Summary:
The paper proposes Q-learning Penalized Transformer (QPT) for safe offline reinforcement learning, addressing the joint challenges of behavior regularization, reward maximization, and constraint satisfaction. QPT is a conditional sequence model that predicts actions conditioned on history, return-to-go, and cost-to-go (Section 3.2), and integrates double Q-learning for reward and cost with n-step targets; the policy objective adds a reward-Q bonus and a cost-Q penalty normalized across datasets (Eqs. 6–10; Eq. 8 in Section 3.3). To cope with infeasible target pairs and improve stitching, it augments data by relabeling to the safest high-reward trajectories (Eqs. 11–12; Algorithm 2) and uses an ensemble inference that samples multiple RTG/CTG pairs and selects actions via the learned Q-networks (Eqs. 13–14; Algorithm 1; Section 3.4). Theoretically, Theorem 3.1 shows that, under return/cost coverage and near-determinism, the penalized objective aligns the learned policy with near-optimal reward while bounding costs. Empirically, across 38 DSRL tasks spanning Safety-Gymnasium, Bullet-Safety-Gym, and MetaDrive, QPT consistently attains safe behavior with strong rewards and outperforms state-of-the-art baselines (Table 1), with ablations confirming the roles of each component and hyperparameters (Table 2, Figure 1). QPT further enables zero-shot adaptation to different cost thresholds through conditioning, surpassing CDT in safe regimes (Figure 2).

Strengths:
1. Clear, controllable objective that unifies the trilogy. The policy loss in Eq. 8 (Section 3.3) cleanly composes behavior regularization (DT MSE) with a reward-Q bonus and a cost-Q penalty, with dataset-scale–aware normalization (Eqs. 9–10). This explicit formulation makes the reward–safety trade-off tunable and portable across datasets—an advantage over Lagrangian schemes discussed in Section 3.1.

2. Principled value-learning backend tailored to sequence models. The reward and cost Q-functions are trained with double Q-learning and n-step targets (Eqs. 6–7), matching the K-step context of the conditional Transformer (Section 3.2). This closes the “stitching” gap of pure sequence modeling by injecting evaluative signals that prefer high-return/low-cost actions during learning.

3. Practical solution to infeasible target pairs without discarding data. The data augmentation that relabels to the “safest max-reward” trajectory for a target (ρ, κ) (Eqs. 11–12; Algorithm 2; Appendix C.2) is a targeted way to retain high-reward information while enforcing safety priorities, addressing the safe/unsafe data mixture problem noted in Section 3.1.

4. Efficient, parallelizable ensemble inference. The multi-pair RTG/CTG sampling with Q-guided selection (Eqs. 13–14; Section 3.4; Algorithm 1) removes manual target tuning typical of CSM methods, is GPU-parallelizable, and demonstrably helps (Table 2, Exp 5–8; Table 5).

5. Zero-shot adaptation across constraint thresholds with empirical validation. The method adapts to varying cost thresholds at deployment via conditioning (Section 3.4), with clear evidence that QPT maintains or improves safety while raising reward when feasible and outperforming CDT in safe regimes (Figure 2).

6. Theoretical alignment beyond standard CSM guarantees. Theorem 3.1 (Section 3.5; Appendix B) extends alignment-style results to the reward–cost setting, showing near-optimal reward and bounded cost under coverage and near-determinism, with improvement terms (±Hσ) over the DT-style baseline (Remark B.5).

7. Strong, broad empirical evidence with safety-first evaluation. Results span 38 tasks across three suites with consistent protocols (Section 4), and QPT is the only approach that stays safe across all tasks while achieving competitive or best returns (Table 1). This breadth and the safety emphasis (Equations 15–16; fixed κ = 10) substantiate the central claims.

8. Component-wise causality of gains. The ablations isolate contributions of reward-Q, cost-Q, data augmentation, and ensemble (Table 2), and the η1/η2 sweeps (Figure 1) expose interpretable reward–cost trade-offs, indicating the method’s knobs map meaningfully to behavior.

9. Robustness to dataset/value-scale differences. The normalization of Q penalties (Eqs. 9–10) is a simple but impactful design choice that stabilizes training across diverse tasks (Section 3.3), aiding reproducibility and deployment on heterogeneous datasets.

10. Reproducibility and clarity of pipeline. The paper provides full training and inference pseudocode (Algorithm 1), task coverage summaries (Table 3; Section D.1), hyperparameters (Table 4), and ensemble-size sensitivity (Table 5), making the approach straightforward to implement and tune.

11. Addresses key limitations of offline Lagrangian methods. By decoupling training from a fixed κ and supporting post-hoc constraint selection (Section 3.1), QPT removes the need to retrain for every new threshold—important for real-world deployment settings with variable safety budgets.

12. Sound architectural match to the problem. Using a conditional Transformer with return-to-go and cost-to-go tokens (Section 3.2) leverages behavioral regularization from sequence modeling while the Q-penalization resolves the optimization conflict between safety and utility, yielding the consistent safe-high-reward behavior seen in Table 1.

Weaknesses:
1. Theoretical support hinges on restrictive and partly exogenous assumptions.
- Evidence: Theorem 3.1 assumes binary rewards/costs, near-deterministic dynamics, and time-consistent conditioning functions (Section 3.5; Assumptions 1–3). It further requires action-selection probability improvements σr, σc that are postulated, not derived from Eq. 8 (Remark B.4).
- Why it matters: Binary signals and near-determinism seldom hold in the evaluated domains; σr/σc are not controlled by the algorithm, so the bounds do not certify the behavior of QPT in the settings it is tested on.
- Actionable: (a) Generalize the analysis to bounded real-valued rewards/costs and stochastic transitions; even a high-level finite-sample error bound relating performance to Q-function estimation error and the penalty weights (η1, η2 in Eqs. 9–10) would make the result informative for practice. (b) Replace the σr/σc assumptions with quantities tied to Eq. 8, e.g., lower bounds on the advantage under Qr and upper bounds on Qc error, to show when the penalization provably changes selection probabilities. (c) Empirically stress-test the assumptions by injecting controlled transition stochasticity and non-binary costs and reporting degradation relative to the bound’s predictions.

2. Safety is not guaranteed under function approximation and Q-bias, yet the method enforces constraints via learned Qc only at training and inference.
- Evidence: Constraint handling is via a cost-Q penalty in the policy loss (Eq. 8) and a hard Qc filter at inference (Eqs. 13–14; Section 3.4); no robustness mechanism or uncertainty calibration is used.
- Why it matters: Offline Q-learning is known to be biased outside the dataset support; violating safety in deployment due to optimistic Qc is a central risk in safe offline RL.
- Actionable: (a) Calibrate the cost filter by using ensembles or quantiles of Qc (you already train double Q; extend to an uncertainty-aware selection) and report safety–reward curves. (b) Add reliability diagnostics for Qc: constraint satisfaction vs. predicted Qc thresholds (reliability plots) and violation rates at high-confidence settings. (c) Include ablations where you deliberately perturb the dataset support to test robustness of constraint satisfaction.

3. Data augmentation could distort target conditioning and Pareto structure and is evaluated too narrowly.
- Evidence: The augmentation relabels RTG/CTG by shifting the returns of the “safest max-reward” trajectory τ* for a target (ρ, κ) (Eqs. 11–12; Algorithm 2; Appendix C.2). Component benefits are shown on only two tasks (Table 2).
- Why it matters: Element-wise relabeling changes conditioning tokens without changing the state–action sequence, which may create infeasible conditioning distributions; the RF(κ, D) reliance presumes good safe coverage near each κ; and computational cost of repeatedly finding τ* is unclear.
- Actionable: (a) Expand ablations to the full benchmark (or a representative subset per suite) to quantify when augmentation helps/hurts. (b) Report computational overhead of building augmented sets and sensitivity to the number N in Algorithm 2. (c) Validate that augmentation does not degrade support alignment: show density-ratio or nearest-neighbor distances between augmented and original conditioning distributions, and a sweep over augmentation strength (fraction of augmented samples).

4. Ensemble inference fairness, scalability, and sensitivity are under-characterized.
- Evidence: Inference samples many RTG/CTG pairs and selects actions via Qr/Qc (Section 3.4; Eqs. 13–14). Sensitivity to ensemble size is reported only for MetaDrive-harddense (Table 5). Baselines like CDT rely on manual target selection, whereas QPT benefits from parallel candidate sampling and Q-guided selection.
- Why it matters: Gains may partly stem from extra search compute at inference; fairness and deployability depend on compute budgets and latency.
- Actionable: (a) Report wall-clock training and inference latency and FLOPs for QPT versus baselines at the settings used in Table 1, including candidate counts. (b) Provide ensemble-size sweeps on several tasks per benchmark (not just one) to establish robustness. (c) For fairness, give CDT a comparable target-pair ensemble (without Q selection, use evaluation rollouts or a simple heuristic) and report results under matched inference budgets.

5. Novelty over closely related Q-regularized sequence models is incremental and could be clarified with stronger baselines.
- Evidence: The main training objective adds a reward-Q bonus and a cost-Q penalty to DT (Eq. 8), building on Q-value regularization for Transformers (Hu et al., 2024a) and cost conditioning in CDT (Liu et al., 2023b). The new ingredients are the explicit cost-Q term and the specific augmentation/ensemble pipeline (Sections 3.3–3.4).
- Why it matters: To establish distinct contribution, comparisons should isolate what QPT adds beyond prior Q-regularized DTs and beyond CDT.
- Actionable: (a) Include a “QDT+cost-conditioning” baseline (reward-Q regularization as in Hu et al., 2024a plus cost-to-go token, but without your augmentation/ensemble) to quantify the net gain of your additions. (b) Add a Lagrangian-DT baseline (reward–λ·cost penalty in the loss with learned λ) to show why your two-Q formulation outperforms standard constrained training for CSM.

6. Empirical claims would be stronger with broader statistical reporting and protocol transparency for baselines.
- Evidence: Table 1 reports means over 3 seeds and 20 episodes but no variances/confidence intervals; Table 2 contains corrupted entries, and the setup for target conditioning in CDT is not fully specified beyond a qualitative remark (Section 4; Section 3.4).
- Why it matters: Safety conclusions rely on small seed counts and may be sensitive to target-conditioning choices in sequence models.

Summary:
The paper introduces ActiveCQ, a unified Bayesian framework for actively estimating a broad class of causal quantities (ATE, CATE, ATT, and ATE under distribution shift) from observational data. It reframes these quantities as integrals of an outcome regression function and models the regression with a Gaussian Process, pairing it with two alternatives for the distribution component: a conditional density estimator and, more centrally, conditional mean embeddings (CMEs) in an RKHS. The CME-based formulation yields closed-form GP posteriors for the target causal quantity, avoids explicit density estimation, and stays aligned with the GP’s feature space (Sec. 4.2–4.3; Prop. 1). Building on this posterior, the authors derive CQ-specific acquisition rules that directly reduce uncertainty of the estimator, instantiating information gain and total variance reduction with batch (greedy) selection (Sec. 4.5; Alg. 1). They provide convergence guarantees showing uncertainty decay rates under submodularity assumptions (Theorem 2; Sec. 4.6; App. E). Extensive simulations and semi-synthetic studies (IHDP, LaLonde) demonstrate consistent sample-efficiency gains over baselines across multiple CQs, especially under distribution shift (Fig. 2–5; App. F.6). The framework is modular and compatible with scalable GP approximations and alternative kernels (Remark 2; App. F.2, F.6.2).

Strengths:
1. Clear, general problem formulation that goes beyond CATE. The paper crisply defines Active Estimation of Causal Quantities (ActiveCQ) and unifies ATE, CATE, ATT, and ATEDS via an integral representation (Lemma 1; Remark 1; Sec. 3). Including ATEDS (distribution shift) in the active estimation scope is particularly valuable for practice.

2. Technically elegant CME–GP unification yielding analytic posteriors for CQs. The use of Conditional Mean Embeddings with a GP regression gives closed-form mean/covariance of the CQ posterior (Proposition 1; Eq. 6), avoiding explicit conditional density estimation and Monte Carlo over s (Sec. 4.3). Operating in the same RKHS as the GP and updating the CME features after each round is a well-motivated, task-aligned design.

3. CQ-aware acquisition rules that target the estimator’s uncertainty directly. The IG and TVR criteria are instantiated for the CQ posterior (Eqs. 8–9; Sec. 4.5), with batch selection via a greedy scheme that promotes diversity (Eq. 10). The paper clearly explains their geometric differences through eigenvalue views (App. D.5, A- vs D-optimality), which is rare and insightful.

4. Theoretical uncertainty-decay guarantee tailored to the transductive, integral-estimation setting. Theorem 2 bounds the estimator variance by irreducible uncertainty plus a term scaling with γnB/√nB (Sec. 4.6), supported by a careful construction (Def. 2, Def. 5) and submodularity justification (App. E.1). Extending TAL-style analysis to distributional integrals is a meaningful theoretical contribution.

5. Strong empirical support across diverse CQs and settings. The method consistently improves sample efficiency in simulations and semi-synthetic data, most prominently under shift (DS) where gains are substantial (Fig. 2, DS panel; Fig. 5; Tables 1–2; App. F.6). Visualizations show that acquisitions align with the target distribution (Fig. 3), directly evidencing the intended behavior.

6. Thorough robustness and practicality analysis. The paper examines batch sizes, warm starts, pool sizes, kernels, and heteroscedasticity (Fig. 12–16; Fig. 11; App. F.6.2), and provides a running-time and complexity breakdown contrasting IG vs TVR (Fig. 4; App. F.5). This level of scrutiny is unusual and increases confidence in practical deployment.

7. Modular framework that clarifies where the gains come from. By providing both CDE/MDN and CME instantiations under a shared GP regressor, the paper isolates the value of the CME approach (Sec. 4.2–4.3; App. F.2–F.3). The analysis in App. G.2 convincingly argues why CME’s feature-aligned embeddings are advantageous in the active loop.

8. Careful derivations for multiple CQs and integral estimators. The appendices give step-by-step expansions for CATE, ATE, ATT, and ATEDS (App. D.1–D.4), all cast as standard GP predictions at “effective” inputs (feature tensors with mean/conditional embeddings). This unification improves clarity and reproducibility.

9. Precise positioning relative to neighboring fields. The distinctions from active causal discovery/ABCI and from transductive AL are carefully laid out (Sec. 6; App. B.2–B.3), making clear both the methodological and problem-setting differences and why previous methods are not baselines in this scenario.

10. Evaluation design that matches the learning objective. The paper explicitly defines the target set (Sec. 4.4) and justifies AMSE as the central metric rather than internal uncertainty (App. F.4.1), ensuring alignment between acquisition, estimation, and evaluation.

11. Reproducibility and implementation transparency. Detailed dataset generation, benchmarks, hyperparameters, and training protocols (App. F.1–F.3), plus an algorithmic overview (Alg. 1), support reuse and verification.

12. Elegant handling of distribution shift without density estimation. For ATEDS, the target population is incorporated via empirical mean embeddings (App. D.4; Eqs. 37–40), cleanly bridging source-trained regressors to new populations—a practically important and methodologically neat component.

Weaknesses:
1. Theory hinges on strong, partly unverified assumptions; bounds are indirect and potentially loose.
   - The variance decay (Theorem 2; Sec. 4.6; App. E) relies on submodularity (Assumption 1). App. E.1 explicitly notes that for CATE and ATT “the assumption may not strictly hold,” and the proof appeals to weak submodularity via an Information Ratio.    - Actionable: (i) Empirically verify (approximate) submodularity/diminishing-returns for IG/TVR on your settings; (ii) quantify constants (or provide kernel-dependent rates) for common kernels; (iii) tighten the analysis by directly bounding the CQ-level information gain (instead of via f), or provide an upper bound linking the two; (iv) add experiments showing empirical variance-vs-budget curves to assess the γnB/√nB trend.

2. Acquisition scalability remains a bottleneck; continuous treatments are curtailed by IG instability.
   - Despite the modularity claim (Remark 2), results and complexity still reflect O(nT^3) GP training and expensive greedy updates (Fig. 4; App. F.5).    - Actionable: (i) Implement sparse/inducing-point or SKI GPs and lazy/stochastic greedy (with incremental Cholesky) to show scalability; (ii) stabilize IG using logdet via Cholesky/LDLT with jitter, pivoted-Cholesky/Lanczos approximations, or Hutch++ trace-log estimators; (iii) approximate IG for continuous a via low-rank Nyström/Random Features on the CQ posterior and subsampled treatment grids; (iv) report wall-clock and accuracy on a larger pool (nP ≫ 10^3).

   - While baselines include µ-BALD, TVR, and QHTE (Sec. 5; App. F.2.3), transductive AL methods that reweight or select pool points to match a target distribution are discussed (App. B.2) but not instantiated.    - The framework assumes positivity (Sec. 2; App. C.1) but in observational pools, parts of (a, z, s) relevant for P∗CQ may have weak support. The current utilities can still prioritize such regions, but labeling cannot fix structural gaps, leading to extrapolation risk.

   - Prop. 1 requires features ϕ(a), ϕ(z), ϕ(s) to “be updated after each batch” to match the GP’s product kernel (Sec. 4.3), yet the CME bandwidth is median-heuristic with a learnable λ (App. F.2.2). Kernel misalignment can bias the effective kernel k̄ and CQ posterior.
   - Actionable: Jointly learn CME and GP kernels by maximizing a CQ-marginal-likelihood (induced by Eqs. 6, 30–35), or employ deep kernels shared by both GP and CME; add ablations where GP–CME kernels are intentionally misaligned to demonstrate sensitivity/resilience.

   - Batch selection uses greedy maximization of U(Xb) (Eq. 10), which triggers repeated posterior updates and high cost, and diversity is only implicitly enforced by the marginal-gain structure (Sec. 4.5; Fig. 4; App. F.5).

Summary:
The paper identifies a previously overlooked failure mode in attention-based MIL for whole-slide imaging—unstable attention dynamics—and quantifies it via epoch-to-epoch Jensen–Shannon divergence (Figure 1, Section 3.3). To address this, it proposes ASMIL, a unified framework that (i) stabilizes attention with an EMA-updated anchor model and aligns the online attention to the anchor via a KL loss (Section 4.1, Eq. 7), (ii) mitigates over-concentration by replacing softmax with a normalized sigmoid function (NSF) in the anchor, theoretically showing NSF’s selective flattening advantage (Theorem 1, Eq. 5), and (iii) reduces overfitting through token random dropping over trainable FEAT tokens (Section 4.3). The overall objective couples cross-entropy with attention stabilization (Eq. 9), and the anchor is discarded at inference (Figure 2). Empirically, ASMIL achieves state-of-the-art or competitive performance on CAMELYON-16/17 and BRACS, with F1 improvements up to 6.49% over prior methods (Table 1), and its anchor+NSF plug-in consistently boosts existing MIL models with gains up to 10.73% F1 (Table 2). It also improves tumor localization (higher FROC and Dice; Table 13), generalizes to survival prediction and non-WSI MIL benchmarks (Tables 16 and 18), and adds minimal training overhead while keeping inference cost unchanged (Appendix M, Table 15). Ablations confirm each component’s contribution (Table 3) and show robustness to key hyperparameters (Appendix K).

Strengths:
1. Novel problem identification and quantification. The paper isolates “unstable attention dynamics” in attention-based MIL and makes it measurable via epoch-to-epoch JSD (Eq. 3), with compelling visual and quantitative evidence (Figure 1; Appendix P across methods/datasets). This is a concrete and substantively new failure mode in WSI MIL beyond overfitting/over-concentration.

2. Principled stabilization mechanism tailored to attention. The EMA “anchor model” with KL alignment directly regularizes attention distributions rather than downstream features (Section 4.1; Eq. 4, 7). The paper justifies why scalar regularizers are insufficient (Remark 1) and why matching softmax bag features cannot stabilize attention due to non-injectivity under affine dependence (Appendix I; Table 8).

3. Theoretical contribution with actionable design. Theorem 1 (Section 4.2; Appendix E) proves the “selective flattening” property of the normalized sigmoid (NSF) and the impossibility for a single-temperature softmax to simultaneously achieve equalization among high tokens and suppression of low tokens. This provides a crisp mathematical rationale for the NSF-in-anchor design.

4. Careful architectural placement to avoid gradient issues. The decision to use NSF only in the anchor (not online) is validated empirically: applying NSF online degrades performance (Table 6) and a trainable softmax–NSF mixture converges to softmax (Table 7), supporting the paper’s gradient analysis (Eq. 8) and design choice.

5. Strong, consistent empirical gains with broad coverage. ASMIL achieves SOTA or competitive results on three WSI benchmarks (Table 1), including +6.49% F1 on CAMELYON-17, and yields better localization (FROC/Dice; Table 13; Figure 4). The anchor+NSF plug-in improves diverse MIL backbones with up to +10.73% F1 (Table 2), showing method generality.

6. External validity beyond subtyping. The framework extends to survival prediction (discrete-time incidence formulation) with top mean C-index across five TCGA cohorts (Table 16), and to classic non-WSI MIL datasets with best or tied-best accuracy on 4/5 tasks (Table 18). It also improves atop WSI foundation-model features (UNI, PATHGEN-CLIP; Table 9).

7. Stability and representation evidence beyond metrics. The paper links stabilized attention to cleaner bag-level clusters via t-SNE (Appendix C; Figures 5–6), and shows reduced JSD/CE oscillations throughout training (Figure 1), substantiating the intended mechanism.

8. Thorough alternatives analysis. The paper systematically contrasts NSF with temperature-scaled softmax (Figure 7–8; Table 4) and with entmax, showing lower accuracy and notably higher compute for entmax (Table 5). It also discusses (and discards) per-slide temporal ensembling due to memory and target limitations (Appendix H).

9. Regularization tailored to the architecture. Token random dropping operates on trainable FEAT tokens, preserving the one-to-one correspondence required by anchor alignment (Section 4.3). The paper pinpoints effective regimes (peak around B≈0.5; Appendix K.4, Figure 11) and demonstrates mitigation of overfitting over epochs (Appendix K.5, Figure 12).

10. Robust ablations and sensitivity analyses. Component-wise ablation isolates contributions (Table 3); hyperparameter robustness (β plateau in [0.5, 1.5], Appendix K.1; FEAT-token counts, Table 10), and design sensitivities (anchor update frequency; batch-wise superior in Table 11) are all documented. Statistical significance is established (Table 12).

11. Efficiency and deployability. The anchor is “discarded at inference” (Section 4.1), so deployment cost is unchanged. Training overhead is modest across backbones (Appendix M; Table 15), while ASMIL’s inference compute/latency/memory are competitive or better than strong baselines (Table 14).

12. Reproducibility and fair comparisons. The paper fixes feature extractors across methods (Appendix B.1), uses macro-F1/AUC for class imbalance (Appendix D), reports splits/protocols clearly (Appendix B.3), and releases code/checkpoints. This strengthens credibility and reuse.

Collectively, the work combines a clearly framed new problem, a theoretically grounded and practically effective solution (anchor+NSF), and comprehensive validation across tasks, models, and datasets, with attention to design alternatives, statistical significance, and compute trade-offs.

Weaknesses:
1. Causal link between stability and performance/interpretability is suggestive but not established. While JSD reductions correlate with smoother training (Figure 1; Appendix P) and the anchor improves F1/AUC (Table 3), the paper does not quantify how much accuracy/localization improves as a direct function of stability. Actionable: (i) report across-seed correlations between late-epoch stability metrics (e.g., mean/variance of JSD over last K epochs) and test F1/AUC; (ii) perform controlled interventions that change stability without changing capacity (e.g., vary β in Eq. 9 and EMA m in Eq. 4 across a grid) and plot accuracy vs. stability; (iii) add an “Attention Stability Index” (e.g., moving-window JSD or variance) and show predictive power for generalization and localization.

2. Theory focuses on NSF vs softmax temperature but not on the anchoring/stability mechanism itself. Theorem 1 (Section 4.2; Appendix E) gives a clean advantage of NSF, yet there is no analysis of why EMA anchoring plus KL (Eq. 7–9) should reduce oscillations (e.g., bounds on JSD(αt, αt+1) or contraction properties under Eq. 8). Actionable: formalize how EMA momentum m and β control drift of α across epochs (e.g., show exponential smoothing of attention fixed points or a stability region), or at least provide empirical phase diagrams over (m, β) demonstrating monotone effects on JSD with confidence intervals.

3. Competing normalizations are under-tested and partially scoped. Entmax is evaluated on a single dataset (Table 5), and softmax temperature is tested on BRACS (Table 4; Figure 7–8). It remains unclear if NSF’s advantage persists broadly. Actionable: (i) repeat entmax/temperature comparisons on CAMELYON-17 and BRACS with statistical tests; (ii) include additional baselines such as logit clipping or top-k/sparse attention and report top-k mass, entropy, and Gini of attention to substantiate “selective flattening” beyond visuals (Figure 3).

4. Attention matching is done over FEAT tokens, not tiles; stabilization of tile-level attention is assumed. Section 4.1/5.3 aggregate per-tile attention from FEAT-to-tile edges, but the KL (Eq. 7) constrains FEAT-token distributions. Actionable: (i) directly measure JSD of tile-level attention before/after ASMIL on the same slides (as in Figure 1) and report reductions; (ii) consider a multi-level objective that also aligns projected tile distributions from the anchor to ensure the claimed interpretability gains propagate to tiles (Appendix L).

5. Plug-in improvements lack significance testing and calibration. Table 2 shows consistent gains, but only ASMIL vs. w/o-anchor is tested for significance (Table 12). Actionable: report paired significance tests (e.g., DeLong/permutation) for +Anchor and +Anchor+NSF across all baselines and datasets in Table 2, and provide per-method calibration (reliability diagrams) to rule out thresholding artifacts, since F1 uses a fixed 0.5 threshold (Appendix D.1).

6. Random dropping is compared only to “no drop,” not to state-of-the-art MIL regularizers. Section 4.3 argues MIL-dropout is not easily integrated due to one-to-one correspondence needs, but this remains unverified experimentally. Actionable: (i) implement and compare against MIL-Dropout/TopK dropping (Zhu et al., 2025) by aligning anchor over the subset of retained FEAT tokens, or by computing KL on the intersection subset; (ii) compare against bag-splitting (Zhang et al., 2022) and entropy-based flattening (Zhang et al., 2025b) under the same backbone to isolate the value of the proposed drop.

7. Localization evaluation could more directly validate interpretability claims. CAMELYON-16 FROC/Dice/specificity (Table 13) are helpful, but the claim that stability improves interpretability (Section 1; Figure 1 bottom) would benefit from per-slide consistency metrics. Actionable: (i) compute per-slide overlap between attention maps across late epochs (IoU/DSC) and relate to Dice/FROC; (ii) report small-lesion sensitivity stratified by lesion size bins, given the known failure on tiny foci (Appendix Q; Figure 26).

8. Handling tiny foci remains a documented limitation (Appendix Q). NSF’s flattening can downweight small lesions in presence of large ones. Actionable: (i) add a small-lesion-aware auxiliary loss (e.g., top-k tail boosting, size-aware curriculum, or class-balanced focal reweighting over tiles); (ii) adopt multi-threshold ensembling for localization maps or a dual-branch scheme where one anchor is tuned for high sensitivity (smaller τ-like effect) and another for specificity, with consistency regularization between branches.

9. Scope of datasets for subtyping is relatively narrow for pathology heterogeneity. The paper uses CAMELYON-16/17 and BRACS (Sections 5.1–5.3); although survival and non-WSI results broaden scope (Tables 16, 18), subtyping conclusions would be stronger with additional disease sites or multi-class organ datasets. Actionable: include at least one more heterogeneous multi-class WSI cohort and report both subtyping and localization to assess robustness to staining/site shifts beyond CAMELYON-17’s OOD split (Appendix B.3).

10. Compute–accuracy trade-offs are not fully characterized as capacity/scales change. While inference cost is reported (Table 14–15) and FEAT-token counts are ablated (Table 10), there is no scaling curve of accuracy and stability vs. FEAT-token budget and bag size. Actionable: provide scaling plots of (accuracy, JSD, time/memory) vs. N FEAT and mean tiles-per-bag to guide practitioners, and add a momentum schedule study for m (Appendix K mentions it but does not show results in the main text).

11. Alternative stabilizers are not empirically compared. Appendix H discusses per-slide temporal ensembling as memory-heavy, but there is no empirical baseline showing its performance/stability relative to the anchor. Actionable: implement the per-slide EMA target (Eq. 36) on a subset (e.g., CAMELYON-16 with compressed attention) to quantify the claimed drawbacks (memory/speed) and performance gap.

12. Presentation/formatting frictions in key results tables. Table 1–2 have misalignments/overflows (e.g., broken columns/rows), which make it hard to audit improvements and may obscure edge cases (e.g., DSMIL slight drop). Actionable: fix table layouts, include confidence intervals, and highlight statistically significant improvements.

These additions would more rigorously connect stability to downstream gains, strengthen the case for NSF and the anchor beyond alternatives, and address documented failure modes (tiny foci) and robustness across datasets—moving the work closer to its goals of stable, generalizable, and interpretable WSI MIL.

Suggestions/Questions:
1. Quantify stability–performance linkage
   - Section 3.3 defines JSD (Eq. 3) and Figure 1/Appendix P show reduced oscillations, but the causal link to F1/AUC is not quantified. Please report across-seed correlations between late-epoch stability metrics (e.g., mean/variance of JSD over last K epochs) and test F1/AUC, and a sweep over β (Eq. 9) and momentum m (Eq. 4) showing accuracy vs. stability curves. A concise “Attention Stability Index” and its predictive value for F1/AUC would clarify mechanism.

2. Why anchoring reduces oscillations
   - You provide the gradient form ∂KL(αnsf∥α)/∂zi = αi − αnsf,i (Eq. 8), but no analysis of how EMA anchoring changes the drift of αt across epochs. Can you add a stability argument (even under simplifying assumptions) or a controlled experiment demonstrating monotone JSD reduction as a function of (m, β)? A small phase diagram of mean JSD vs. (m, β) would help.

3. Tile-level stability vs FEAT-token matching
   - The KL loss aligns FEAT-token attention distributions (Figure 2; Section 4.1–4.2), while localization aggregates FEAT→tile attentions (Section 5.3; Appendix L). Please quantify improvements in tile-level stability directly (JSD of per-tile distributions across epochs, as in Figure 1), and clarify whether any additional projection/alignment to tile space was used. If not, could you add a lightweight auxiliary tile-level alignment and report the delta?

4. NSF vs alternatives beyond a single dataset
   - Theorem 1 (Section 4.2; Appendix E) motivates NSF; empirical comparisons show temperature-scaled softmax on BRACS (Table 4; Figure 7–8) and entmax on CAMELYON-16 (Table 5). To strengthen generality, could you repeat these comparisons on CAMELYON-17 and BRACS for entmax and on CAMELYON-16/17 for temperature scaling, with statistical tests? Also report attention concentration metrics (entropy, top-k mass, Gini/HHI) to substantiate “selective flattening” (Figure 3).

5. Significance and calibration for plug-in gains
   - Table 2 shows consistent improvements when adding Anchor/Anchor+NSF to baselines. Please add paired significance tests (DeLong/permutation) per method/dataset, and provide calibration plots (reliability curves) or PR-AUC. Since macro-F1 uses a fixed 0.5 threshold (Appendix D.1), also report macro-F1 at a validation-tuned threshold to rule out thresholding artifacts.

6. Random drop vs state-of-the-art MIL regularizers
   - Section 4.3 argues MIL-Dropout/top-K dropping (Zhu et al., 2025) is hard to integrate due to one-to-one correspondence. Could you provide an empirical comparison by computing KL on the intersection of retained FEAT tokens (or aligning only over kept indices) and compare against: (i) MIL-Dropout/TopK, (ii) bag splitting (Zhang et al., 2022), and (iii) entropy regularization (Zhang et al., 2025b), holding the rest fixed?

7. Tiny foci sensitivity and interpretability
   - Appendix Q/Figure 26 document misses on tiny lesions; Table 19 counts slides without missed regions but not size-stratified sensitivity. Please report FROC/Dice or sensitivity broken down by lesion size bins, and the consistency of attention maps across late epochs (IoU/DSC of attention masks over epochs), to connect stability to interpretability more directly.

8. Anchor momentum schedule and update frequency
   - Table 11 shows batch-wise anchor updates outperform epoch-wise. Could you also provide an ablation over EMA momentum m (mentioned in Section 4.4 and Appendix K) with both accuracy and mean JSD, and discuss any best-practice schedule (e.g., warm-up, cosine)?

9. Per-slide temporal ensembling baseline
   - Appendix H argues against per-slide EMA targets (Eq. 36) on memory grounds. A compact experiment on CAMELYON-16 with compressed/low-precision per-slide attention would quantify overhead and performance/stability vs. your anchor. Even a small subset would make the comparison concrete.

10. Scaling guidance for FEAT tokens and bag size
   - Table 10 ablates #FEAT tokens, but practitioners also need guidance vs. tiles-per-bag. Can you provide scaling plots of F1/AUC and stability (mean JSD) vs. NFEAT and average bag size, with corresponding training/inference time/memory (extending Tables 14–15), to show the accuracy–compute frontier?

11. Theorem-to-practice bridge
   - Theorem 1 assumes z ∈ S(τ, γ, H, L). Could you estimate empirical τ and γ from score histograms (Figure 8a) and report how often slides approximately satisfy these conditions? A brief empirical check that NSF approximately equalizes top tokens and suppresses lows as in Eq. (6) would ground the theory.

12. Clarify implementation details of αnsf and attention layers
   - Figure 2 shows multi-head attention blocks. Which layer’s attention scores z feed αsmx/αnsf? Is α computed over heads (averaged) or a specific head? Are anchor and online attention modules truly architecturally identical except for normalization? These details affect reproducibility and the applicability of the plug-in in Table 2.

13. Localization pipeline specifics
   - Section 5.3/Appendix L: please provide the exact formula used to obtain per-tile scores from FEAT-token attentions (e.g., mean over tokens/heads), any smoothing/morphological steps, and thresholding sensitivity analyses (FROC/Dice vs. threshold). This will help interpret Figure 4 and Table 13.

14. Early stopping and overfitting
   - Appendix K.5 (Figure 12) shows random drop mitigates late-epoch degradation. For completeness, could you compare baselines with early stopping on validation AUC/F1 to ensure the observed gains are not primarily due to training longer without overfitting?

15. Broader dataset coverage for subtyping
   - Sections 5.1–5.3 focus on CAMELYON-16/17 and BRACS; Appendix J adds foundation-model features. If feasible in rebuttal, adding one additional multi-class WSI subtyping dataset (even smaller-scale) would strengthen claims of robustness to staining/site shifts beyond CAMELYON-17’s OOD split (Appendix B.3).

16. Reproducibility artifacts
   - The Reproducibility Statement notes an anonymized repository. For review, please ensure it includes: (i) scripts to compute and plot JSD (Eq. 3) and attention stability diagnostics, (ii) exact seeds/configs for Tables 1–3, 12–15, (iii) code to reproduce Theorem 1 comparisons (Tables 4–5, Figures 7–8), and (iv) a minimal example showing how to wrap an existing MIL method with your Anchor+NSF plug-in (Table 2).

Soundness: 4

Presentation: 3

Contribution: 4

Overall: 8

Confidence: 4

Conduct: NO

Ethics: No ethics review needed.

Summary:
This paper introduces World2Minecraft, a reality-to-simulation pipeline that reconstructs real indoor scenes as editable Minecraft environments by leveraging 3D semantic occupancy prediction and multi-view fusion (Sec. 3.2; Fig. 1; Alg. 1, Eqs. 1–5). The system post-processes fused occupancy with density-based clustering and retrieval-based template matching to generate executable Minecraft building commands, and provides an interactive refinement tool, SceneForge, for light manual correction (App. J). To enable downstream research, the authors build MinecraftVLN, a VLN dataset with Next-View and Next-Action tasks derived from reconstructed and community scenes (3,801 items total; Table 9; Fig. 2), and demonstrate fine-tuning of Qwen2.5-VL and real-time control with Gemini-2.5-Pro (Sec. 4.3; Fig. 5). To address the data bottleneck in occupancy prediction, they propose an automated, low-cost data generation pipeline and release MinecraftOcc, a large-scale semantic occupancy dataset (100,165 images, 156 scenes, 1,452 classes; Sec. 3.4; Table 1; Fig. 3). Experiments show that state-of-the-art occupancy models underperform on MinecraftOcc, while mixed training with NYUv2 improves generalization (Tables 4–5). The paper further evidences practical advantages over layout-based generation for functional reconstruction and reports significant efficiency gains from refinement vs. building from scratch (Tables 6–7).

Strengths:
1. Occupancy-to-voxel alignment enables editable, physically grounded reconstructions. The paper exploits the structural match between 3D semantic occupancy and Minecraft’s voxel world, bypassing mesh-to-block conversion and yielding scenes that are immediately editable and actionable for embodied tasks (Sec. 3.2; Fig. 1; Alg. 1; Eqs. 1–5). The density-based center extraction, DBSCAN instance consolidation, and rotation-aware template retrieval (Eq. 5) are a well-engineered combination that improves geometric fidelity beyond a naïve voxel→block mapping.

2. A truly low-cost, automated labeling pipeline with deterministic semantics. MinecraftOcc labels are obtained by querying the map function M_world that “maps any coordinate v to a semantic label s” (Sec. 3.4; Eqs. 8–9), eliminating manual annotation and sensor artifacts. The viewpoint-aware volume construction f(Pplayer, θ, w, h, d) and fallback strategy (Eqs. 6–7; Fig. 3) plus camera-model-based culling (App. E; Eq. 16) are concrete technical choices that raise label precision.

3. High-quality, large-scale dataset with clear, quantitative evidence. MinecraftOcc delivers 100,165 images, 156 scenes, and 1,452 classes at 1920×1129 (Table 1) and outperforms NYUv2/OccScanNet on NIQE/PIQE/LV (Table 3: NIQE 9.97 vs. 14.96/17.63; LV 274,305 vs. 57,369/10,352), supporting its visual realism and utility for perception.

4. A challenging benchmark that exposes generalization limits of SOTA occupancy models. Multiple methods experience substantial mIoU drops on MinecraftOcc across data scales (Table 4), demonstrating the dataset’s novelty and difficulty. This is not merely bigger data; it shifts distributions enough to invalidate overfitting to NYUv2-style scans.

5. Demonstrated complementarity to real-world datasets. Mixed training on MinecraftOcc (8k) + NYUv2 with Symphonies improves NYUv2 performance (Table 5: IoU +0.43, mIoU +0.21), providing concrete evidence that the synthetic data adds useful bias/variance trade-offs rather than just domain drift.

6. End-to-end downstream validation for VLN, not only perception. The paper builds MinecraftVLN with two tasks tied to reconstructed scenes (Fig. 2; Table 9) and shows consistent gains from SFT/RFT over no-train on both Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B (Table 2), plus a live control demo with Gemini-2.5-Pro (Fig. 5). This closes the loop from reconstruction to embodied behavior.

7. Strong functional advantages over layout-based scene generation. Against LayoutGPT/I-Design/LayoutVLM, the proposed pipeline achieves markedly lower OOB and collisions and higher semantic integrity and visual realism (Table 6), supporting the claim that occupancy-driven reconstruction better preserves geometry critical for navigation and interaction.

8. Practical workflow efficiency with quantification. Manual touch-ups after automated reconstruction are far cheaper than building from scratch: 7.5× faster and 13.9× fewer operations (Table 7), with a breakdown of typical fixes (hole filling, noise deletion, orientation tweaks). This makes the approach feasible at scale.

9. Reproducible, well-specified camera modeling and fusion details. Intrinsics/extrinsics derivations (App. D; Eqs. 10–15) and visibility culling (App. E; Eq. 16) remove ambiguity in data generation and fusion. Algorithm 1 concretely specifies the full reconstruction pipeline, increasing reproducibility.

10. Tooling that supports inspection and refinement. The SceneForge web tool (App. J) provides category-aware, interactive 3D visualization and editing of occupancy/centers, which is rare in this line of work and directly useful for dataset curation and error analysis.

11. Thoughtful use of the Minecraft mod ecosystem to narrow the reality gap. Integrating TMEO’s >1,400 semantically labeled objects and PBR/dynamic lighting (App. B.2–B.3) results in complex, diverse, and visually realistic indoor scenes—substantiated by the statistics (Table 1) and image quality metrics (Table 3)—addressing the “blocky” domain gap that limits prior Minecraft-based embodied research.

12. Clear scoping of contributions beyond a dataset release. The work delivers a coherent triad—pipeline (World2Minecraft), benchmark (MinecraftOcc), and downstream task suite (MinecraftVLN)—with empirical evidence at each stage (Figs. 1–5; Tables 1–7, 9–11), elevating the paper from a single resource to a usable research stack.

Weaknesses:
1. Limited end-to-end automation and selection bias in VLN scenes
- Evidence: “selected 15 scenes for manual refinement” (Sec. 3.3) and “selected 30 scenes for meticulous manual refinement… 15 high-quality scenes were chosen” (Sec. 4.2).
- Why it matters: The core claim is a low-cost, scalable reality-to-Minecraft pipeline (Abstract; Sec. 3.2–3.4), yet VLN evaluation relies on a small, hand-picked, manually cleaned subset, weakening claims of scalability and robustness.
- Actionable: Report quantitative pre-/post-refinement fidelity (e.g., voxel IoU to EmbodiedOcc-ScanNet labels, block placement error) and downstream VLN impact with vs. without manual edits. Scale VLN to all reconstructed validation scenes to reduce selection bias, or provide controlled sampling and confidence intervals.

2. Sparse analysis of negative scaling on MinecraftOcc
- Evidence: In Table 4, most methods degrade as the dataset grows from 8k → 50k → 100k (e.g., Symphonies mIoU 21.56 → 19.61 → 13.08).
- Why it matters: The dataset is positioned as “low-cost, automated, and scalable” (Abstract; Sec. 3.4), but training at larger scales yields worse outcomes without diagnosis.
- Actionable: Add analyses of class/scene imbalance, viewpoint case distribution (axis-aligned vs. diagonal; Sec. 3.4), and training protocol sensitivity (LR, batch size, schedule). Provide learning curves and per-class mIoU vs. data size. Try balanced sampling, curriculum on viewpoint cases, and augmentations matched to PBR lighting.

3. Missing ablations for key reconstruction components and hyperparameters
- Evidence: Density threshold τ and kernel K (Eq. 3), DBSCAN distance η (Eq. 4), template-library L coverage and rotation sampling δ (Eq. 5), fallback offset ε (Eq. 7) are central to quality (Sec. 3.2–3.4) but never ablated.
- Why it matters: These choices likely drive reconstruction fidelity and downstream VLN metrics (Tables 6–7) and may explain manual refinement needs.
- Actionable: Provide ablations and sensitivity plots for τ/K/η/ε and rotation discretization. Compare: (a) no clustering, (b) voxel-to-block direct mapping, (c) retrieval + rotation. Report block-level IoU to occupancy, OOB/collision rates (Table 6 metrics), and VLN accuracy (Table 2) per variant.

4. No quantitative evaluation of template retrieval and library coverage
- Evidence: Shape retrieval via IoU matching to L (Eq. 5) is key to “geometric fidelity” (Sec. 3.2), but there is no metric for retrieval correctness or library recall.
- Why it matters: Mismatched shapes/orientations propagate to navigation geometry (Table 6 metrics) and to the need for manual orientation fixes (Table 7).
- Actionable: Report retrieval top-k IoU distribution, orientation error histograms, and library coverage (fraction of instances with a high-IoU template). Add a baseline without retrieval to quantify benefit.

5. VLN evaluation is small-scale and lacks standard embodied metrics
- Evidence: MinecraftVLN has 3,801 items across tasks/datasets (Table 9), with only 15 reconstructed scenes contributing to Base (Sec. 3.3; 4.2–4.3). Results are reported as Accuracy only (Table 2). The real-time demo (Fig. 5) is anecdotal.
- Why it matters: Without success rate or path-efficiency metrics, it is hard to judge embodied competence and navigability of reconstructed scenes.
- Actionable: Add success rate, SPL/NE, and stop accuracy; report cross-scene generalization (train on one set of scenes, test on unseen scenes). Provide per-scene breakdowns and confidence intervals. Include multiple rollouts and aggregate success for the Gemini-2.5-Pro agent demo.

6. Confounded evaluation in VLN due to mixing community-built and reconstructed scenes
- Evidence: To increase difficulty, Extend uses 5 community-created scenes (Sec. 3.3; Fig. 6; Table 8), then Combined merges Base+Extend (Sec. 4.3).
- Why it matters: Mixing sources blurs whether improvements come from high-fidelity reconstructions or simply from dataset composition. It also weakens claims that the reconstructed environments are immediately useful for VLN.
- Actionable: Report separate training/evaluation where both train and test are strictly on reconstructed scenes; and a transfer setting trained on reconstructed scenes and tested on community scenes (and vice versa) to isolate the contribution of reconstruction.

7. Reconstruction fidelity lacks quantitative validation against ground-truth occupancy
- Evidence: Qualitative examples are shown (Fig. 4), but there is no quantitative comparison (IoU/mIoU) between fused predictions (ˆOscene; Eq. 2) and EmbodiedOcc-ScanNet ground truth, nor between the final block world and the fused occupancy it purports to implement.
- Why it matters: The central promise is faithful, editable reconstruction (Sec. 3.2; Fig. 1), which should be validated numerically.
- Actionable: Evaluate voxel-level IoU of fused occupancy vs. ground truth and block-level agreement after command execution. Report per-class metrics and errors due to fusion/clustering/template steps.

8. Fairness and robustness of layout-based comparison are limited
- Evidence: Inputs for layout methods come from GPT-4o-generated text from images, and three perceptual metrics are GPT-4o scores (Table 6). Methods are designed for text→layout, not image→layout, which may disadvantage them.
- Why it matters: The comparison supports claims that occupancy-based reconstruction better preserves geometry for VLN (Sec. 4.5), but pipeline and scoring choices introduce confounds.
- Actionable: Add human evaluation (blind, multi-rater) for Visual/Complete/Aesthetic with inter-rater reliability. Provide an image-conditioned layout baseline (e.g., using detected 2D/3D boxes from the same inputs). Ensure identical room envelopes and object libraries. Report OOB/Collision sensitivity to the translation layer used for each method.

9. Realism claims rely on limited no-reference metrics and small samples
- Evidence: NIQE/PIQE/LV computed on 100 randomly sampled images per dataset (Sec. 4.4; Table 3).
- Why it matters: No-reference metrics on a small sample may not reflect domain closeness for embodied perception under PBR lighting and complex geometry.
- Actionable: Report metrics over the full test sets with confidence intervals; add task-driven realism proxies (e.g., zero-shot transfer of real-image-pretrained classifiers/detectors to MinecraftOcc images) to quantify domain gap in features used by perception models.

10. Label generation heuristics for viewpoint handling lack error analysis
- Evidence: Two yaw cases (axis-aligned/diagonal) with fallback offset ε (Eqs. 6–7; Fig. 3) and projection-based culling (App. E; Eq. 16) are used to approximate visible voxels.
- Why it matters: Heuristic volume placement and expansion may include/exclude wrong voxels, contributing to training noise and the negative scaling in Table 4.
- Actionable: Validate visibility by ray-casting from the camera against the map (ground-truth geometry) and quantify precision/recall vs. the proposed f(·) + ε approach. Ablate culling (Eq. 16) and show label-quality vs. model mIoU trade-offs.

11. Cross-dataset class mapping collapses fine-grained semantics without analysis
- Evidence: 1,452 MinecraftOcc classes are mapped to 13 categories for evaluation (Sec. 4.4; App. G).
- Why it matters: Collapsing may hide failure modes and bias results toward structure classes (empty/ceiling/floor/wall).
- Actionable: Provide per-superclass frequency distributions, confusion matrices, and results on a mid-granularity taxonomy. Report performance on furniture-only subsets to probe semantic generalization beyond structure.

12. Throughput and compute efficiency of the pipeline are under-specified
- Evidence: Manual refinement efficiency is quantified (Table 7), but end-to-end runtime (occupancy inference, fusion, clustering, retrieval, command execution) is not.
- Why it matters: Claims of scalability (Abstract; Sec. 3.2–3.4) hinge on throughput.
- Actionable: Report per-scene wall-clock for each stage and GPU/CPU resources; include batched reconstruction throughput and cost per scene. Add a scale-up study (e.g., 100→1,000 scenes).

Suggestions/Questions:
1) Reconstruction pipeline: parameters, ablations, and fidelity
- Please report the voxel resolution (X×Y×Z) used in O_mono and Ô_scene (Eqs. 1–2), and the Minecraft block-to-voxel scale you enforce. How sensitive is reconstruction to this resolution?
- Provide ablations for the key hyperparameters in Sec. 3.2: density kernel K and threshold τ (Eq. 3), DBSCAN distance η and min_samples (Eq. 4), rotation discretization δ and library size L (Eq. 5). Which components most affect geometric errors and manual edits?
- Quantify reconstruction fidelity: (a) voxel IoU between Ô_scene and the ground-truth occupancy from EmbodiedOcc-ScanNet for the same viewpoints, and (b) voxel/block-level agreement between Ô_scene and the final built Minecraft scene (post command execution). This would substantiate the qualitative examples in Fig. 4.
- How do you handle scaling and alignment of the fused occupancy to the room envelope before command generation (Alg. 1, lines 12–14)? Any drift corrections?

2) Template retrieval (Eq. 5)
- Please detail the template library L: number of templates per category, source, licensing, and coverage. What fraction of instances attain IoU ≥ {0.5, 0.7} to some template after rotation search? A top-k IoU histogram and orientation error distribution would clarify the benefit.
- Compare against a “no-retrieval” baseline (direct voxel→block fill) to isolate the contribution of retrieval to the metrics in Table 6 (OOB/Collisions/Semantic Integrity) and to the reduction in manual orientation adjustments in Table 7.

3) Fusion and visibility modeling
- App. E proposes projection-based culling (Eq. 16) while Sec. 3.4 uses a viewpoint-aware volume with fallback offset ε (Eqs. 6–7; Fig. 3). Can you quantify label precision/recall of this heuristic against exact ray-casting in Minecraft (which is feasible given access to M_world)? This could illuminate the negative scaling trend in Table 4.
- How were ε and the volume dimensions (w,h,d) chosen across axis-aligned vs. diagonal cases? Provide sensitivity curves (label density/precision vs. ε) and the distribution of the two yaw cases in MinecraftOcc.

4) Negative scaling on MinecraftOcc (Table 4)
- Many methods degrade from 8k→50k→100k (e.g., Symphonies mIoU 21.56→19.61→13.08). Were total optimization steps/epochs held constant across scales? If so, could underfitting explain the drop? Please report training schedules, effective updates per sample, and learning curves.

Summary:
The paper identifies a robustness-security paradox in deep post-processing image watermarks: distortion-aware training increases embedding redundancy, causing watermark “feature leakage” that neural networks can learn and exploit (Sec. 4.1; Fig. 4). It introduces DAPAO, a no-box, single-image attack framework that uses multi-channel feature learning: a pretrained feature extractor and K-Means localize leakage channels W, then PGD optimizes perturbations for watermark removal (Eq. 1) and a two-stage procedure for forgery with semantic alignment (Eq. 2) (Fig. 5; Alg. A.4). Evaluated on COCO and DIV2K across five representative post-processing schemes (RivaGAN, StegaStamp, HiDDeN, PIMoG, CIN), DAPAO achieves high success while preserving visual quality, outperforming prior attacks by 52.9% in removal SR and 9.6% in forgery SR (Tables 1–2, 12). Ablations validate the roles of feature extraction and leakage-channel selection (Tables 3–4), and analyses highlight when semantics-watermark coupling constrains forgery transfer (Table 13). The paper further explores an adaptive defense that reduces DAPAO’s success but weakens robustness to natural distortions, illustrating the trade-off (App. A.1.2; Table 6). Code is released to support reproducibility (Sec. 8).

Strengths:
1. Clear and original conceptual insight. The paper articulates a “robustness‑security paradox” specific to deep post‑processing watermarks with distortion layers: robustness training induces embedding redundancy that manifests as learnable “feature leakage” (Sec. 4.1). This extends classic robustness–invisibility trade-offs to modern learning-based pipelines and is empirically grounded via feature visualizations evidencing cross-image, channel-specific invariances (Fig. 4).

2. Practical attack model with strong constraints. DAPAO operates in a strict no-box setting with only a single watermarked image (Sec. 3), addressing a realistic and hard threat model compared to prior works needing encoder/detector access or large data (Sec. 1; Sec. 6). This significantly raises the relevance of the results.

3. Simple, unified pipeline that generalizes. The multi-channel feature learning approach—pretrained feature extractor + K-Means to localize leakage channels W, followed by task-specific PGD objectives (Eq. 1–2; Fig. 5; Alg. A.4)—is elegant and re-usable. It unifies removal and forgery within one framework, requiring only loss swaps and the two-stage procedure for semantic alignment.

4. Strong, consistent empirical gains under broad coverage. Across five representative post‑processing schemes (RivaGAN, StegaStamp, HiDDeN, PIMoG, CIN) and two datasets, DAPAO substantially outperforms baselines in removal (Table 1; Table 12) and forgery (Table 2), while preserving visual quality (e.g., removal on StegaStamp SR=1 with SSIM=0.895; Table 1). The reported average improvements (52.9% in removal SR; 9.6% in forgery SR) are meaningful at scale (Sec. 5.2).

5. Insightful analysis of semantics–watermark coupling. The staged forgery (Stage I vs Stage II; Table 4) reveals when semantics alignment matters: Stage I alone suffices for PIMoG/StegaStamp/CIN but not for RivaGAN/HiDDeN. The targeted overlay study (Table 13) further confirms RivaGAN’s tighter coupling, offering design-relevant diagnostics beyond raw attack scores.

6. Defense‑oriented contribution. The adaptive defense experiment (App. A.1.2; Table 6) is a valuable addition: mitigating leakage reduces DAPAO SR but simultaneously weakens robustness to common distortions (JPEG SR rises), concretely evidencing the proposed trade-off and informing future watermark design.

7. Strong ablation and sensitivity coverage. The paper rigorously validates components: feature extraction and selective channel localization (Table 3), staged losses for forgery (Table 4), clustering parameters k,n (Tables 7–8), loss choices (Table 9), and backbone independence (ResNet vs DenseNet; Tables 10–11). This breadth supports stability and transferability of the core mechanism.

8. Clarity of methodological exposition. The high-level pipeline and objectives are easy to follow (Fig. 5; Eq. 1–2), and the background situates the approach within modern distortion-aware training (Fig. 2; Sec. 2.1). Despite minor formatting glitches elsewhere, core methodological parts are conveyed crisply.

9. Reproducibility and transparency. The release of code and scripts (Sec. 1 “Code is available…”; Sec. 8) plus detailed hyperparameters and pseudocode (Sec. 5.1; App. A.4) enhance credibility and facilitate adoption and follow-up work.

Weaknesses:
1. Limited evaluation scale and statistical rigor. The core results use only 100 watermarked images per dataset and 100 image pairs for forgery (Sec. 5.1). Tables 1–2 and 12 report point estimates without confidence intervals or significance tests. Actionable: increase sample sizes by at least an order of magnitude, report per‑scheme mean±std/CIs, and run multiple random seeds for clustering/optimizers to quantify stability.

2. Heuristic leakage localization without guarantees. The key step selects “the n clusters with the fewest samples” over feature channels (Sec. 4.2, Extraction Stage; Fig. 5). This criterion is ad‑hoc and lacks evidence it consistently isolates watermark leakage. Actionable: compare against principled outlier/structure discovery (e.g., robust PCA, isolation forests, sparsity scoring, spectral saliency) and provide quantitative localization diagnostics (e.g., ablate removing top‑k channels ranked by the chosen method vs competitors).

3. Ambiguity and potential mismatch in W definition/usage. W is described as “channel indices” (Sec. 4.2) but later treated as weights/masks (“transform the channel feature indices … into weights” in Alg. A.4). This affects the validity of the feature-space losses in Eq. 1–2. Actionable: formalize W as a binary/real mask, specify how it is computed from clustering, and show sensitivity to W’s sparsity/threshold.

4. Forgery generality is uneven and underexplored. Forgery success sharply drops on RivaGAN (SR=0.24 in Table 2) and needs Stage II alignment for HiDDeN (Table 4), indicating scheme‑dependent limitations. Actionable: analyze failure cases beyond Table 13 by quantifying a “semantics‑coupling index” per scheme (e.g., success vs strength of content‑conditioned decoding), and test additional in‑between schemes or training variants that modulate coupling.

5. Insufficient robustness testing under real distribution shifts. The attack is evaluated on canonical images with the watermark decoder directly (Sec. 5.1). In practice, content passes through unpredictable pipelines (resizing, cropping, color conversion, multiple compressions). Actionable: evaluate whether DAPAO’s removal/forgery survives typical platform transforms and mild physical changes (print‑scan/screen‑capture), mirroring the distortion layer in Fig. 2 but as post‑attack stress tests.

6. No assessment of runtime and scalability. DAPAO optimizes per image (Eq. 1–2; Alg. A.4), but the computational cost and wall‑time are not reported. Actionable: provide per‑image runtimes on RTX 3090, PGD iteration counts for success, and explore amortized/universal perturbations to reduce cost; report success‑time trade‑offs.

7. Dependence on a specific feature backbone and layer choice is only partially tested. While DenseNet vs ResNet appears similar (App. A.2; Tables 10–11), the layer(s) used and their impact on leakage detectability are not analyzed. Actionable: perform layer‑wise ablations (early/mid/late features; multi‑scale fusion) and include modern backbones (e.g., ViT) to ensure the leakage phenomenon is not an artifact of CNN inductive biases.

8. Visual quality evaluation is narrow. SSIM/PSNR can be insensitive to perceptual artifacts; ablations show quality can degrade severely without selective channels (Table 3). Actionable: add LPIPS and no‑reference IQA, and a small user study to confirm imperceptibility. For semantic preservation claims, report CLIP similarity before/after attacks.

9. Threshold reporting focuses on a single operating point in the main text. Although full thresholds are in the appendix (Sec. 5.2; “Detailed results … Appendix A.3.2/3”), Tables 1–2 only show one threshold per method, which can mask sensitivity. Actionable: summarize ROC‑style curves or AUC over thresholds in the main paper, and report results at the p<0.05 binomial threshold per method alongside fixed thresholds.

10. Defense analysis is too narrow to substantiate the trade‑off broadly. The adaptive defense is demonstrated only on HiDDeN and only against JPEG as a proxy distortion (App. A.1.2; Table 6). Actionable: replicate on multiple schemes (at least PIMoG, StegaStamp) and include diverse distortions (blur, resize, noise) to confirm the robustness‑security trade‑off generality.

11. Lack of keying/instance diversity in target schemes. Many watermark systems instantiate per‑key encoders/decoders. The evaluation uses public implementations (Sec. 5.1) but does not vary keys/initializations. Actionable: for each scheme, evaluate across multiple random keys or independently trained instances and report how single‑image leakage extraction transfers across instances.

12. Fragility to post‑attack resizing/cropping is unknown. Since δ is image‑aligned (Eq. 1), small resampling could break evasion/forgery. Actionable: measure success after down/up‑sampling, small crops/pads, and color‑space conversions to bound the real‑world reliability of the attack.

13. Large L∞ budgets without sensitivity analysis. The chosen budgets are ϵ1=0.08 (removal), ϵ1=0.08/ϵ2=0.018 (forgery) (Sec. 5.1), which may be perceptible on 0–1 scaling. Actionable: sweep ϵ across [0.005, 0.08], report detection‑evasion curves vs imperceptibility metrics, and identify minimally‑visible operating points.

14. Forgery is limited to transplanting an observed watermark, not targeting arbitrary IDs. The current method extracts leaked patterns from a single watermarked image and transfers them (Sec. 4.2, Forgery). Actionable: explore whether partial control is possible (e.g., flipping bits or composing leakage from multiple sources) and quantify the ability to impersonate specific IDs under the same no‑box constraint.

15. Presentation issues impede reproducibility. Several tables/algorithms are misformatted or garbled (e.g., Tables 1–2 and 12 headers; Table 4 “1 0.701”; Algorithms in App. A.4). Actionable: fix all formatting; provide clean, executable pseudocode and detailed implementation notes (exact layers used, normalization of features, clustering space), as these details are critical for the leakage extraction step.

16. Limited coverage of in‑processing schemes and clear success boundary. The only in‑processing test (Tree‑Ring) shows low SR=0.12 (App. A.1.1; Table 5). Actionable: extend experiments to at least one more in‑processing method and articulate a measurable criterion (e.g., leakage score) that predicts DAPAO feasibility, enabling practitioners to assess risk before deployment.

17. Missing cross‑detector analysis for forgeries. It is unclear whether forged images inadvertently trigger other detectors or are specific to the target scheme. Actionable: evaluate cross‑watermark false positives/negatives to understand collateral risks and the specificity of the leakage‑based forgery.

Collectively, addressing these points—especially scaling experiments with stronger statistical reporting, broadening robustness and defense analyses, formalizing leakage localization, and tightening presentation—would substantially strengthen the paper’s claims and practical relevance.

Suggestions/Questions:
1. Formalization of leakage-channel mask W
- In Sec. 4.2 (“Extracting Leakage Features”), W is described as “channel indices,” while Alg. A.4 says “transform the channel feature indices … into weights.” Please precisely define W (binary mask vs real weights), how it’s computed from K-Means, and how it’s applied to F(·) in Eq. (1)–(2). Clarify whether clustering is performed on per-channel feature vectors (which representation?), per spatial position, or statistics (e.g., mean/variance). A concise mathematical description would remove ambiguity.

2. Which feature layer(s) are used and how are features normalized?
- Sec. 5.1 states DenseNet is used as F, but not which layer(s). Do you pool across blocks or use a single intermediate layer? Are features standardized (per-channel z-score, L2-norm) prior to clustering and losses? A layer-wise ablation (early/mid/late; single vs multi-scale fusion) would clarify where leakage is most pronounced (cf. Fig. 4).

3. Stability of leakage localization with K-Means
- The “fewest-samples clusters” heuristic (Sec. 4.2; Fig. 5) is central but potentially sensitive to K-Means init and k,n choices. Beyond Tables 7–8, can you report variability over multiple random seeds (initial centers and PGD seeds) and provide CIs for SR in Tables 1–2? A comparison to alternative outlier discovery (robust PCA, isolation forest, sparsity ranking) would strengthen the claim that the selected channels truly capture leakage.

4. Loss L on feature maps and use of SSIM
- You write “We used SSIM loss” (Sec. 5.1) and Table 9 compares SSIM/L1/L2. In Eq. (1)–(2), L acts on W·F(·). Do you compute SSIM directly on feature maps as images? If so, what window/stride and normalization are used, and why is SSIM preferable to cosine/L2 in feature space? Please provide a brief justification and implementation details; this affects reproducibility.

5. Sign conventions and the role of δ in forgery
- In Sec. 4.2 (Forgery), Stage I optimizes Eq. (1) (maximize divergence of W·F(Iwm) and W·F(Iwm+δ)), then the forged image is I′−δ (or I′−δ+δs). If δ was learned to disrupt or move away from leakage features (removal), why does −δ approximate the watermark to add? Please reconcile this with the statement “This learned δ approximates the watermark pattern” and clarify whether Stage I for forgery uses a different sign/objective than removal.

6. Budgets and imperceptibility
- The chosen budgets are ε1=0.08 (removal) and ε1=0.08/ε2=0.018 (forgery) (Sec. 5.1). Please (a) state the input scaling, (b) include a sensitivity sweep (ε vs SR and visual quality), and (c) report perceptual metrics (e.g., LPIPS) and CLIP similarity to support imperceptibility and semantic preservation beyond SSIM/PSNR (Tables 1–2).

7. Runtime, iteration counts, and convergence
- What are typical wall-times per image (removal/forgery) on RTX 3090, PGD iteration counts, and step sizes? Do you observe diminishing returns beyond a certain number of steps? This would be useful for practitioners and for assessing practicality relative to WmRobust/WmAttacker.

8. Statistical reporting and scale
- The main experiments use 100 images/pairs per dataset (Sec. 5.1). Could you provide mean±std or 95% CIs for SR/bit-accuracy in Tables 1–2 and 12, aggregated over multiple random seeds? Even if you cannot substantially scale up in the rebuttal, reporting uncertainty would strengthen your claims.

9. Detector thresholds and operating points
- Sec. 5.1 mentions FPR=0.05 thresholds “according to the default configuration,” yet Tables 1–2 report fixed thresholds (e.g., “PIMoG(th=0.6)”). Please clarify how these numbers correspond to FPR=0.05 and to the binomial p<0.05 criterion. A compact ROC/AUC summary or success-vs-threshold plot in the main paper (not only App. A.3) would aid interpretability.

10. Post-attack robustness under platform transforms
- Since robust watermarks are designed to withstand pipelines (Fig. 2), how stable are DAPAO results after common post-attack transforms (resize/downsample/upscale, small crop/pad, JPEG recompression, color-space conversion)? A small stress-test would demonstrate real-world reliability.

11. Physical-world stress tests
- If feasible, please include limited screen-capture or print-scan simulations to test whether δ remains effective in conditions for which these watermark schemes were trained (Sec. 2.1).

12. Keys/instances and message diversity
- Many systems use different keys or independently trained instances. In Sec. 5.1, do you fix one instance per scheme? Are watermark messages identical across images or randomized? Please evaluate (or comment on) (a) cross-instance/keys transfer of single-image δ and (b) whether forgery succeeds when the target clean image expects a different bit pattern than the source from which δ was derived.

13. Scope of forgery: can you target or edit IDs?
- The current forgery transfers whatever leakage is extracted from Iwm (Sec. 4.2). Is there any leverage to flip bits or steer toward a specific ID without detector access by composing δ from multiple sources or using Stage II constraints? Even negative results would help delineate the attack boundary.

14. Quantifying semantics–watermark coupling
- You argue coupling explains poor forgery on RivaGAN/HiDDeN (Table 4; App. A.3.6, Table 13). Could you propose and report a quantitative proxy (e.g., dependence of decoder output on (1−W) channels, or a coupling index measured via counterfactuals) across schemes? This would generalize the insight beyond a single case study.

15. Generality across backbones and layers (CNN vs ViT)
- App. A.2 (Tables 10–11) compares DenseNet vs ResNet. Can you add a transformer backbone (e.g., ViT) and a brief layer-wise study to ensure leakage is not an artifact of CNN inductive biases?

16. Post-attack survivability of forgeries across different detectors
- Do forged images for scheme A inadvertently trigger other detectors (B–E) or remain specific? A small cross-detector evaluation would clarify collateral risks and specificity of learned leak patterns.

17. Defense generality and formalization
- The adaptive defense (App. A.1.2; Table 6) is shown only for HiDDeN and JPEG. Please (a) formalize the training objective that “guides leakage-related features to align with semantics,” (b) test on ≥1 additional scheme and additional distortions (blur, noise, resize), and (c) present a trade-off curve (robustness to distortions vs DAPAO SR) to substantiate the robustness–security paradox.

18. Single-image claim vs feasibility study with multiple images
- Sec. 4.1 feasibility “embed watermarks into multiple images,” yet the attack claims single-image operation (Sec. 3; Fig. 1/5). Please confirm that the extraction stage (clustering, W) uses only the single input at test time and that no extra watermarked images are needed for parameter selection.

19. Visualizing and quantifying W-selected channels
- Beyond Fig. 4, could you show representative W-selected channel maps and report how many channels are selected per scheme on average, together with a simple invariance metric across images (e.g., correlation of W·F across contents)? This would substantiate that W isolates shared watermark structure.

20. Pseudocode and formatting for reproducibility
- Algorithms in App. A.4 are currently garbled (e.g., line breaks, symbols) and Table 4 has a broken entry (“1 0.701”). Please provide clean pseudocode specifying: exact feature layer(s), feature normalization, K-Means init/stop, PGD step sizes/iters, and how W is constructed/applied. This will materially help others reproduce your results.
