Summary:
This paper proposes GLaVE-Cap, a global–local aligned framework for detailed video captioning that integrates vision experts (Fig. 2). The TrackFusion module (Sec. 3.2) combines Grounding DINO and SAM2 to track objects and create visual prompts with IDs, and uses a dual-stream design to separately capture inter-frame dynamics (differential captions) and intra-frame static details (detailed captions), merging them into fine-grained local captions. The CaptionBridge module (Sec. 3.3) injects a globally generated overview caption to guide local captioning and performs adaptive, semantically coherent scene segmentation and summarization (supported by PySceneDetect) to form the final video caption. The authors introduce GLaVE-Bench (Sec. 4.1, Table 1), a multi-scene evaluation set with 55 videos and 6,491 QAs—about 5× more QAs per video than prior work—and “scene-hints” to reduce ambiguity, evaluated via a caption-as-proxy protocol. They also release GLaVE-1.2M (Sec. 4.2), comprising 15,814 videos, 16k fine-grained captions, and 1.176M QA pairs, and train a student model, GLaVE-7B, showing strong results (Table 3). Experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance of GLaVE-Cap on GLaVE-Bench, VidCapBench, Video-MME, and MVBench with both GPT-4o and Qwen2.5-VL-72B backbones, with ablations validating the contribution of each module (Tables 2, 4–5).

Strengths:
1. Clear algorithmic advance over local-to-global pipelines: the two-module design explicitly targets three documented failure modes (Fig. 1) with (i) expert-guided object tracking and ID-tagged visual prompts plus a dual-stream local captioner to decouple dynamics from static details (TrackFusion, Sec. 3.2; Fig. 3), and (ii) bidirectional local–global interaction via overview-caption injection and adaptive, semantics-aware scene segmentation (CaptionBridge, Sec. 3.3; Eqs. 1–6; Fig. 2).  
2. Technically concrete and reproducible design: inputs/outputs and formulae are specified for each substep, including the role of overview captions and scene splits (Eqs. 1–6). The tracking pipeline combines Grounding DINO and SAM2 with ID assignment and Set-of-Mark visualization (Sec. 3.2), a pragmatic, well-justified expert integration (Appendix B).  
3. Strong, multi-backbone SOTA with broad coverage: consistent improvements on GLaVE-Bench, Video-MME(-S), VidCapBench, and MVBench using both GPT-4o and Qwen2.5‑VL‑72B (Table 2), demonstrating generality beyond a single proprietary model.  
4. Fine-grained benchmark contribution with novel disambiguation: GLaVE-Bench offers ~5× more QAs/video than prior work and includes scene-hints to resolve multi-scene ambiguity (Sec. 4.1; Table 1; Appendix C.2). The evaluation protocol quantifies accuracy, hallucination, and coverage with an LLM judge and an explicit “Not mentioned” option (Sec. 4.1).  
5. Large-scale data resource with demonstrated utility: GLaVE‑1.2M (15,814 videos, 1.176M QA pairs) is curated for fine-grained supervision (Sec. 4.2). The student model GLaVE‑7B trained on it outperforms strong baselines on GLaVE‑Bench (Table 3), evidencing dataset value.  
6. Targeted ablations and diagnostics that go beyond accuracy:  
   - Component removals produce sizable, interpretable drops (Tables 4–5; 15).  
   - Counting-specific benefits from visual prompts are shown across datasets (Table 5).  
   - Quantified gains in descriptive richness, contextual consistency, and detail retention during summarization (Appendix K.1–K.3; Tables 9–11) directly validate the paper’s core claims.  
7. Careful evaluation design to mitigate confounds: baseline implementations documented (Appendix E), average frame counts reported (Table 7), repeated LLM-judge runs with stability analysis and error taxonomy (Table 8; Appendix H.2), and a hallucination accumulation check (Table 6).  
8. Practicality for downstream generation: captions from GLaVE‑Cap guide video generation better than a strong baseline, with qualitative showcases and a user study (Appendix F; Fig. 8–9), indicating real utility beyond benchmark scores.  
9. Extensive prompts, settings, and training details in appendices (P, Q, I, J) and an explicit plan to open-source code, weights, benchmark, and dataset, supporting community adoption (Ethics/Availability statement; end of Sec. 6).  
10. Measured discussion of limitations and future directions (Appendix R), showing awareness of remaining bottlenecks (e.g., many-object scenes) and a plausible path (object-centric captioning).

Weaknesses:
1. Evaluation circularity and dependence on LLM judging
   - The main claims rely on QA derived from captions produced by the authors’ own pipeline (Appendix C.1), and evaluation is performed by GPT‑4o reading generated captions (Sec. 4.1). Although captions are regenerated at test time and multiple runs are reported (Table 8), this still risks favoring styles/content emphasized by GLaVE‑Cap and inherits judge/model biases. Actionable: add a human study on factual alignment of captions to videos; evaluate on VQA sets whose QAs are authored directly from videos and independent of your captions; include a second, open-source judge and report agreement (e.g., Cohen’s κ) and confidence intervals.

2. Small and potentially unrepresentative benchmark
   - GLaVE‑Bench comprises only 55 videos, all selected from the Video‑MME short subset (Sec. 4.1; Table 1). Per‑video QA density is high, but the number of source videos is limited, which may inflate variance and limit ecological validity. Actionable: expand to hundreds of videos with stratified sampling across the six Video‑MME categories (Appendix C.5), and report per‑category results and confidence intervals.

3. Possible train–test contamination and data provenance gaps
   - GLaVE‑1.2M is built from LLaVA‑Video‑178K (Sec. 4.2), while GLaVE‑Bench samples videos from Video‑MME‑S (Sec. 4.1). The paper does not quantify overlap or near-duplicates between training sources (including any other datasets used in base models) and the 55 evaluation videos. Actionable: perform video‑level deduplication via perceptual hashing/fingerprints and release a leakage report; ensure no-caption/no-QA derived from any evaluation video/near-duplicate appears in GLaVE‑1.2M; add a “clean” split evaluation.

4. Baseline fairness and comparability
   - Several baselines are re‑implemented (Appendix E), and frame sampling is not unified; Table 7 shows large differences in average frame counts. Vript originally uses audio transcripts but the reproduction omits audio (Appendix E). These choices can understate baselines. Actionable: provide a matched‑budget comparison with equal keyframe counts, resolution, and token budgets; re‑run Vript with audio; add an experiment fixing identical scene boundaries across methods.

5. Limited analysis of computational cost and scalability
   - The pipeline integrates Grounding‑DINO + SAM2 tracking, dual‑stream captioning, and multiple LLM calls (Sec. 3; Fig. 2), but there is no report of runtime, GPU/CPU hours, token usage, or cost vs. video length. Summary:
This paper studies the probabilistic bisection algorithm (PBA) for noisy 1-D threshold/root finding and proves it achieves geometric convergence for a fixed (non-Bayesian) ground truth. The main result (Section 2.2, Theorem 1) shows E|θ̂n−θ*| ≤ 3e−Cn for a constant C depending only on the noise level p∈(0,1/2), matching the optimal noiseless binary search rate. The analysis hinges on new tools that directly characterize PBA’s query dynamics (Subsection 2.3): two propositions (Propositions 1–2) establish that a carefully chosen ratio of posterior masses Mn forms a supermartingale that decays exponentially while the queries oscillate across the truth with linearly many crossings in expectation. The proof technique departs from prior discretized/Bayesian analyses that rely on location-independent expected improvements (Eq. 3), and instead tracks location-dependent updates via posterior mass partitions and stopping-time arguments. The paper also treats more general noise models with error rate at most p (Appendix B). Beyond 1-D, it constructs a PBA-based estimator for Hölder-smooth decision boundaries with nearly minimax L1 rates (Appendix C, Theorem 2), and proves an exponential L1 rate for linear boundaries (Theorem 3). Simulations (Appendix D, Figure 1) illustrate the exponential error decay and the dependence of the constant on p.

Strengths:
1. Resolves a concrete open question with a sharp result. Section 2.2 (Theorem 1) proves geometric convergence in the fixed-truth setting, E|θ̂n−θ*| ≤ 3e−Cn, with C depending only on p. The paper explicitly argues this rate matches noiseless binary search (lines 091–095), settling the question of whether PBA’s empirical efficiency persists under noise.

2. Novel, location-aware analysis of query dynamics. Subsection 2.3 introduces a fine-grained partition of the domain I1/I2/I3 and ties query locations to posterior mass via the median property Pn(Xn+1)=1/2 (Eq. 4). This departs from prior analyses that rely on location-independent drift (Eq. 3) and that “breaks down” for the original PBA (lines 210–215).

3. New supermartingale and stopping-time machinery tailored to PBA. The definition of Mn = a(3)n/a(2)n (Eq. 7) is carefully chosen to recover monotonicity in expectation (Remark 3). Proposition 1 shows exponential decay of Mn via log-supermartingale increments verified case-by-case (Case 2 and 3 in “Proof of Proposition 1”), and Azuma–Hoeffding is applied after lower-bounding the number of effective decrease steps.

4. Quantified oscillation around the truth with linear crossing rate. Proposition 2 proves E(T) ≥ ηn for the number of truth crossings (Eq. 5), giving a precise and interpretable dynamic: queries “oscillate across the truth” with shrinking amplitude (Implications). This insight is new and operationally useful for understanding adaptive posterior-updating algorithms.

5. Robustness beyond the symmetric noise model. Appendix B extends the result to general responses with P(Y≠hθ*(X)) ≤ p, noting that the key contraction of E(Mi/Mi−1) improves as the error probability drops and that T remains Θ(n). This broadens applicability without altering the core analysis.

6. Careful handling of boundary cases and tight tail control. The proof of Theorem 1 reduces to an upper-tail bound (Eq. 2) and uses a gridding-plus-Markov argument (Appendix A). Corner cases θ*∈{0,1} are treated separately via Lemma 2, showing P(a(3)n ≤ e−C1 n) with the same exponential decay flavor.

7. Meaningful high-dimensional extensions with near-minimax guarantees. Appendix C constructs a practical grid-lines-plus-1D-PBA estimator and proves E||ĝn−g*||1 ≤ O((log n/n)^{α/(d−1)}) (Theorem 2), explicitly leveraging Theorem 1 in the sample allocation (Eq. 10–15). It also proves an exponential L1 rate for linear boundaries (Theorem 3), close to best possible in this structured setting.

8. Clear exposition that aids verification and reuse. The paper includes targeted remarks (Remark 2 on the role of a(j)i, Remark 3 on the design of Mn), a succinct proof sketch (Implications and “Proof Sketch” under Subsection 2.3), and a structured, stepwise proof of Proposition 1 (Steps 1–3). The algebraic checks (e.g., monotonicity of h(x) and the bound −ln 2 + H(p) < 0 in Case 3; Eq. 6 drift bounds) are explicit and easy to follow.

Summary:
The paper proposes a hybrid explainability framework that converts LLM Q&A outputs into structured “Feature Trees” (with fields such as Root, KeyFactors, Process, Limitations, NextSteps, Resources) and merges them into a global “Uber Tree” using chunked LLM-based semantic merging with a deterministic recursive fallback (Section 3; Figure 1). It adds an automated consistency verification step in which an LLM audits alignment between individual trees and the Uber Tree, producing scores and issue lists (Section 3.3). Evaluated on 1000 mortgage-compliance Q&A pairs with a 100-tree holdout (Section 4.1), the method achieved 100% valid tree generation (Section 5.1), produced a more abstract and compact Uber Tree with 12 coherent top-level categories than algorithmic baselines (Table 2), and yielded high consistency (average 0.95; 95/100 fully consistent) with mostly minor terminological/granularity issues (Section 5.3). A human study with three domain experts over 30 Q&A pairs found Feature Trees clearer than Chain-of-Thought explanations, with a trade-off in perceived comprehensiveness and similar ease of verification (Table 3; Section 5.4). The authors position the approach as a practical path to auditable, enterprise-ready LLMs and note planned code/data release (Section 6, Conclusion).

Strengths:
Strengths

1. Clear local-to-global explainability formulation. The paper’s core idea—structuring per-QA explanations as Feature Trees and merging them into an Uber Tree—cleanly separates local rationale from a global, auditable knowledge map (Section 3; Figure 1). This “local-to-global” bridge is a concrete, original problem framing for XAI in LLMs.

2. Practical hybrid merging design with operational robustness. The chunked LLM-based semantic merging combined with a deterministic recursive fallback (Sections 3.2.1–3.2.2) is both creative and pragmatic. The fallback is specified with alignment heuristics (normalized Levenshtein, embedding cosine similarity with τ=0.72) and complexity analysis, including memoization and backtracking rules—an unusually thorough engineering treatment for explainability work.

3. Explicit, auditable schema for local explanations. The Feature Tree schema—Root, KeyFactors, Process, Limitations, NextSteps, Resources (Section 3.1)—encourages complete, multi-faceted justifications rather than free-text rationales. This design makes downstream verification tractable (Section 3.3) and aligns well with regulated workflows.

4. Systematic consistency verification protocol. The use of a held-out set V and a structured “auditor” prompt that reports a numerical score and issue lists (Section 3.3) is well operationalized. Beyond a single scalar, the protocol surfaces “contradictions,” “missing key factors,” and “structural discrepancies,” creating an actionable audit trail rather than a black-box metric.

5. Strong reliability in structured generation at scale. The paper demonstrates 100% valid JSON generation across 1000 Q&A pairs with all required fields present (Section 5.1), indicating that, with careful prompting and error handling (JSON mode, retries; Section 4.2), LLMs can reliably produce machine-verifiable explanations.

6. Evidence that LLM merging achieves meaningful abstraction. Table 2 shows a large reduction in top-level nodes (12 vs. 37 for the purely algorithmic baseline) with similar or slightly greater depth (5 vs. 4), suggesting genuine consolidation rather than shallow pruning (Section 5.2). The resulting 12-category taxonomy is interpretable for the domain (e.g., “Regulatory Compliance,” “Fees & Closing Costs,” “Documentation & Verification”).

7. Useful failure-mode analysis that informs governance. The paper does not stop at reporting high consistency (average 0.95; Section 5.3); it categorizes the 5% inconsistent cases (e.g., appraisal, compensation, marketing claims) and translates them into targeted Uber Tree improvements. This closes a practical loop between verification and curation.

8. Domain significance and realistic coverage. The dataset spans 1000 mortgage-compliance Q&A pairs covering TRID, RESPA, TILA, ECOA, ATR/QM, SAFE Act, and state rules (Section 4.1). Applying the method to a multi-regulation, high-stakes setting substantiates the paper’s enterprise-facing claims.

9. Reproducible and transparent implementation details. The paper documents concrete choices—APIs and versions, temperatures, token budgets, chunk sizes, thresholds, backoff policies (Section 4.2)—and includes prompt templates and pipeline scripts (Appendix A.2; “build uber tree llm.py,” “evaluate uber tree.py”), increasing reproducibility and easing adoption.

10. Thoughtful evaluation design and statistical reporting. The research questions are pre-specified with metrics (Table 1). The human study reports t-stats, p-values, and effect sizes (Table 3), and the main consistency result includes 95% CIs and SD (Section 5.3). Section 4.2 notes bootstrap intervals and multiple-comparisons corrections, signaling methodological care.

11. Justified similarity thresholding for the fallback. The embedding similarity cutoff (τ=0.72) is empirically validated on 200 annotated node pairs with 92% agreement to human judgment (text adjacent to Section 4.1), lending credibility to the deterministic merger when the LLM is unavailable.

12. Cohesive narrative connecting XAI to knowledge governance. The Discussion explicitly positions the Uber Tree plus verification as a mechanism for “knowledge base governance” and continuous auditing (Section 6.1), which is a meaningful and underexplored angle in LLM explainability for regulated domains.

13. Clear, high-level pipeline visualization. Figure 1 succinctly captures the staged process—tree generation, chunked merging, and consistency verification—improving comprehensibility of the end-to-end system.

Weaknesses:
Weaknesses and actionable improvements

1. Circular consistency evaluation without independent ground truth
- Evidence: The consistency audit uses the same class of LLM to both construct the Uber Tree and judge alignment (“We prompt the LLM to act as an auditor… outputs a structured consistency report,” Section 3.3), yielding ¯s = 0.95 (Section 5.3). No human or rule-based adjudication is reported.
- Why it matters: Self-auditing risks confirmation bias and inflated scores; “No factual contradictions” (Section 5.3) could be false negatives.
- Actionable: (a) Add a human-judged alignment benchmark on the 100 held-out trees V with double annotation and inter-annotator agreement. (b) Triangulate with cross-model audits (e.g., a different LLM family) and prompt variants to assess test–retest reliability of scores. (c) Incorporate a rule-based compliance engine or checklist for a subset of regulations (e.g., TRID/RESPA items listed in Section 4.1) to serve as an external reference for contradiction/gap detection. Report calibration plots mapping LLM scores to human judgments.

2. Underspecified and weak baselines for merging quality
- Evidence: Table 2 lists “SHAP-based Clustering” and “Attention-based Grouping” without methodological detail or citations; only structural counts (Top-Level Nodes/Depth/Total Nodes) are compared. Table 1 mentions “Expert evaluation of coherence and coverage,” but these scores are not reported in Section 5.2.
- Why it matters: Structural compression (12 vs. 37 top-level nodes) does not establish semantic quality or coverage.
- Actionable: (a) Fully specify baseline pipelines, hyperparameters, and references. (b) Report the promised expert coherence/coverage ratings for each method (Table 1) with effect sizes. (c) Add ontology/schema alignment baselines from ontology matching (Section 2.5; Euzenat & Shvaiko, 2013) and evaluate with standard alignment metrics (e.g., precision/recall of node mappings against a human-curated mini-taxonomy). (d) Measure duplication rate, misclassification rate, and concept coverage against a gold taxonomy for a representative subset.

3. Claims of auditability not borne out by user study design
- Evidence: The human study (3 experts, 30 Q&A) finds no significant improvement in “Ease of Verification” (Table 3), yet the Abstract/Conclusion claim gains in “auditability.”
- Why it matters: Auditability should be task-based (e.g., time-to-verify, error detection), not just Likert perceptions.
- Actionable: Redesign the study around auditor tasks: (a) time-to-locate relevant policy for a claim; (b) accuracy in spotting planted contradictions; (c) completeness in identifying mandatory factors. Report objective metrics and confidence intervals. Include a within-subjects design controlling token length so CoT and Feature Trees have comparable content budgets.

4. Inconsistent reporting and numerous formatting/reproducibility issues
- Evidence: Section 4.1 states 1000 training trees and 100 held-out; Section 6.4 “Experimental Limitations” refers to “100 Q&A pairs.” Appendix A.2/A.4 contain garbled prompts and broken JSON; several references are incomplete/garbled around lines 536–565.
- Why it matters: These issues hinder verification and replication.
- Actionable: (a) Resolve internal inconsistencies on dataset sizes. (b) Clean and validate all prompt templates and JSON examples (Appendix A.2, A.4) with a JSON schema and unit tests. (c) Provide complete bibliographic entries. (d) Release the promised code/data with exact prompts, schemas, seeds, and scripts to reproduce Tables 2–3 and Section 5.3.

5. Faithfulness of the Uber Tree to regulatory sources is not tested
- Evidence: Section 5.3 reports terminological/granularity mismatches but “No factual contradictions,” without checking against authoritative regulations; “Resources” links are not validated (Section 3.1).
- Why it matters: A compact taxonomy can omit or distort requirements; high internal consistency does not imply external correctness.
- Actionable: (a) Build a small, human-verified checklist per regulation (e.g., top TRID disclosures, ECOA adverse action items) and measure Uber Tree recall/precision. (b) Validate a sample of “Resources” URLs for correctness, relevance, and currency. (c) Conduct an adversarial evaluation by injecting known contradictions or outdated requirements into feature trees and measuring detection rates.

6. Limited analysis of robustness, parameter sensitivity, and scalability
- Evidence: Chunk size K=10 is “determined through empirical testing” (Section 4.2) with no ablations; the fallback algorithm’s complexity is given (Section 3.2.2) but no runtime/cost measurements; the pipeline targets “enterprise scale” (Sections 1, 6.3) without performance evidence.
- Why it matters: Practical deployment depends on latency, cost, and stability under varying loads.
- Actionable: (a) Report wall-clock time, API cost, and token usage for generation/merging/verification at 100/1k/10k trees; include failure rates triggering the fallback. (b) Ablate K, temperatures (T=1.0/0.1), and τ=0.72 on merging quality and consistency scores. (c) Stress-test with longer/deeper trees and measure degradation.

7. Lack of formal definition and reliability of the “consistency score”
- Evidence: Section 3.3 defines s_i ∈ [0,1] as LLM output without rubric/scale anchors; Section 5.3 reports mean/SD but not reliability.
- Why it matters: Without a scoring rubric and reliability analysis, scores are hard to interpret or compare.
- Actionable: (a) Specify a scoring rubric mapping issue types/severity to score deductions; provide examples. (b) Report test–retest reliability (same input, different prompts/seeds) and inter-model agreement (two LLMs). (c) Calibrate scores to human labels via isotonic/logistic calibration and report Brier scores.

8. Missing comparisons to structured knowledge construction literature
- Evidence: The paper cites Knowledge Graphs (Section 2.2; Hogan et al., 2021) and ontology alignment (Section 2.5) but does not empirically compare to KG/ontology construction pipelines on consolidation and verifiability.
- Why it matters: Uber Tree may replicate ontology induction; without comparison, novelty and advantage remain unclear.
- Actionable: Implement a KG/ontology baseline with lightweight schema induction and entity linking on a subset; compare on coherence, coverage, and verification effort with expert raters. Discuss trade-offs in flexibility vs. formal semantics.

9. Dataset provenance, sampling, and ethics not documented
- Evidence: Section 4.1 describes “1000 real-world Question-Answer pairs” across regulations but omits source, anonymization, and approvals; no Code-of-Ethics discussion despite potential human subject data.
- Why it matters: Enterprise deployment requires documented provenance and privacy compliance.
- Actionable: Provide dataset sourcing, de-identification procedures, license, and (if applicable) IRB/ethics review. Release distribution statistics across regulations and question types; deduplication checks; leakage controls between training and verification sets.

10. Limited “closed-loop” improvement demonstration
- Evidence: Section 5.3 identifies five systematic gap categories (e.g., “appraisal process,” “compensation/commission”) but does not show Uber Tree revision and re-verification.
- Why it matters: Governance claims (Section 6.1) hinge on iterative improvement.
- Actionable: Show a loop: (a) incorporate missing categories; (b) re-run verification; (c) report delta in consistency and expert coverage; (d) quantify curator effort.

11. Fallback algorithm validation is narrow
- Evidence: τ=0.72 is “empirically validated… 200 node pairs, 92% accuracy” (text adjacent to Section 4.1) with no details on annotator protocol or error modes.
- Why it matters: Deterministic merging is safety-critical during API failures.
- Actionable: Expand the validation with balanced positives/negatives, multiple annotators, confusion analysis, and calibration of τ via ROC/PR curves. Report the end-to-end quality of merged trees produced entirely by the fallback on a held-out subset.

Collectively, addressing these points would substantiate the claimed advances in explainability and auditability: replace self-referential scoring with externally validated measures, provide rigorous baselines and task-based human evaluations, quantify scalability/cost, and demonstrate iterative governance that improves the Uber Tree over time.

Suggestions/Questions:
1. Dataset size, split, and leakage controls
- Section 4.1 states “1000 … Q&A pairs” with a 100-tree holdout V, while Section 6.4 (“Experimental Limitations”) refers to “100 Q&A pairs.” Please reconcile this and provide: (a) exact train/verification counts; (b) distribution across regulations (TRID, RESPA, TILA, ECOA, ATR/QM, SAFE Act, state rules); (c) de-duplication and leakage checks between the 1000 trees used to build TU and the 100 used for verification.

2. Baselines in Table 2: methods, citations, and tuning
- Table 2 lists “SHAP-based Clustering” and “Attention-based Grouping” but no pipeline/citations. Please specify for each: the underlying model/features, how SHAP or attention was derived for tree nodes, clustering algorithm/hyperparameters, and references. Include how you controlled for node label normalization and synonymy (cf. Section 3.2.2 thresholds). Without this, the structural comparison (12 vs. 37 top-level nodes) is hard to interpret.

3. Expert coherence/coverage ratings promised for RQ2
- Table 1 includes “Qualitative: Expert evaluation of coherence and coverage,” but Section 5.2 reports only structural counts and a narrative. Please provide the missing expert scores (means, CIs), rater identities/experience, rubric, and inter-rater agreement for all merging methods in Table 2. These could materially change the assessment of Uber Tree quality.

4. Consistency audit circularity and score reliability
- In Section 3.3, “We prompt the LLM to act as an auditor… outputs a structured consistency report.” To mitigate self-audit bias, can you add in rebuttal: (a) cross-model auditing (a different LLM family) and report inter-model agreement; (b) test–retest reliability with prompt/seed variants; (c) a small human-judged subset (e.g., 30 trees) with double annotation and κ to calibrate s_i? Also, please share the scoring rubric that maps issue types to s_i ∈ [0,1] (currently unspecified).

5. “No factual contradictions” claim (Section 5.3)
- Please provide 3–5 representative audit reports R_i showing how contradictions/gaps would be flagged. Also, can you run an adversarial check by injecting known regulatory contradictions or outdated requirements into a subset of trees and report detection rates? This would substantiate the “No factual contradictions” finding.

6. External correctness against authoritative sources
- Beyond internal alignment, can you benchmark TU against a small, human-curated mini-taxonomy/checklist for one or two regulations (e.g., TRID disclosures, ECOA adverse action)? Report recall/precision of required concepts and show mappings via the “Resources” field (Section 3.1). Even a focused subset could strengthen the claim of “auditability.”

7. Runtime, token, and cost profile at 1k trees
- Section 4.2 describes temperatures, chunk size K=10, and token budgets but no resource/cost accounting. Please provide: (a) number of API calls and tokens per stage (generation/merging/verification); (b) wall-clock times; (c) proportion of merges that fell back to the deterministic algorithm; (d) total cost estimates. These are important for the “enterprise-scale” claim (Sections 1, 6.3).

8. Sensitivity analyses for K, temperatures, and τ
- K=10 and τ=0.72 are “empirically validated,” but ablations are missing. Could you add a concise ablation (e.g., K ∈ {5,10,20}, temperatures ∈ {0.0–0.7}, τ ∈ {0.65–0.80}) reporting effects on Table 2 structure metrics and the average consistency ¯s (Section 5.3)? This would clarify robustness.

9. Fallback merger validation details
- The τ=0.72 threshold is said to achieve “92% accuracy” on 200 node pairs (text adjacent to Section 4.1). Please provide: (a) annotation protocol (positives/negatives balance), inter-annotator agreement, and a confusion matrix; (b) ROC/PR curves to motivate τ; (c) quality of a TU produced entirely by the fallback on a held-out subset (structure metrics and expert rating as in RQ2).

10. Human evaluation design and “Ease of Verification”
- Table 3 shows improved “Clarity” but no gain in “Ease of Verification.” Could you augment with task-based measures (time-to-verify a claim, accuracy in spotting a planted inconsistency, completeness in listing mandatory factors) under matched-length conditions for FT vs. CoT? Also report expert backgrounds, instructions, and any counterbalancing. Even a small add-on study could clarify auditability.

11. Uber Tree coverage and the five “gap” areas
- Section 5.3 lists five inconsistent themes (e.g., “appraisal process,” “compensation/commission”). Can you show: (a) where these gaps appear in TU (node-level coverage statistics per top-level category); (b) a minimal revision to TU addressing them; and (c) re-run of the verification on the same 100 trees with Δ in ¯s? This would concretely demonstrate the governance loop (Section 6.1).

- Appendix A.2/A.4 show garbled prompt text and broken JSON; several references around lines 536–565 are incomplete. For rebuttal, please provide: (a) a clean JSON schema for Feature Trees and the merged tree; (b) exact, validated prompt templates (Section A.2) and example valid trees (A.4); (c) corrected bibliographic entries. A link to the promised code/data (Conclusion) with seeds and scripts to reproduce Table 2 and Table 3 would significantly improve confidence.

- Section 4.1 mentions “1000 real-world Q&A pairs” but not sourcing/anonymization. Please describe provenance, de-identification, licensing, and any ethics/IRB review per the Code of Ethics. If the Q&A include customer interactions, clarify consent and privacy safeguards.

- The “Resources” field (Section 3.1) is central for audit trails. Have you validated link availability and currency (e.g., % of dead/outdated URLs)? A brief audit with statistics and examples would strengthen the claim that outputs are actionable for compliance reviewers.

Summary:
This paper addresses overthinking in large reasoning models by showing that GRPO’s group-relative advantage turns length-penalized but correct rollouts into negative advantages, which misguides learning (Section 3; Figure 1; Table 3). The authors propose Decoupled Reward Policy Optimization (DRPO), which decouples signals for correct and incorrect samples so that length rewards for correct rollouts are normalized only within the positive group (Section 4). Built on a discriminative constrained objective (DisCO; Section 4.1), DRPO integrates an optimized positive-data distribution that maximizes a length reward under a KL regularization and derives a closed-form solution (Eq. 6), enabling efficient on-policy training via importance weighting (Eq. 7). The formulation is general and can incorporate other rewards on positive data beyond length (Section 4.2). Experiments on math reasoning benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH-500, OlympiadBench, AIME) and models of 1.5B/7B/8B parameters show substantial length reductions with minimal accuracy loss, consistently outperforming six efficient-reasoning baselines in performance–efficiency trade-offs (Figure 3; Figure 4; Table 1), with training dynamics illustrating controllable length via λ (Figure 2). Additional studies include generalization to logic puzzles (Appendix A.4; Figure 5), ablations on length reward shapes (Appendix A.5; Figure 6), robustness with pass@16 (Figure 7), and qualitative cases showing markedly shorter, less redundant reasoning paths (Figures 8–10).

Strengths:
1. Clear, convincing diagnosis of GRPO’s failure under composite rewards. Section 3 shows that adding length penalties can flip advantages of correct-but-long rollouts to negative, misguiding learning; this is crisply illustrated in Figure 1 and systematically across diverse reward designs in Appendix A.3 (Table 3). The analysis generalizes beyond GRPO to other REINFORCE-style estimators that couple positives and negatives.

2. Conceptually simple but original decoupling principle. DRPO normalizes length rewards only within the positive group, ensuring verbose correct rollouts receive reduced but never negative signals (Section 4; lines 069–072). This directly removes the identified optimization barrier without introducing heavy machinery.

3. Strong theoretical grounding with a tractable, closed-form construction. The positive-sample distribution P∗ that maximizes the length reward under a KL regularizer is derived in closed form (Eq. (6); proof in Appendix A.1, Eqns. (11)–(12)). This yields a practical weighting scheme for positives computable from on-policy data (Eq. (7)).

4. Principled integration into a discriminative RL objective. Building on DisCO (Section 4.1; Eq. (3)), DRPO cleanly integrates P∗ into a discriminative max–min style objective (Eq. (7)), combining positive-only, length-weighted likelihood maximization with a log-sum-exp over negatives—well-aligned with classical discriminative learning.

5. Stable, implementable training recipe. The method includes a trust-region style KL constraint with a practical penalty relaxation and an explicit algorithm (Algorithm 1), making adoption straightforward. The scoring function sθ and KL estimator are specified in detail.

6. Consistent, state-of-the-art accuracy–efficiency trade-offs across scales. DRPO dominates baselines on 1.5B/7B/8B models in Figure 3, e.g., 7B: reducing average length from 3053 to 1502 (≈51%) with only 2.6% pass@1 loss. DRPO achieves positive AES while baselines are largely negative (Table 1; detailed per-dataset AES in Appendix A.6, Tables 4–6).

7. Controllable efficiency via a single knob. Training dynamics (Figure 2) show λ smoothly trades off length and accuracy: smaller λ dramatically shortens generations (e.g., >50% reduction at λ=0.1) with marginal training-time performance impact, offering practitioners fine-grained control.

8. Difficulty-aware evaluation clarifies where efficiency gains are “free.” Figure 4 decomposes results by benchmark difficulty, showing very large gains with negligible loss on easy tasks (GSM8K: 1.5B, 77.2% length reduction with −1.1% accuracy; 7B, 73.1% with −0.6%), and sensible trends as difficulty increases.

9. Generalization beyond math reasoning. DRPO’s decoupling benefits transfer to logic puzzles (Appendix A.4; Figure 5), achieving a 33.2% length reduction with no accuracy drop (0.972→0.974), indicating the principle is task-agnostic.

10. Robustness across metrics and reward shapes. DRPO maintains superior trade-offs under pass@16 (Figure 7) and works well with multiple length reward forms (linear/concave/cosine in Appendix A.5; Figure 6), with linear rewards offering the broadest operating range.

11. High-quality diagnostic tooling for the community. The paper catalogs prevalent length-reward designs (Appendix A.2/A.3; Table 2) and explicitly demonstrates their failure modes under group-relative advantages (Table 3), providing actionable insight for practitioners debugging overthinking.

12. Persuasive qualitative evidence of reduced redundancy. Case studies (Figures 8–10) show markedly shorter chains with fewer reflection tokens and repeated answers, aligning human-interpretable reasoning behavior with the quantitative gains.

13. Reproducibility and experimental transparency. Training settings, hyperparameter sweeps, generation budgets, and evaluation protocols are detailed (Section 5; Appendix A.2), and a Reproducibility Statement notes code availability in the supplementary materials.

Weaknesses:
1. Limited novelty relative to existing discriminative RL formulations
- Evidence: The closed-form solution for P∗ (Appendix A.1; Eq. (11)–(12)) is a standard exponential tilting under a KL regularizer, closely paralleling DPO-style derivations (Rafailov et al., 2023) and f-divergence preference optimization (Go et al., 2023). The overall objective extends DisCO (Section 4.1; Eq. (3)) by reweighting positives with exp(rl/λ) normalized within positives (Section 4.2; Eq. (7)).
- Why it matters: The key mechanistic novelty is the decoupling/normalization within the positive set, which could be perceived as a targeted design choice atop known discriminative machinery.
- Actionable: (a) Provide a head-to-head comparison to a simple “positive-only normalization” baseline without the KL-derived P∗ to isolate gains from the exponential reweighting vs. decoupling itself. (b) Clarify theoretical distinctions vs. DisCO/DPO/FDPO, e.g., show that the DRPO gradient cannot be obtained by a straightforward reparameterization of those objectives.

2. No formal guarantees on accuracy preservation or “never-negative” learning signals
- Evidence: The paper argues DRPO “never pushes [correct rollouts] into negative territory” (Section 4, lines 069–072), but offers no formal bound relating λ, the positive/negative class separation, and accuracy retention.
- Why it matters: The central claim is preserving performance while shortening reasoning (Figures 2–4; Table 1). Formal guarantees (even in simplified settings) would strengthen confidence beyond empirical evidence.
- Actionable: Provide propositions bounding the sign and magnitude of positive-sample learning signals under Eq. (7), and, if possible, a toy analysis (bandit or linearized model) showing conditions under which accuracy cannot decrease as λ shrinks within a range.

3. Baseline comparability and tuning may bias conclusions
- Evidence: Some baselines are evaluated using authors’ released models rather than fully controlled retraining (Section 5, Baselines). For trained baselines, hyperparameter sweeps are narrow (e.g., α ∈ {0.05, 0.1, 0.2} for RLOO-LP; β ∈ {1e−9, 1e−8, 1e−7} for ALP; w ∈ {0.01, 0.1, 1} for HAPO), potentially underexploring accuracy–efficiency trade-offs (Figure 3; Table 1).
- Why it matters: AES is sensitive to the accuracy drop (Table 1; Appendix A.6), and stronger tuning could change rankings.
- Actionable: (a) Retrain all baselines under the same data, steps, generation budget, and decoding (Section 5, Training Details). (b) Expand sweeps (including α/β/w beyond the reported sets) and report best-of-sweep with error bars over multiple seeds (Appendix A.6 currently lacks variance).

4. Compute/latency benefits not quantified
- Evidence: Results emphasize token-length reductions (Figures 2–4; Table 1) but omit wall-clock time, throughput, or energy/FLOPs gains.
- Why it matters: The practical motivation is reducing inference cost and latency (Introduction; lines 044–053).
- Actionable: Report end-to-end latency and throughput gains vs. reference (squares in Figure 3), including variance across prompts and hardware, and normalize by system-level overheads (e.g., verifier calls).

5. Sensitivity to positive-rate sparsity and weight variance unaddressed
- Evidence: DRPO relies on positive-only reweighting ω(o|q) with per-question normalization (Section 4.2; Eq. (7); Algorithm 1). Early in training or on harder datasets (Figure 4, right panels), positives can be rare.
- Why it matters: Rare positives can cause high-variance gradients or degenerate normalization.
- Actionable: (a) Plot positive fraction over steps and stability metrics. (b) Add safeguards (e.g., ω clipping, moving-average denominators, or mixing λ=+∞ updates when |S+q| is small). (c) Ablate these stabilizers to quantify impact.

6. Global λ is coarse; difficulty-aware control left to future work
- Evidence: Figure 4 shows increasing performance cost on harder datasets; the paper itself notes adapting λ by difficulty as future work (lines 509–513).
- Why it matters: A single λ trades off aggressively across tasks of varying difficulty, leaving performance on hard sets exposed.
- Actionable: Implement and evaluate question-conditioned λ (e.g., based on pass rate, verifier confidence, or stepwise perplexity), and show that it preserves the strong GSM8K gains while mitigating drops on OlympiadBench/AIME.

7. Choice and calibration of the length scale C are not analyzed
- Evidence: Length reward uses C as maximum response length (Section 4.2), but sensitivity to C is not reported.
- Why it matters: Miscalibrated C can saturate weights or distort incentives across datasets and models.
- Actionable: Provide sensitivity plots over C (per dataset/model), or learn C adaptively (e.g., from running quantiles of |o|).

8. Limited ablations on DRPO’s own regularizers and scoring temperature
- Evidence: Key training hyperparameters (δ, β0, τ in Algorithm 1/Section 4.2) are fixed without sensitivity studies.
- Why it matters: The KL constraint (δ) and τ in the log-sum-exp for negatives control stability and hardness emphasis.
- Actionable: Ablate δ, β0, and τ to show robustness of the trade-off curves (Figure 3) and AES (Table 1).

9. Generalization beyond math is thin
- Evidence: Only one non-math task is included (logic puzzles; Appendix A.4; Figure 5).
- Why it matters: The claim of a general mechanism for efficient reasoning would be stronger with diverse domains.
- Actionable: Evaluate at least one additional domain (e.g., scientific QA or program synthesis) under the same training/eval protocol to test transferability of the decoupled positive weighting.

10. Lack of a GRPO-style decoupling baseline to isolate the “group-advantage” factor
- Evidence: The paper diagnoses GRPO’s group-relative advantage as the root cause (Section 3; Figure 1; Table 3) but does not show a GRPO variant with positive-only normalization.
- Why it matters: It is unclear how much of DRPO’s gain stems from discriminative training vs. decoupling itself.
- Actionable: Add a “GRPO-PosNorm” baseline that computes advantages normalized within positives, holding other GRPO elements fixed, to attribute gains more precisely.

11. Statistical reporting is minimal
- Evidence: Figures 2–4 and Table 1 present point estimates without confidence intervals; pass@1 is averaged over 16 completions (Section 5, Evaluation) but seed variability is not shown.
- Why it matters: Differences between methods can be within noise for some settings, especially averaged across datasets (Figure 3).
- Actionable: Report mean±std over multiple seeds for key settings and per-dataset confidence intervals, and include significance tests where appropriate.

12. Behavioral analysis is anecdotal
- Evidence: Case studies (Figures 8–10) qualitatively show fewer reflections and repeated answers.
- Why it matters: Quantitative behavioral metrics would generalize the claim that DRPO reduces redundant back-and-forth.
- Actionable: Track reflection-token rates, repetition counts, and premature-final-answer rates across benchmarks, correlating them with accuracy and length to substantiate behavioral mechanisms beyond examples.

Suggestions/Questions:
1. Clarify novelty relative to DisCO/DPO/FDPO
- Section 4.2 derives P∗ via an exponential tilting under a KL regularizer (Eq. 5–6), akin to DPO-style results (Appendix A.1, Eq. 11–12). Please provide a formal comparison: can DRPO’s gradient (Eq. 7; Algorithm 1, step 9) be reduced to a reparameterization of DisCO/DPO under some choice of rewards, or is it genuinely distinct? A short derivation showing why DisCO with heuristic positive-only normalization cannot recover DRPO’s update would sharpen the conceptual contribution.

2. Formalize the “never-negative” learning signal claim
- The paper states DRPO “never pushes [positive rollouts] into negative territory” (Section 4; lines 069–072), since positives are normalized within S+q. Can you state and prove a proposition that the per-positive gradient contribution is always non-negative under Eq. 7 (accounting for the negative log-sum-exp term over S−q and the KL penalty)? A toy analysis (e.g., linearized model) bounding the net positive term would substantiate the central claim.

3. Robustness when S+q is small or empty
- Algorithm 1 (step 6–9) normalizes by ∑o∈S+q exp(rl/λ). What is the fallback when S+q=∅ or very small (early training or on AIME/OlympiadBench; Figure 4 right panels)? Do you (a) skip the positive term, (b) back off to λ=+∞ (DisCO) for that question, or (c) use a moving-average denominator? Please describe safeguards and their empirical impact.

4. Weight variance and stability of ω(o|q)
- In Eq. 7/Algorithm 1, ω(o|q) ∝ exp(rl/λ) within S+q. Can you report histograms of ω and the positive fraction over steps, to assess variance and stability on hard sets? Were any weight clipping or temperature adjustments applied in practice? This would help interpret convergence behavior in Figure 2.

5. Sensitivity to the length scale C
- Section 4.2 sets rl(o)=1−|o|/C, with C the “maximum response length.” Is C fixed (e.g., the 8k generation budget in Section 5) or question/model-specific? Please provide sensitivity curves for C (per-dataset and model) and discuss how to set/learn C (e.g., running quantiles of |o|) to avoid reward saturation or miscalibration.

6. Difficulty-aware λ
- Figure 4 shows large “free” gains on GSM8K but increasing costs on OlympiadBench/AIME. Since lines 509–513 suggest adapting λ by difficulty, could you add a simple question-conditioned λ (e.g., based on pass rate or verifier confidence) and report its effect on the hard sets, holding easy-set gains?

7. Baseline comparability and tuning scope
- Section 5 (Baselines) mixes retrained models and released checkpoints (L1-MAX, LASER-D, SB). Summary:
The paper proposes LOTION, a principled loss-smoothing framework for quantization-aware optimization that replaces the discontinuous quantized loss with its expectation under unbiased randomized rounding noise, yielding an almost-everywhere differentiable objective with preserved global minima (Section 3; Lemma 2). For neural networks, the authors derive a second-order approximation showing LOTION induces a curvature-aware ℓ2-style regularizer via the (diagonal) Gauss–Newton term weighted by the rounding noise variance (Section 3.3, Equation 3), and they analyze the quadratic case to relate randomized-rounding training to unbiased gradient estimation (Section 3.2; Lemma 3). The method targets fine-grained shared-scale quantization schemes (Section 2.1) and is optimizer-agnostic; in large models they estimate curvature using the empirical Fisher as in Adam (Section 4.3). Empirically, LOTION improves quantized performance over STE-based QAT and PTQ on synthetic linear regression and linear networks (Figures 2–3, 7–8). On 150M- and 300M-parameter language models trained on C4, LOTION achieves lower INT4/INT8/FP4 validation cross-entropy than baselines, with gaps most pronounced at lower precision (Figures 1, 4–5; Tables 1–2).

Strengths:
1. Principled surrogate with preserved optima. The paper replaces the discontinuous quantized objective with the expected loss under unbiased randomized rounding, proving continuity and that “global minima match the global minima of the quantized loss function” (Section 3.1; Lemma 1–2; Appendix A.2). This addresses a core weakness of STE-based QAT with formal guarantees rather than heuristic gradients.

2. Clear, general definition of randomized rounding. Definition 1 (Section 3.1) specifies RR as a mapping into distributions over the quantization lattice Q with W2-continuity and a fixed-point property on quantized points. This formalization is precise and reusable across rounding schemes.

3. Transparent second-order interpretation. The quadratic warm-up and neural-network extension yield a closed-form, curvature-aware ℓ2-style ridge regularizer weighted by the rounding-noise covariance (Section 3.2–3.3). In particular, σi2 = sB(i)2 Δi(1−Δi) and the Gauss–Newton diagonal gii(w) produce the regularizer in Equation 3, making explicit how quantization interacts with curvature and why the method stabilizes training.

4. Insightful analysis of QAT’s limits. For quadratic losses, RAT (random-rounding in the forward pass) provides an unbiased estimator of the original gradient (Lemma 3, Section 3.2), implying QAT/RAT offer at best PTQ-like behavior in this regime, while LOTION improves via loss smoothing. This clarifies when and why smoothing outperforms gradient surrogates.

5. Alignment with practical quantization. The method directly targets widely used fine-grained shared-scale schemes with absmax scaling (Section 2.1), and the noise model and covariance derivation follow from this design. The moving quantization lattice during training is explicitly acknowledged and leveraged in the analysis.

6. Optimizer-agnostic with existing curvature proxies. The Gauss–Newton diagonal can be estimated from quantities already tracked by common optimizers (e.g., empirical Fisher via gradient squares as in Adam), enabling straightforward integration (Section 3.3, “Interpretation and optimization”).

7. Strong synthetic evidence with spectrum-aware setups. The linear regression toy problem uses inputs with a power-law Hessian spectrum mimicking modern nets (Section 4.1), and LOTION substantially beats QAT/PTQ on INT4 (Figure 2; Figure 7). The two-layer linear network study connects improvements to model scaling and shows LOTION maintains an edge as capacity grows (Figure 3; Figure 8).

8. LLM-scale validation at multiple precisions. On 150M and 300M models trained on C4, LOTION consistently lowers quantized validation cross-entropy versus QAT/PTQ at INT4/INT8 (Figures 1, 4; Tables 1–2). Representative gains: 150M INT4, LOTION RTN 3.276 vs QAT RTN 3.315 and PTQ RTN 3.864 (Table 1); 300M INT4, LOTION RTN 3.1031 vs QAT RTN 3.223 (Table 2). The advantage persists even with extended training budgets (Figure 10).

9. Generalization to non-uniform formats. Despite reduced quantization error in FP4, LOTION still improves over QAT/PTQ (Figure 5), demonstrating applicability beyond uniform INT and to modern formats used in practice.

10. Consistent evaluation protocol across rounding rules. The experiments report results under both round-to-nearest and randomized rounding at evaluation and plot the best variant for each method (e.g., Figure 1; Figure 2; Tables 1–2). This avoids single-policy cherry-picking and strengthens claims of robustness.

11. Practicality and low overhead. All computations run in FP32 with simulated quantization; the per-parameter variance Var[εi] = sB2 Δi(1−Δi) is computed once from existing scaling factors and distances to bin boundaries and can be parallelized at low cost (Section 4).

12. Clear exposition with proofs and helpful visuals. The core claims are supported by concise proofs (Appendix A.2 for Lemmas 1–3). The conceptual picture of loss smoothing vs quantized loss is well illustrated (Appendix Figure 6), and hyperparameters are tabulated (Appendix A.5), aiding reproducibility.

13. Well-situated within prior art with concrete contrasts. Related work draws sharp distinctions from STE/QAT, noise-proxy methods like NIPQ, and curvature-aware PTQ (Section 1.1). The paper explicitly addresses limitations of proxy noise (“does not capture its full structure”) and explains how LOTION avoids extra learned parameters while adding guarantees.

14. Scalability of insights from theory to practice. The shift from exact second-order analysis to a Gauss–Newton diagonal and empirical Fisher in large models (Sections 3.3, 4.3) is justified and empirically validated at 150M/300M scales, showing the theoretical framing meaningfully guides practical design.

Weaknesses:
1. “Parameter-free” claim vs. required tuning at scale
- Weakness: The method is positioned as “fully principled, parameter-free” (lines 047–051), but large-model training introduces a regularization coefficient λ for the Gauss–Newton diagonal (Section 4.3: “we weight the regularization term by a hyperparameter, λ”). This weakens the core positioning and blurs the end-to-end guarantee when the curvature term is only an approximation.
- Actionable: (a) Provide a principled calibration of λ from first principles, e.g., tying λ to the expected variance sB2 Δi(1−Δi), learning rate, or batch size; (b) add sensitivity curves for λ on the 150M/300M LMs; (c) report whether the same λ transfers across precisions (INT4/INT8/FP4) and scales.

2. Assumptions behind smoothing guarantees with moving scales are underdeveloped
- Weakness: Scales sB depend on w and move the quantization lattice (Section 2.1: “scale parameters {sB} depend on wi, so the quantization lattice moves as optimization proceeds”). Lemma 1–2 (Section 3.1; Appendix A.2) require continuity of RR(w) in W2, but the paper does not prove this property for the specific “absmax, shared-scale” rule when sB(w) changes discontinuously (e.g., when the block abs-max changes).
- Actionable: (a) Prove W2-continuity (or quantify violations) for RR under absmax scaling with blockwise maxima; (b) characterize conditions on data/weights ensuring rare rescaling events; (c) include a stress test where heavy-tailed weights cause frequent scale changes, measuring whether the claimed smoothness still holds.

3. Smoothed-vs-quantized objective gap lacks bounds away from minima
- Weakness: While Lemma 2 ensures the global minima are preserved, there is no bound on the suboptimality gap between minimizers of Esmooth and L(cast(w)) away from minima, nor on the error from the second-order truncation and Gauss–Newton substitution (Section 3.3; “Equation 3”).
- Actionable: (a) Provide a local third-order remainder bound for Equation 3; (b) bound the bias between smoothed and quantized objectives as a function of curvature and Var[ε]; (c) empirically plot both objectives during training (not just the final quantized loss), correlating gaps with curvature estimates.

4. Limited baseline coverage for QAT and noise-based methods
- Weakness: Experiments compare to a basic STE QAT and PTQ, but omit strong QAT baselines that specifically address instability (e.g., LSQ, Esser et al., 2020; OCS/MAD, Sakr et al., 2022; PROFIT, Park & Yoo, 2020) and noise-annealing STE variants (Spallanzani et al., 2022) discussed in Section 1.1. This leaves open whether LOTION outperforms the best current QAT practices.
- Actionable: Add at least LSQ and OCS/MAD as baselines on synthetic and one LLM setting; include a noise-injection training baseline (Défossez et al., 2022) to isolate the benefit of loss-level smoothing versus forward-noise proxies.

5. Evaluation protocol can inflate gains by picking the best rounding per method
- Weakness: Several plots select “the variant that yields the lowest validation loss” among RTN and RR for each method (Figure 1; Figure 2 caption, Figure 7). In deployment, a single rounding rule is used.
- Actionable: (a) Report side-by-side results under a fixed, deployment-realistic rounding (e.g., RTN for INT/FP formats) without best-of-two selection; (b) add a table of relative deltas under the same rounding for all methods (as in Tables 1–2, which help but still mix RR/RTN rows).

6. Statistical robustness and variance are missing
- Weakness: All curves appear single-seed with no error bars or confidence intervals (Figures 1–5, 9–12). Given known instability at 4-bit, conclusions need variability reporting.
- Actionable: Run ≥3 seeds for each setting; report mean±std of final quantized loss (Tables 1–2) and confidence bands on curves; quantify effect sizes.

7. Overhead and practicality are not measured
- Weakness: The method requires per-parameter Δi and Var[εi] and curvature tracking (Section 4: “can be done in parallel at very low cost”), yet no wall-clock, memory, or throughput measurements are reported relative to QAT/PTQ.
- Actionable: Provide training-time overhead (step time, memory) and inference-time impact (no change expected, but confirm) on 150M/300M runs; include FLOP estimates for the curvature proxy vs. baseline Adam.

8. Scope limited to weight-only quantization
- Weakness: The paper targets weight-only quantization; activation and KV-cache quantization are not addressed (Section 5 lists this as future work). The primary inference bottleneck often includes activations and KV cache on LLM decoding.
- Actionable: Add a small-scale activation-quantization study (INT8/FP8 activations) on the 150M model using the same smoothing framework; report whether the curvature-aware term remains effective and how Var[ε] is defined for activations.

9. Gap between “fine-grained shared-scale” framing and per-tensor practice in experiments
- Weakness: Section 2.1 emphasizes blockwise (fine-grained) scales, but Section 4 states “we scale the entire tensor into the dynamic range of the format,” i.e., per-tensor scaling in practice. This can misrepresent the intended deployment setting and affect curvature/noise statistics.
- Actionable: Evaluate per-channel/per-group scaling (typical for weight-only LLM quantization) and vary block size B; report how Equation 3’s regularizer and performance change with block granularity.

10. Generalization beyond C4 cross-entropy is untested
- Weakness: Large-model results use C4 validation cross-entropy only (Figures 1, 4–5; Tables 1–2), which may not capture downstream resilience to quantization.
- Actionable: Add lightweight, widely used zero-shot evaluations for small models (e.g., a subset of language modeling benchmarks) or at least hold-out corpora distinct from C4 to demonstrate robustness of the quantized models.

11. Missing ablations on curvature estimator choices
- Weakness: Section 3.3 suggests two options (extra backprop with sampled labels as in Sophia vs. empirical Fisher via gradient squares), but experiments fix the empirical Fisher and do not explore estimator quality vs. cost.
- Actionable: Compare (i) empirical Fisher, (ii) Sophia-style diagonal GN, and (iii) a cheaper moving-average proxy on the 150M model; quantify accuracy/overhead trade-offs and whether λ needs retuning across estimators.

12. Theoretical overstatement on convergence
- Weakness: Early claims imply “standard optimizers are guaranteed to converge to a local minimum” on the smoothed loss (lines 052–053), but the objective remains nonconvex and only “almost everywhere” differentiable; Davis et al. (2018) provide convergence of subgradient methods to stationary points, not local minima.
- Actionable: Rephrase claims to stationary-point convergence and, if possible, cite the precise conditions under which the chosen optimizer (e.g., Adam-like) converges for the smoothed objective.

Suggestions/Questions:
1. “Parameter-free” vs λ in large models
- Section 4.3 introduces a scalar λ to weight the Gauss–Newton regularizer, while the intro (lines 047–051) positions LOTION as parameter-free. Please clarify:
  a) How λ is chosen in practice (search ranges in Appendix A.5 show {3000,10000,30000,100000}); 
  b) Whether a principled scaling (e.g., with Var[ε], batch size, or step size) can eliminate tuning;
  c) How sensitive 150M/300M results (Figures 1, 4–5; Tables 1–2) are to λ; include sensitivity curves and whether one λ transfers across INT4/INT8/FP4 and across model sizes.

2. Continuity of RR under moving scales
- Section 2.1 notes sB depends on w (absmax), so the quantization lattice moves as optimization proceeds. Lemma 1 requires W2-continuity of RR(w) (Section 3.1; Appendix A.2). Can you prove or empirically validate W2-continuity (or quantify violations) for RR with absmax shared scales, where scale updates occur at blockwise max changes? A stress test with heavy-tailed weights triggering frequent rescalings would help.

3. Objective gap and approximation error
- Section 3.3 derives Equation 3 via a second-order expansion with a Gauss–Newton substitution. Can you provide:
  a) A local remainder bound for the Taylor truncation;
  b) A bound (or characterization) of the bias between Esmooth and L(cast(w)) away from minima as a function of curvature and Var[ε] = sB(i)2Δi(1−Δi);
  c) Empirical tracking of Esmooth (your working objective) vs the true quantized loss during training on the 150M model.

4. Curvature estimator choices
- Section 3.3 mentions two options (Sophia-style extra pass vs empirical Fisher/Adam squares), and Section 4.3 states you use the empirical Fisher without differentiating through it. Please add an ablation on the 150M setting comparing:
  i) empirical Fisher;
  ii) Sophia-style diagonal Gauss–Newton;
  iii) a cheaper moving-average proxy.
Report accuracy, overhead, and whether λ needs retuning across estimators.

5. Baseline coverage for strong QAT variants
- Related work (Section 1.1) cites LSQ (Esser et al., 2020) and OCS/MAD (Sakr et al., 2022) designed to stabilize low-bit QAT. Adding at least LSQ and OCS/MAD on the linear regression toy (Figure 2) and one LLM setting (e.g., 150M INT4 in Figure 9/Table 1) would clarify whether LOTION still leads against best-practice QAT.

6. Noise-based training baselines
- Since Section 1.1 contrasts LOTION with noise-injection proxies (e.g., Défossez et al., 2022) and annealing (Spallanzani et al., 2022), please include a “pseudo quantization noise” baseline on 150M INT4 and the linear regression toy. This would isolate the benefit of loss-level smoothing vs forward noise proxies.

7. Evaluation under a single deployment rounding
- Several figures choose, per method, the best between RTN and RR at evaluation (e.g., Figure 1; Figure 2 caption; Figure 7). For deployment realism, please report side-by-side results when all methods are evaluated with the same deterministic rounding (e.g., RTN for INT/FP formats). Tables 1–2 partially help; a unified “same-rounding” table for 150M/300M INT4/INT8/FP4 would remove ambiguity.

8. Statistical robustness
- Figures 1, 4–5, 9–12 appear single-seed. Can you add ≥3 seeds with mean±std for the final quantized validation loss (Tables 1–2) and bands on the curves for at least the 150M INT4/FP4 plots (Figure 9; Figure 12)? Low-bit training is known to be volatile; variance would strengthen claims.

9. Practical overhead
- Section 4 claims low overhead to compute Var[εi] and apply Equation 3. Please quantify training-time step latency, memory footprint, and throughput vs QAT/PTQ for the 150M and 300M runs, and specify how often Δi and sB are recomputed (every step? every N steps?). A small table next to Figure 4 would be helpful.

10. Reconciling “fine-grained shared-scale” with per-tensor scaling
- Section 2.1 emphasizes fine-grained shared-scale blocks, but Section 4 states “we scale the entire tensor” for experiments. Please clarify the actual scaling granularity used for LLM runs and how Equation 3’s regularizer and performance change with block size (per-tensor vs per-channel/group). An ablation on block size for the 150M INT4 case would be informative.

11. Activation quantization
- Section 5 lists activation quantization as future work. Given the generality of Equation 3, could you provide a small-scale 150M study with INT8 or FP8 activations using the same smoothing (defining Δi and Var[ε] for activations), even if only for a few layers, to demonstrate feasibility?

12. Convergence claim precision
- Lines 052–053 state “any standard first- or second-order optimizer can be used with its usual convergence guarantees (in particular, non-smooth convergence guarantees (Davis et al., 2018)).” Please clarify the exact notion (e.g., convergence to a Clarke stationary point) and assumptions that your smoothed objective satisfies, and whether these guarantees extend to Adam-like methods actually used in Section 4.3.

13. RAT baseline at 300M and INT2 probing
- RAT is included at 150M (Figure 9; Table 1) but not at 300M (Figure 11; Table 2). Please add RAT at 300M to complete the forward-noise comparison. Also, since instability is most acute at 2–4 bits (Section 1.1), a small INT2 experiment on the toy setting would clarify LOTION’s regime of benefit.

14. RR definition and unbiasedness with moving scales
- Appendix A.2.4 gives a scalar RR scheme and Section 3.2 uses E[ε]=0. With sB(w) changing over time, is E[ε|w] still 0 at each step under your implementation? Please state the conditioning explicitly and confirm that unbiasedness holds per-step with shared scales across coordinates.

15. Correlation of curvature and gains
- Equation 3 predicts larger regularization in sharp directions. Can you empirically correlate per-layer (or per-parameter-group) Gauss–Newton diagonals with realized quantized loss improvements under LOTION vs QAT/PTQ on the 150M model? A scatter or rank correlation would substantiate the curvature-aware interpretation.
