Summary:
The paper proposes DLER, a reinforcement learning recipe for efficient reasoning that revisits the simplest length penalty—truncation—and shows that prior accuracy loss stems from suboptimal optimization rather than the penalty itself. The method addresses three issues identified under truncation—biased advantage estimates with GRPO, entropy collapse from clipping, and sparse/imbalanced rewards—by combining batch-wise reward normalization (Sec. 3.1, Eq. 3), a higher asymmetric clipping threshold to keep gradients on exploratory tokens (Sec. 3.2; Fig. 2, Fig. 4b), and dynamic sampling to exclude all‑0/all‑1 reward prompts (Sec. 3.3; Fig. 3). The resulting DLER models achieve state-of-the-art accuracy–length trade-offs on DeepSeek-R1-1.5B/7B, reducing average tokens by 69–80% while matching or improving accuracy across MATH, AIME-24, AMC, Minerva, and Olympiad (Sec. 4.2; Table 1; Fig. 7, Fig. 10). The paper further introduces DA-DLER, which adaptively tightens truncation for easy questions to gain additional length reductions without hurting accuracy (Sec. 3.5; Table 1). DLER also enables superior test-time scaling via parallel thinking, delivering higher Pass@K at much lower latency than baselines (Sec. 4.4; Fig. 1b; Fig. 5; Fig. 8; Table 4). Finally, an update-selective weight merging strategy restores baseline accuracy when training data are limited while retaining large token savings (Sec. 4.6; Table 2).

Strengths:
1. Clear diagnosis of why truncation underperforms in prior RL setups, backed by concrete measurements and analysis. Sec. 3.1 quantifies increased variance from aggressive truncation and provides a bias derivation for GRPO-style advantage estimators (Appendix B), then validates the fix via batch-wise normalization (Eq. 3) with improved training dynamics (Fig. 9).

2. Insightful token-level investigation of entropy collapse tied to clipping. Sec. 3.2 shows clipped tokens are disproportionately “transitional” and high-entropy (Fig. 2a–b) and demonstrates that asymmetric higher clipping selectively restores gradients on exploratory tokens and reverses entropy collapse (Fig. 4a→4b), a concrete and actionable optimization knob.

3. Well-motivated remedy for sparse/imbalanced rewards that emerges specifically under truncation. Sec. 3.3 quantifies the prevalence of all‑0/all‑1 prompts early in training (Fig. 3) and shows dynamic sampling curbs this bias and helps the model utilize the length budget effectively (Fig. 4c).

4. A simple, coherent recipe (DLER) that combines the above ingredients and demonstrably changes the training regime, evidenced by distinct entropy and length trajectories (Sec. 3.4; Fig. 4c) and by accuracy recovery versus plain batch-wise normalization (Appendix C; Fig. 10).

5. Strong, consistent state-of-the-art accuracy–length trade-offs across datasets and scales. Table 1 shows −69% to −80% average token reductions with equal or improved accuracy on MATH, AIME‑24, AMC, Minerva, and Olympiad for both 1.5B and 7B. These are large, practically meaningful gains relative to strong baselines (e.g., Laser-DE, AdaptThink, LCR1, R1-VeriThinker).

6. Clear evidence that optimization, not penalty sophistication, determines the frontier. Sec. 4.5 (Fig. 6) shows DLER dominates the Pareto frontier across multiple length penalties (Truncation, Cosine, L1‑Max, Laser), with penalties moving along the frontier rather than extending it; truncation is competitive while being compute-efficient because rollouts stop at cutoff.

7. Practical test-time scaling benefits quantified with wall-clock latency. Sec. 4.4 and Fig. 1b/Table 4 report 4× faster single-response latency and substantially higher Pass@K at the same or less time (e.g., DLER‑7B reaches 83.33% in 85.43s with 256 rollouts vs. 221.22s for DeepSeek‑7B with 16 rollouts). Sec. 4.3 (Fig. 5, Fig. 11) further shows robustness across length cutoffs and K.

8. Difficulty-aware extension is simple and effective. Sec. 3.5 and Table 1 show DA‑DLER yields an additional 11–15% length reduction on top of DLER while preserving accuracy, with an easily implementable rule using correctness ratios and tiered cutoffs.

9. Practical pathway when high-quality proprietary data are unavailable. Sec. 4.6 proposes update-selective merging (top 25% deltas, scaled 0.7) that restores baseline accuracy on harder sets (AIME‑24, MATH) while keeping large token savings (−46%) (Table 2), addressing a common deployment constraint.

10. Mechanistic analyses support claims beyond headline metrics. Appendix G.1 (Fig. 12) shows DLER slightly increases high-entropy token mass versus Laser-DE’s contraction, aligning with exploration claims, while Appendix G.2 (Table 5) shows large reductions in reasoning steps and transition keywords—especially on incorrect cases—consistent with mitigating overthinking.

11. Reproducibility and comparability are facilitated by explicit configurations and consistent evaluation. Sec. 4.1 details datasets, generation settings (temperature/top‑p/max length), rollouts, and batch sizes; Appendix D (Table 3) lists veRL hyperparameters, enabling faithful replication of the training setup.

12. Results are communicated with informative training-dynamics figures that tie diagnosis to outcomes. The sequence from variance/bias (Sec. 3.1), entropy behavior (Sec. 3.2), reward sparsity (Sec. 3.3), to the integrated DLER trajectory (Sec. 3.4; Fig. 4, Fig. 10) provides unusually transparent empirical evidence for each design choice.

Weaknesses:
1. Incremental algorithmic novelty; reliance on known ingredients without rigorous disentanglement of what is new.
   - The three key components—batch-wise normalization (Sec. 3.1; Eq. 3), higher/asymmetric clipping (Sec. 3.2; Fig. 4a→4b), and dynamic sampling that filters all‑0/all‑1 prompts (Sec. 3.3; Fig. 3)—are all close to existing practices (batch normalization in Reinforce++ (Hu et al., 2025), exploration-preserving PPO variants, and DAPO-style filtering/curriculum (Yu et al., 2025)). The paper’s main novelty is the diagnosis of truncation-induced pathologies and the specific combination.
   - Actionable: (i) Reproduce strong prior recipes (e.g., DAPO/ProRL) with truncation and report matched results to show that DLER’s gains are not solely from adopting these known knobs. (ii) Provide a component-level comparison against the closest prior instantiations (batch-wise norm vs Reinforce++ norm; filtering vs DAPO filter-groups; asymmetric clip vs decoupled-PPO variants) under the same data/compute to establish incremental novelty.

2. Limited domain coverage; all training/evaluation is math-centric.
   - Training uses DeepScaleR-Preview math problems (Sec. 4.1); evaluation spans MATH, AIME‑24, AMC, Minerva, Olympiad (Table 1; largely quantitative/math). Claims about “efficient reasoning” and “test-time scaling” may not transfer to code, symbolic logic, tool-use, or long-form QA.
   - Actionable: Add at least one non-math reasoning domain (e.g., code generation or symbolic reasoning) and one long-context setting to test whether truncation plus DLER maintains accuracy when long chains are necessary.

3. Statistical robustness is not reported.
   - Key results (Table 1; Fig. 5; Fig. 6) are single-run means without confidence intervals or multi-seed variance; some deltas are modest (e.g., AIME-24: 55.2 vs 55.62 for Laser-DE‑7B vs DLER‑7B). Training dynamics (Fig. 4, Fig. 9, Fig. 10) show single trajectories only.
   - Actionable: Report ≥3 seeds for principal tables/figures with mean±std and bootstrap CIs for Pass@K; include seed sensitivity for DA-DLER and for the high-clip threshold.

4. Fairness of comparisons when demonstrating “optimization over penalty design” is not airtight.
   - In Fig. 6, DLER variants dominate the frontier, but comparisons include “Original Laser-DE/D” using publicly released checkpoints versus DLER-Laser retrained with the new recipe. This mixes training pipelines.
   - Actionable: Re-train Laser-DE/D and L1-Max with their original recipes under matched compute and also re-train DLER‑Truncation with the original recipes. A 2×2 comparison (with/without DLER; with/without each penalty) would more cleanly establish causality.

5. DA-DLER hyperparameters and behavior on hard/easy subsets are under-explored.
   - DA-DLER uses a correctness-ratio threshold of 0.5 and two truncation lengths (Sec. 3.5), but no sweeps or difficulty-stratified accuracy are shown. Filtering easy/hard prompts (Sec. 3.3; Fig. 3) plus DA-DLER may bias training toward medium difficulty.
   - Actionable: Provide sensitivity studies over thresholds and tier counts, and report per-difficulty accuracy/length to ensure no regressions on the hard tail.

6. Dynamic sampling may induce distribution shift by discarding extremes.
   - Filtering out all‑0 and all‑1 prompts (Sec. 3.3; Fig. 3) stabilizes training but risks undertraining very hard/easy items and could reduce robustness to extremes at inference.
   - Actionable: Compare filtering vs. reweighting/importance sampling curricula; report evaluation stratified by item difficulty and by required solution length to verify that hard, long-reasoning cases remain accurate.

7. Theoretical analysis of advantage bias is stylized and loosely tied to practice.
   - Appendix B assumes i.i.d. Gaussian rewards and analyzes group-wise normalization bias at the prompt level, while the objective is token-level (Eq. 2). The link between this stylized bias and the observed degradation under truncation remains heuristic.
   - Actionable: Validate the theory with controlled synthetic environments that vary reward variance/shape and measure empirical bias; extend analysis beyond Gaussian assumptions and to token-level credit assignment.

8. Weight-merging section is promising but under-evaluated and narrowly scoped.
   - Only one base (Nemotron‑8B) and one merged configuration (top‑25% deltas, scale 0.7) are shown (Sec. 4.6; Table 2). Naive baselines are mentioned but not quantified; no comparison to standard merging schemes (e.g., TIES-merging with its recommended settings).
   - Actionable: Add sweeps over delta percentiles and scaling; compare against TIES-merging baselines; test merging on R1-7B to demonstrate generality; report trade-offs between recovered accuracy and residual length reduction.

9. Compute and reproducibility details for training are incomplete.
   - While hyperparameters are summarized (Appendix D; Table 3), total training FLOPs/GPU-days and per-step token budgets are not reported; comparisons to released baselines may differ in compute.
   - Actionable: Report training compute for each run and, where possible, normalize comparisons by total sampled tokens or GPU-days to strengthen claims of efficiency.

10. Latency measurements are narrow and lack token-throughput normalization.
   - Test-time scaling is reported on AIME‑24 with one GPU (Sec. 4.4; Fig. 1b; Table 4). Wall-clock latency favors shorter generations by construction; without tokens/sec and memory/KV-cache details, engine-level factors may confound conclusions.
   - Actionable: Add tokens/sec and tokens/J metrics; report memory footprint and KV-cache configs; include latency on at least one additional benchmark to rule out dataset-specific artifacts.

11. Entropy/tokens-as-causal evidence is suggestive but not causal.
   - Sec. 3.2 and Appendix G.1 (Fig. 12) link higher-entropy/clipped “transition” tokens to exploration and length control, but only correlational evidence is provided on AIME-24.
   - Actionable: Perform targeted interventions (e.g., masking or boosting transition-token logits) during inference/training to demonstrate causal effects on length and accuracy; replicate token-entropy analyses on non-math datasets.

Suggestions/Questions:
1. Compute budget and fairness of comparisons
   - Please report total training compute (GPU type/count, hours, tokens sampled) for each run, including DLER, DA-DLER, and the non-DLER baselines you retrain. This will help calibrate the gains shown in Table 1 and Fig. 6. Also clarify whether public baselines (e.g., “Original Laser-DE/D” in Sec. 4.5; Fig. 6) were trained with more/less compute than your DLER variants.

2. Definition of “Pass@1” under multiple samples
   - Sec. 4.1 says “generate 16 samples and report average pass@1 accuracy.” Is pass@1 computed from a single decoded sample per prompt, averaged across multiple stochastic trials, or is it the max over the 16 samples? Please formalize the estimator and provide CIs/SEs.

3. Token counting protocol
   - Table 1 and Fig. 1a show large length reductions. Do token counts include prompt/system tokens, reasoning plus final answer, and tool-calls (if any)? Are tokenizer and special tokens identical across models? Please specify the exact counting method and release code for this.

4. Multi-seed robustness
   - Key results (Table 1; Fig. 5; Fig. 6; Fig. 7–8) appear single-seed. Could you provide mean±std over ≥3 seeds for the main tables/curves and show that conclusions (e.g., DLER frontier dominance in Fig. 6) are statistically stable?

5. Batch-wise normalization details and sensitivity
   - Sec. 3.1/Eq. (3) introduces batch-wise normalization. How sensitive are results to batch size, number of rollouts G, and to mixing heterogeneous difficulties in a batch? Please report an ablation varying batch size and G (keeping total tokens fixed) and include a stability plot akin to Fig. 9.

6. Higher/asymmetric clipping clarification
   - In Sec. 3.2 you decouple upper/lower clip thresholds; Table 3 shows 0.2/0.28. Please state the general rule you use, how you select the upper bound, and provide a sweep to show accuracy/entropy/length trends (e.g., reproducing Fig. 4(b) with several upper thresholds). A short formula for the modified objective would help.

7. Evidence linking clipped tokens to “transition” behavior
   - Fig. 2a shows a word cloud; Fig. 2b shows probability/entropy trends. Could you quantify: fraction of clipped tokens that fall into a predefined transition-lexicon vs. baseline; and the effect on length when masking/boosting these tokens during decoding? This would strengthen the causal link.

8. Dynamic sampling mechanics and coverage
   - Sec. 3.3 discards all‑0/all‑1 prompts and resamples. Please: (a) report the resampling rate over training (fraction of prompts replaced), (b) show how often each training example is used (coverage histogram), and (c) evaluate whether extremes (hard/long or very easy/short) suffer at test-time by reporting accuracy stratified by required gold solution length or by empirical difficulty.

9. Curriculum alternatives to filtering
   - To address concerns that discarding extremes shifts the training distribution, could you compare your dynamic sampling to (i) reweighting losses for all‑0/all‑1 prompts, or (ii) a scheduled mixture that gradually decreases the rejection rate? A brief comparison on AIME‑24/MATH would clarify whether filtering is essential.

10. DA-DLER specifics and sensitivity
   - Sec. 3.5 uses a 0.5 correctness-ratio threshold and two target lengths (2000/4000). Please share: (a) a sweep over thresholds and number of tiers, (b) stability to noisy correctness estimates (e.g., using EMA across steps), and (c) per-difficulty accuracy/length to verify no regressions on hard-tail questions.

11. Re-training baselines under native vs DLER recipes
   - Fig. 6 argues the frontier is set by DLER regardless of penalty. To make this airtight, could you run a 2×2 comparison: each penalty with (i) its native training recipe and (ii) your DLER recipe, under matched compute, then plot all four points per penalty on the same charts?

12. Generalization beyond math
   - All experiments are on math-style reasoning (Sec. 4.2). Do the findings transfer to at least one non-math task (e.g., code generation, formal logic) or to long-context QA where long traces are sometimes necessary? A small-scale experiment would substantially broaden the claim.

13. Decontamination / overlap checks
   - Since you train on DeepScaleR-Preview (Sec. 4.1) and test on MATH/AIME/AMC/Minerva/Olympiad, can you provide overlap screening (hash-based or fuzzy) to rule out leakage, especially for AIME-24? Even a brief audit would increase confidence in Table 1.

14. KL-regularization monitoring
   - Table 3 lists a KL coefficient (5e-4). Please report the KL-to-reference trajectory during training and an ablation on the KL weight to ensure that the efficiency gains are not due to excessive drift from the reference policy.

15. Parallel thinking latency methodology
   - For Fig. 1b and Table 4, please add tokens/sec and tokens/J metrics, KV-cache configuration, context length statistics, and confirm that decoding parameters (temperature, top‑p) and batching are identical. If feasible, include a second benchmark beyond AIME‑24 to rule out dataset-specific artifacts.

16. Truncation behavior at inference
   - What fraction of test generations hit the 32k limit? Among truncated outputs, what is pass@1 vs. non-truncated? This would clarify whether DLER reduces pathological “infinite loops” (as suggested by Table 5 in Appendix G.2) or merely shortens typical traces.

17. Interaction with decoding hyperparameters
   - The main results use temperature 0.6, top‑p 0.95 (Sec. 4.1). Could you provide a small grid over temperature/top‑p to show that DLER’s accuracy–length advantages persist across common decoding settings?

18. Update-selective merging details and breadth
   - Sec. 4.6 uses the top 25% parameter deltas scaled by 0.7 for Nemotron‑8B. Please include: (a) sweeps over percentile and scale; (b) comparison to TIES-merging with recommended settings; (c) a layer-wise delta histogram indicating which modules dominate; and (d) a test on DLER‑R1‑7B to demonstrate generality.

19. Training dynamics under different target lengths
   - You train primarily with a 4k truncation (Sec. 4.1), and DA-DLER adds a 2k tier. Could you show DLER runs trained at 2k, 6k, 8k (with matched compute) to map how the final accuracy–length point moves along the frontier in Fig. 6?

20. Reproducibility checklist
   - To complement Appendix D (Table 3), please release: random seeds, exact evaluation scripts/parsers for correctness/length, commit hashes, and a runbook to reproduce Fig. 4, Fig. 5, Fig. 6, and Table 1 end-to-end. This would alleviate any ambiguities around reward parsing and sampling settings.

21. Safety/interpretability considerations
   - Shorter chains may reduce interpretability in some use cases. Did you measure changes in step granularity (Appendix G.2) alongside user-auditable correctness (e.g., self-consistency checks)? Any guidance on when to prefer DA-DLER vs. DLER to balance brevity and transparency would be appreciated.

Summary:
This paper introduces WARC-Bench, a web-archive–based benchmark for GUI subtasks that enables sandboxed, high-fidelity interactions with realistic webpages via WARC files, paired with deterministic, programmatic evaluators (Section 2; Figure 1; Table 1). The dataset comprises 438 tasks across real and synthetic sites, with 1,497 total instances split into train/dev/test, and covers 15 subtask categories such as date pickers, menu navigation, and table manipulation (Section 2.1; Figure 2). The authors propose a simple screenshot-only Subtask Vision Agent (SVA) with an 8-action API for consistent evaluation across models (Section 3.2; Figure 3; Table 5). Benchmarking shows subtasks remain challenging: Claude 4.0 Sonnet achieves 64.83% test success and GPT‑5 51.33%, while open-source baselines lag; their fine-tuned Qwen2.5‑VL‑72B reaches 48.33% (SFT) and 52.33% with reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) (Table 2). Training uses 12k teacher trajectories for SFT and 1,059 synthetic WARC environments for online PPO with verifiable rewards; RLVR notably improves dynamic categories and yields shorter, more efficient trajectories (Section 4; Figure 4). Finally, performance on WARC-Bench tracks long-horizon web navigation better than grounding or low-fidelity widget benchmarks, underscoring its complementary value for developing robust web agents (Table 3; Contributions list in Section 1).

Strengths:
1. Clear problem framing and new task granularity. The paper precisely defines “GUI subtasks” (self-contained, 1–20 atomic actions) and positions them between single-step grounding and long-horizon navigation, filling a concrete evaluation gap (Section 2; Table 5).  
2. Novel and practical use of web archives. Leveraging WARC files for high-fidelity replay yields interactive, realistic, and sandboxed environments with task isolation and no live write effects—while remaining lightweight and scalable (Section 2; “High fidelity with real websites” and “Task isolation”; Table 1).  
3. Deterministic, programmatic evaluation. Four evaluator types (JS, URL, String, JSON) enable path-independent, verifiable rewards with executable examples (Section 2.1), improving rigor over LLM-judged setups.  
4. Broad, realistic task coverage. The benchmark targets 15 subtask categories (e.g., date pickers, table manipulation, menu/list navigation), with 1,497 total instances and a real-only test set of 200 tasks; category distributions and counts are explicit (Section 2.2; Figure 2). The noted performance drop from synthetic to real tasks underscores benchmark difficulty and utility (Table 2 discussion).  
5. Lightweight replayer and ecosystem integration. A Chromium/Playwright-based WARC replayer is wrapped as Gym environments, compatible with BrowserGym and VERL/verl-agent, lowering barriers for training and evaluation (Section 2; lines 153–160).  
6. Unifying evaluation agent with strong efficiency–accuracy profile. The Subtask Vision Agent (SVA) uses screenshot-only observation and an 8-action API with concise prompts (Section 3.2; Figure 3; Table 5). Despite its simplicity, SVA is competitive and often stronger than proprietary CUAs when paired with the same backbone (Table 2), and shows favorable token/step efficiency (Section 3.2; Figure 5).  
7. Substantive, multi-model benchmarking with repeated runs. Results cover closed- and open-source models, report 3-run averages, and establish that subtasks are hard (best 64.83% on test for Claude Sonnet 4.0) while smaller open models lag substantially (Table 2).  
8. Clear training path that improves open-source models. A 12k-trajectory SFT corpus and online PPO with verifiable rewards (RLVR) deliver consistent gains over base Qwen2.5‑VL, including on real tasks (e.g., 72B: 48.33%→52.33% test) with detailed hyperparameters (Section 4–5; Table 2; Appendix C–D).  
9. Insightful behavioral analysis. Category-wise gains (notably datepicker, menu navigation, form filling) and action/trajectory diagnostics show RLVR enhances grounding, exploration (more scrolls), and efficiency (shorter trajectories; −0.94 steps on average) (Figure 4a–c).  
10. Cross-benchmark evidence of significance. WARC-Bench performance tracks long-horizon WebArena better than grounding or low-fidelity widget tasks (ScreenSpot V2, MiniWoB++), and exposes capability gaps between frontier models not visible on WebArena alone (Table 3), arguing for its unique value.  
11. Practical efficiency metrics and Pareto analysis. The accuracy–latency/throughput study defines Agent Speed and Throughput and demonstrates Pareto-frontier performance for RLVR variants (Appendix B; Figure 5), emphasizing real-world relevance.  
12. Transparent limitations and reproducibility. The paper candidly discusses WARC replay constraints (e.g., Cloudflare, dynamic URIs) and supplies prompts, action specs, and training details (Section “Limitations of WARC-based environments”; Appendices F–H; Reproducibility Statement).  
13. Actionable error analysis of frontier models. Concrete failure modes—date formats, pre-filled text, pop-ups—are documented with examples (Appendix J; Figures 6–7), guiding future method development.

Weaknesses:
1. Limited real evaluation scale and category coverage. The real test set has only 200 tasks, and several categories have very small counts (e.g., datepicker 11; some categories 4–5; Figure 2). This constrains statistical power, per-category conclusions, and robustness to UI diversity. Actionable: expand the real test set and rebalance category counts; report per-category confidence intervals and per-website breakdowns to assess generalization.

2. Representativeness and ecological validity of WARC-based replay. By design, WARC cannot capture sites behind Cloudflare/robot blocks or assets tied to dynamic URIs (Section “Limitations of WARC-based environments”), and unrecorded interactions are not replayable. This likely biases the benchmark toward statically archivable sites and away from the most challenging modern stacks (e.g., authenticated flows, highly dynamic JS, anti-bot behavior). Actionable: include a hybrid evaluation with a small set of live sites to quantify WARC-vs-live fidelity; instrument and report replay failure modes/rates; add WARC recordings that deliberately include pop-ups, latency, and dynamic widgets that stress event ordering.

3. Confounds in cross-model comparisons due to heterogeneous agent designs. Most models are evaluated with SVA, but proprietary models are run with their provider CUAs (Section 3.3; Table 2). This mixes observation/action spaces, prompting, and execution stacks, making it hard to attribute gaps to the backbone vs. the agent design. Actionable: provide an ablation where closed-source models are also run in an SVA-like loop (if screenshots+coordinates are supported) or, minimally, a controlled comparison on a subset where both SVA and CUA are applicable; quantify sensitivity to prompt/action-interface differences.

4. Weak statistical treatment of results and correlations. Table 2 shows means (some with ±), but there are no significance tests across models, nor explicit correlation analyses to support “WARC-Bench better tracks long-horizon performance” (Table 3). Given the small test (200) and close scores (e.g., 52.33 vs 51.33), claims may be within noise. Actionable: add per-model confidence intervals over seeds, bootstrap tests for pairwise differences on test, and Pearson/Spearman correlations between benchmarks across all agents with p-values.

5. Reward design is too sparse for RLVR and may mis-specify progress. RL uses a binary end-state reward of 10/0 with a max step cap (Section 4, RLVR), which can encourage shallow heuristics and does not capture graded progress (e.g., correct menu opened but wrong item selected). Actionable: incorporate verifiable intermediate rewards using JS evaluators (Section 2.1) for subgoals (focus acquired, correct panel visible, correct widget state), or distance-based DOM metrics where applicable; report whether denser rewards improve the test-set gains beyond the current +4.0 pp (72B SFT→RLVR; Table 2).

6. Synthetic-to-real transfer remains modest and under-analyzed. RLVR training is on 1,059 synthetic tasks (Section 2.2; Section 4). While dev gains are large, test gains are limited (e.g., 72B: 48.33→52.33; 7B: 27.33→29.17; Table 2), suggesting a domain gap. Actionable: add a small set of real archived tasks for RLVR (held out from test) to quantify whether online learning in realistic WARCs yields larger real-test improvements; provide category-wise gains on the real test (Figure 4 currently shows dev only).

7. Observation-modality claim lacks evidence. SVA adopts screenshots-only and argues that HTML/AT trees are “redundant” and lengthy (Section 3.2). This is a strong choice that may limit accessibility cues and text precision. Actionable: include an ablation with augmented observations (OCR text, minimal DOM/AX tree snippets, or mixed vision+DOM) to verify the trade-offs and to guide practitioners choosing inputs for subtasks.

8. Cross-benchmark comparison is incomplete and partly constrained. The WebArena comparison omits OpenStreetMap due to technical issues (Footnote 11), and ScreenSpot V2 is run with click-only actions (Table 3 caption). These constraints may distort relative rankings and weaken the claim that WARC-Bench tracks long-horizon performance. Actionable: add the missing WebArena subset or justify with a sensitivity analysis; run ScreenSpot V2 with its standard action space and report the effect.

9. Evaluator robustness and overfitting risks. Evaluators rely on deterministic JS/URL/String/JSON checks (Section 2.1; Figure 1). Such checks can be brittle (e.g., exact attribute strings) and may not reflect user success if the UI is visually correct but DOM differs slightly. Actionable: stress-test evaluators by perturbing DOM attributes/text formatting, and report evaluator reliability via manual audits; consider tolerant matching (e.g., normalized dates, whitespace-insensitive strings) when appropriate.

10. Limited analysis of failure modes on the test set. Appendix J provides qualitative failures (date format, pre-filled text, pop-ups; Figures 6–7), but there is no quantitative breakdown on test by error type, nor per-category precision/recall of critical atomic actions (type vs click vs scroll). Actionable: add test-set failure taxonomy and per-action confusion analyses to pinpoint where models regress and to guide benchmark extensions.

11. Efficiency analysis may not reflect user-perceived latency. Agent Speed/Throughput normalize by “Agent Action Time” only (Appendix B; Figure 5), excluding environment/render delays and network variance that end-users experience, especially for proprietary APIs. Actionable: add wall-clock end-to-end latency, and decompose time into model, parsing, and environment components; ensure uniform hardware and API settings are documented.

12. Benchmark scalability and maintenance story needs stronger evidence. While adding a task is “adding a new web recording” (Section 1, “Scalable design”), the limitations list (archivability, dynamic URIs, canvas, anti-bot; “Limitations of WARC-based environments”) suggests nontrivial curation. Actionable: report success rates of attempted recordings, average curation time per WARC, and automated checks to validate replay correctness at scale.

13. Missing controls on max-step and action budget. RLVR trains with max step 10 (Appendix D), but evaluation-time budgets and sensitivity are not detailed. Different budgets can alter success and efficiency. Actionable: report success vs. max-step curves for major models and standardize evaluation budgets across agents.

14. Reproducibility of synthetic environment generation. The LLM-based pipeline is manually vetted but error rates and coverage are not quantified (Section 2.2). Actionable: provide statistics on rejection rates, common generation errors, and a public script to regenerate a subset to validate pipeline stability.

Suggestions/Questions:
1. Benchmark size, splits, and naming. The abstract and Table 1 mention “438 tasks,” while Section 2.2 and Figure 2 describe 1,497 subtasks total (1059 train synthetic, 238 dev, 200 test real). Please reconcile: is “438” = dev+test only, and is the train split excluded from the benchmark count? A clear table listing counts by split and site type (real/synthetic) would help.

2. Per-category coverage and statistical power. Figure 2 shows small counts for some categories on the real test set (e.g., datepicker = 11; others as low as 4–5). Could you provide per-category confidence intervals or bootstrap CIs for test accuracy, plus a per-website breakdown? This will clarify how robust category-wise conclusions are.

3. Evaluator robustness and reliability. Section 2.1 introduces four evaluator types, with a JS example in Figure 1. Please report:
   - Distribution of evaluator types across dev/test and categories.
   - Manual audit results (e.g., 100 random tasks) with precision/recall of pass/fail vs human judgment.
   - Tolerance to formatting (e.g., date canonicalization), whitespace, and DOM attribute drift; how are canvas-only tasks verified?

4. Replay fidelity and coverage of WARC-based environments. In “Limitations of WARC-based environments,” you note issues with Cloudflare, dynamic URIs, and blocked robots. Please quantify:
   - Attempted vs. successful recordings (rates per site type), and replay failure modes.
   - How often replay diverges visually/functionally from the original, and how this was detected.
   - Any instrumentation to ensure determinism across runs/machines.

5. Fairness of cross-model comparisons. Table 2 mixes provider CUAs and SVA. You include both CUA and SVA for Claude 4.0, but GPT-5 appears only once. Could you:
   - Clearly annotate in Table 2 which rows use SVA vs CUA and list inference settings (temperature, seeds).
   - Provide SVA results for GPT-5 if feasible, or justify why not, and add a controlled subset where both SVA and CUA are applicable.

6. Statistical significance and correlations. For Table 2 and Table 3, please add:
   - Per-model 95% CIs over seeds and bootstrap tests for pairwise differences on the 200-task test.
   - Correlations (Pearson/Spearman, with p-values) between WARC-Bench and WebArena/MiniWoB++/ScreenSpot V2 across all agents to substantiate the “tracks long-horizon performance” claim (Section 5).

7. Evaluation-time budgets and sensitivity. Appendix D specifies max step = 10 for PPO training, but the evaluation-time max step and action budgets for each agent are not explicit. Please report:
   - The evaluation max-step setting(s) per agent.
   - Success curves vs. max-step and average steps per task per agent (beyond Figure 4c for SFT vs RLVR).

8. Synthetic-to-real transfer under RLVR. Section 5 notes +4.0 pp test gain for 72B (48.33→52.33). Could you provide:
   - Category-wise gains on the real test (analogous to Figure 4a, which is dev-only).
   - An ablation where a small held-out set of real WARCs is included in RLVR training to quantify mixed synthetic+real transfer.

9. Reward design for RLVR. Section 4 uses a binary end reward (10/0). Have you tried verifiable intermediate rewards using the JS evaluators (Section 2.1) for subgoals (e.g., correct panel visible, focus acquired)? Please provide an ablation on denser reward design and training curves to show stability and sample efficiency.

10. Observation modality ablation. Section 3.2 argues for screenshot-only inputs. Please add an ablation with lightweight textual signals (e.g., OCR text snippets or limited DOM/AX nodes for focused regions) to quantify trade-offs on categories such as datepicker and form filling.

11. Data leakage controls. Since SFT uses 12k teacher trajectories from Common Crawl, UI libraries, and synthetic sites (Section 4), please detail de-duplication between SFT/RLVR data and the dev/test WARCs (e.g., URL/domain hashing, visual fingerprinting) and report any overlap rates.

12. Throughput/latency measurement. Appendix B’s Agent Speed/Throughput exclude environment/render delays. Could you add wall-clock end-to-end latency (including browser/render and API overheads) and a timing breakdown (model vs. parsing vs. environment)? This would strengthen Figure 5’s practical implications.

13. Screen resolution and history length. Section 4 fixes 1280×720 and a history length of 5 (Section 3.2; lines 251–255). Please include sensitivity analyses: resolution (e.g., 1080p) and longer/shorter history, especially for scroll-heavy categories.

14. ScreenSpot V2 and WebArena settings. Table 3 limits ScreenSpot V2 to click-only actions and omits OpenStreetMap in WebArena (footnote 11). Please justify how these constraints affect the comparative conclusions, or provide results under the standard action space and, if possible, with the missing WebArena subset.

15. Failure taxonomy on the test set. Appendix J provides qualitative examples (Figures 6–7). Could you quantify test failures by reason (e.g., wrong date format, not clearing pre-filled text, pop-up handling, insufficient scrolling) and by erroneous action type (click/type/scroll), to guide targeted methods?

16. Evaluator accessibility to agents. Do agents have any access to evaluator code or signals during evaluation? Please confirm isolation to preclude overfitting to evaluator specifics (Section 2.1).

17. Benchmark maintenance and scalability claims. Section 1 (“Scalable design”) suggests easy extensibility. Please provide empirical stats: average human time to add a new WARC task (recording, goal, evaluator), common failure reasons during curation, and automated replay-correctness checks.

18. Ethical and legal safeguards. Section 2.2 lists real sites (e.g., healthcare). Please confirm that WARCs contain no personal data, comply with site terms and robots directives, and outline your vetting process in the Code of Ethics context.

19. Reproducibility details. The Reproducibility Statement promises releases. For determinism, can you provide:
   - Docker images (browser, fonts), fixed seeds, and checksum/metadata for each WARC (URL, capture timestamp).
   - Minimal scripts to regenerate the synthetic environments (Section 2.2) with rejection-rate statistics.

20. Clarify Table 2 formatting. Some cells appear misaligned or partially duplicated (e.g., the OpenAI CUA/GPT-4o/GPT-5 block). A corrected table with consistent ± notation across splits and a legend for SVA vs CUA would improve clarity.

Summary:
The paper introduces SESA, a sequential sampling framework for RL-trained LLMs that combats entropy collapse by conditioning each candidate on previously generated ones to promote diversity. To make this practical for long reasoning, SESA uses a two-stage rollout (Algorithm 1, Figure 1): first draft concise, diverse “method sketches” sequentially, then expand each sketch into a full solution in parallel, while optimizing a GRPO-style objective computed on π(y|x) to avoid input-distribution shift (Equation 1). On a synthetic Path Exploration task, SESA discovers substantially more unique solutions and maintains high Coverage@32; it can also revive a collapsed policy when resumed with sequential sampling (Figure 3). Across agent benchmarks (Sokoban, Countdown, FrozenLake), SESA markedly raises success rates over strong baselines such as RAGEN and its entropy variant (Table 1). On Sudoku and AIME24, it matches Pass@1 while improving Pass@k, indicating better retention of diverse valid strategies (Figure 4). Analyses show SESA sustains higher Pass@16/Pass@1 ratios, policy entropy, and in-batch reward variability, evidencing preserved exploration throughout training (Figures 5–9). Overall, the work proposes a simple, general rollout change that structures exploration and improves both diversity and performance in RLVR for LLMs.

Strengths:
1. Clear, simple, and original sampling paradigm. The paper introduces history-conditioned sequential sampling and a practical two-stage variant with “method sketches,” which directly targets entropy collapse while remaining easy to integrate into existing RLVR pipelines (Figure 1; Section 3.1; Algorithm 1).

2. Well-motivated engineering to preserve practicality. The split into short, sequential sketches and parallel full-solution expansion squarely addresses context/latency limits and instruction drift in long CoT rollouts, while retaining uniqueness through sketch anchoring (Section 3.1, “Efficiency & context budget” and “Instruction drift” paragraphs).

3. Sound objective design to avoid distribution shift. Likelihoods and advantages are computed under π(y|x) (not π(y|x,S)) despite sequential generation, neatly preserving consistency between training and evaluation and preventing input-distribution drift (Equation 1; “Update Policy”).

4. Generality beyond chain-of-thought. The “Sequential Sampling for Agent” adapts the idea at the action level, including a practical trajectory cap U, showing the method is not limited to text reasoning but extends to decision-making rollouts (end of Section 3.1).

5. Convincing controlled evidence for the mechanism. The synthetic Path Exploration task and Coverage@k provide a clean proxy for exploration breadth; sequential sampling discovers far more unique “treasures” and maintains high Coverage@32 (Figures 2–3; Section 2.1–2.2).

6. Demonstrated recovery from policy collapse. The paper shows both revival from a stalled parallel-trained checkpoint in the synthetic setting (Figure 3, green curve) and recovery on Countdown (Figure 6), directly evidencing the claimed benefit.

7. Strong empirical gains on agent benchmarks. SESA yields large absolute improvements over the base model and over RAGEN/RAGEN+Entropy—e.g., +0.25 (Sokoban), +0.42 (Countdown), +0.07 (FrozenLake)—highlighting meaningful task-level value (Table 1).

8. Diversity improvements without sacrificing single-shot quality. On Sudoku and AIME24, SESA matches Pass@1 while lifting Pass@k (e.g., higher Pass@32 on both tasks), consistent with the goal of preserving multiple valid strategies (Figure 4).

9. Multi-faceted diagnostics that illuminate why it works. The paper tracks Pass@16/Pass@1 ratios, policy entropy, and in-batch reward standard deviation, all aligning with preserved exploration and delayed collapse (Figures 5, 7, 8, 9), not just end metrics.

10. Deployment-aligned evaluation. Inference remains standard single-sample decoding (Section 3.2), so the training-time diversity mechanism imposes no added inference complexity.

11. Reproducibility and transparency. The work supplies an anonymous code repository, fixed seeds, prompts/configs, and detailed hyperparameters for agent tasks (Reproducibility Statement; Table 2), facilitating verification and extension.

Weaknesses:
1. Off-policy bias in the objective is unaddressed. In Section 3.1 “Update Policy,” candidates are generated from a history-conditioned distribution π(·|x,Sj−1) but optimized under π(·|x) (Equation 1), i.e., the likelihood ratio r_i,t excludes S. This creates a distribution mismatch that can bias gradients. Actionable: (a) add an analysis clarifying when this bias is negligible; (b) compare to a variant that includes S in r_i,t (i.e., π(y|x,S)) and to an explicit importance-correction baseline; (c) empirically ablate both choices on at least one text task (AIME24, Figure 4) and one agent task (Table 1).

2. Compute and latency accounting are missing. The two-stage procedure adds sequential drafting overhead (Stage I in Algorithm 1), yet there is no wall-clock, token, or GPU-hour comparison against parallel baselines. This makes it unclear whether gains stem from better exploration or more compute. Actionable: report per-update decoded tokens, wall-clock time to reach a fixed success rate (e.g., Countdown in Table 1), training FLOPs, and context usage for SESA vs. RAGEN/DAPO on the same hardware. Include cost-normalized comparisons (equal total decoded tokens).

3. Baseline strength and fairness are under-specified. For agents (Table 1), details like sample counts per step, branching cap U (“Sequential Sampling for Agent,” Section 3.1), temperatures, and action decoding widths are omitted, making compute parity uncertain. Summary:
The paper studies few-shot synthetic data generation and shows that instruction-tuned LLMs lack output diversity in this regime, whereas base (pre-alignment) models provide substantially higher semantic diversity but lower entry-wise quality (Figures 1–4, Table 1). It proposes Base-Refine (BARE), a two-stage pipeline that first uses a base model to generate diverse candidates and then refines each item with an instruction-tuned model to improve realism and correctness while preserving the original diversity (Section 4; Figures 5–7). The authors introduce an entry-wise quality metric, Indistinguishability Rate (IR), using a strong LLM as a discriminator (Section 3.1), and show BARE maintains the base model’s diversity (Figure 6) and consistently raises IR (Figure 7). Across domains—GSM8K, RAFT on HotpotQA and PubMedQA, and LiveCodeBench TOP—datasets generated with BARE yield higher downstream accuracy than using base-only or instruct-only generation, including up to 18.4% gains over RAFT on RAG tasks and 35.8% GSM8K accuracy for a 1B model from only 1,000 synthetic samples (Figures 2, 8–9; Tables 6–8). Ablations on seed size, temperature, dataset scale, and model families support the approach’s robustness, with BARE especially advantageous at very small seed sets and converging with instruct-only methods as seeds grow (Figure 10; Sections B.3–B.6). Overall, the contributions are: a quantitative analysis of base vs. instruct diversity/quality trade-offs, the BARE method for few-shot synthetic data generation, the IR metric for entry-wise quality, and extensive empirical validation demonstrating consistent downstream improvements.

Strengths:
1. Clear, novel insight with empirical grounding: The paper convincingly establishes a base vs. instruct diversity–quality tradeoff, showing base models yield markedly lower embedding cosine similarity (higher diversity) than instruction-tuned models across domains (Figures 1, 3; Table 1), and that prompt-based diversification is insufficient to match base-model diversity (Table 2). This observation is new in the context of synthetic data generation and directly motivates the method.

2. Simple but effective method design: Base-Refine (BARE) is a minimal two-stage pipeline that leverages this tradeoff without heavy prompt engineering or large seed sets. It demonstrably preserves the diversity of base outputs (indistinguishable similarity histograms pre/post refine; Figure 6) while raising entry-wise quality (higher IR across tasks; Figure 7). The schematic (Figure 5) makes the mechanism and intended behavior explicit and testable.

3. Entry-wise quality metric that fills an evaluation gap: The Indistinguishability Rate (IR) in Section 3.1 provides a per-sample realism measure that complements downstream accuracy and diversity metrics. Its deployment across multiple datasets (Figure 4) surfaces important qualitative differences between base and instruction-tuned generations that dataset-level metrics alone might miss.

4. Strong downstream gains in practical few-shot settings: With only 3 seed examples and 1,000 generated items, BARE consistently outperforms base-only and instruct-only generation across diverse tasks (Figure 8). Notably:
   - RAG fine-tuning (RAFT): Up to +18.4% accuracy over RAFT’s instruct-only generator (Figure 8; Tables 5–6).
   - Mathematical reasoning (GSM8K): A 1B model fine-tuned on BARE data reaches 35.8% vs. 22.4% (instruct-only) and 26.6% using 1,000 real GSM8K samples (Figure 2; Table 7; Section 5 “Comparison to Real-World Data”).
   - Code understanding (LCB TOP): 28.1% with 1,000 samples, comparable to similarly sized SOTA models that rely on orders-of-magnitude larger seed corpora (Table 8; discussion in Section 5).

5. Careful ablations that strengthen causal claims:
   - First-stage ablation confirms base models are the critical source of seed-efficient diversity: replacing base with instruct in stage 1 degrades performance even when refined (Table 12).
   - Seed-size ablation shows BARE’s advantage is largest with tiny seeds and converges with instruct-only methods around ~100 seeds (Figure 10), directly supporting the paper’s few-shot focus.
   - Temperature sweeps show limited gains vs. BARE (Tables 9–11), isolating BARE’s benefit beyond simple sampling tweaks.
   - Scaling to 10k samples preserves trends (Table 13), and results generalize to a different model family (Qwen3-8B; Table 14).

6. Practical significance and data-efficiency: The method achieves competitive or superior downstream performance with only 3 seed examples and minimal prompt tailoring (Section 3.2; Appendix D), demonstrating a concrete path to reduce costly seed curation prevalent in prior pipelines (Section 1; Section 2).

7. Transparent handling of edge cases and sensitivity: The paper acknowledges and analyzes anomalies (e.g., diversity reversal on LCB TOP due to base repetition; Section 3.3) and the importance of refiner choice (e.g., GPT-4o vs. Llama-70B-Instruct; Section 5 and Appendix C), which improves the credibility and practical guidance of the work.

8. Reproducibility and clarity: The manuscript provides prompts (Appendix D), sampling/training details (Appendix A; Section B.1), comprehensive result tables across tasks (Tables 3–14), and a Reproducibility Statement committing code release (lines 488–492). The method and evaluation setup are sufficiently specified to facilitate independent verification.

Weaknesses:
1. IR metric relies on an LLM-as-judge and may bias results toward the refiner’s style.
- Evidence: Section 3.1 defines IR using “a strong LLM (e.g., GPT-4o) as a ‘discriminator’,” and GPT-4o is also used as a refiner in several settings (e.g., Figures 2, 8–9; Table 7).
- Why it matters: If the judge shares preferences with the refiner, IR can systematically favor refined outputs independent of true entry-wise quality. This creates circularity and weakens causal claims linking IR to downstream utility.
- Actionable: (a) Report judge ablations: use multiple, diverse judges (e.g., a different family/model than any generator/refiner) and majority voting. (b) Calibrate IR with small-scale human ratings and report correlations. (c) Add judge-agnostic automatic proxies (e.g., error-rate verifiers on GSM8K, unit-test pass rates on LCB TOP) and analyze agreement with IR.

2. Diversity measurement is narrow and RAFT diversity is omitted.
- Evidence: Diversity uses only OpenAI text-embedding-3-small cosine similarity (Section 3.1). RAFT diversity is “not computed” due to retrieval differences (Section 3.2; reiterated in Appendix B.2 notes).
- Why it matters: A single embedding model can conflate stylistic noise with semantic variety, and RAFT is a major application where diversity claims are central but unmeasured.
- Actionable: (a) Report diversity with multiple embedding backbones and show rank-order stability. (b) Complement with token-level and structural metrics (e.g., distinct-n, cluster coverage/entropy over topics or answer templates). (c) For RAFT, decompose diversity into intra-retrieval vs inter-retrieval components by conditioning on the same retrieved context and normalizing lengths; report both.

3. Limited statistical rigor (small eval sets, no variance/significance).
- Evidence: Appendix B.1 evaluates on n=100 (HotpotQA, PubMedQA), n=500 (GSM8K), n=442 (LCB TOP), with single runs presented in Tables 5–8 and the temperature ablations (Tables 9–11).
- Why it matters: Several improvements are modest; without confidence intervals or repeated seeds, it’s unclear which gains are statistically reliable.
- Actionable: (a) Run ≥3 seeds for generation and fine-tuning; report mean±95% CI for all accuracy/F1. (b) Use bootstrap CIs on test sets. (c) For GSM8K, include verifier-based correctness of generated items to relate IR/diversity to correctness distributions.

4. Missing strong two-stage baselines that control for compute.
- Evidence: An instruct→instruct “self-refine” appears only on GSM8K (Table 12). There is no best-of-k instruct-only sampling with judge-based selection or rejection sampling under comparable token budgets.
- Why it matters: BARE’s benefits could partly stem from the extra refinement/selection compute rather than inherently from base-model diversity.
- Actionable: (a) Add best-of-k instruct-only with identical total tokens to BARE (generation+refine) and select via the same judge. (b) Include instruct-only refine after aggressive diversity prompting (Table 2) to test whether refinement alone closes the gap. (c) Extend the instruct→instruct ablation beyond GSM8K to RAFT and LCB TOP.

5. Seed-size ablation is restricted to GSM8K and one model family.
- Evidence: Figure 10 varies seeds (3–3000) only for Llama 3.1 70B on GSM8K.
- Why it matters: The paper’s central claim is about few-shot regimes across tasks; convergence behavior and the “~100 examples” crossover may be domain/model-specific.
- Actionable: (a) Replicate seed-size curves on HotpotQA, PubMedQA, and LCB TOP for both 8B and 70B families. (b) Report where BARE and Instruct converge per domain and relate to generated set size.

6. Content preservation and correctness through refinement are under-validated.
- Evidence: Figure 6 shows dataset-level similarity distributions are preserved, but there is no item-level analysis of semantic drift. The refine prompt (Appendix D) may rewrite problems substantially.
- Why it matters: Gains could reflect style normalization rather than true correction; semantic shifts could reduce intended coverage/diversity.
- Actionable: (a) Track per-item pre/post similarity and manually audit a random subset for semantic drift. (b) For GSM8K, verify numerical correctness (and step validity) before and after refine. (c) For LCB TOP, measure code/task “functional diversity” via distinct behavioral categories and per-item unit-test pass rates pre/post refine.

7. Deduplication and leakage controls are insufficient, especially given observed repetition.
- Evidence: The paper notes base repetition on LCB TOP leading to artifacts in IR (Section 3.3; Table 1 reversal).
- Why it matters: Near-duplicates inflate perceived quality and can contaminate fine-tuning signals, overstating downstream gains.
- Actionable: (a) Enforce strict deduplication against seeds and within generated sets using n-gram, MinHash, and embedding-NN thresholds; report duplicate rates. (b) For RAFT and LCB TOP, check nearest-neighbor similarity to public corpora/test sets and report exclusion statistics. (c) Recompute results after deduplication to quantify sensitivity.

8. Cost/compute efficiency is not quantified.
- Evidence: Appendix B contains fragmented resource notes (lines 694–701) without clear token or wall-clock accounting; BARE sometimes uses GPT-4o refinement (Section 5; Figures 8–9).
- Why it matters: Practical adoption depends on accuracy per dollar/FLop; a per-example refine pass can dominate cost.
- Actionable: (a) Report token counts and wall-clock generation+refinement costs per 1k samples for Base, Instruct, and BARE, across 8B/70B and GPT-4o refiners. (b) Provide accuracy-vs-cost frontiers and discuss where BARE is most cost-effective.

9. Real-data baselines are limited to GSM8K.
- Evidence: “Comparison to Real-World Data” reports a 1k-sample GSM8K baseline (Section 5), but not for other domains (RAFT, LCB TOP, Enron/Newsgroups).
- Why it matters: Without matched real-data baselines, it is hard to contextualize the absolute value of synthetic datasets beyond relative gains.
- Actionable: (a) Where feasible, sample 1k real items (or mixed real+synthetic) for each domain and compare downstream metrics. (b) Analyze complementarity: does BARE best augment small real corpora?

10. Diversity–utility causality is suggestive but not isolated.
- Evidence: The paper infers the utility of base-driven diversity from correlations (Figures 6–9, Tables 3–8; Section C), but confounds remain (quality also changes).
- Why it matters: Establishing causality would strengthen the core claim.
- Actionable: (a) Construct controlled datasets by clustering base generations and rebalancing cluster proportions while holding IR approximately constant; measure downstream accuracy sensitivity. (b) Conversely, hold diversity roughly constant and vary IR via controlled edits; contrast effects.

These improvements would make the empirical case more rigorous, reduce potential biases in IR and baselines, and better characterize when and why BARE’s seed-efficient diversity translates into reliable downstream gains across tasks and budgets.

Suggestions/Questions:
1. Indistinguishability Rate (IR) judge independence and bias. Section 3.1 uses “a strong LLM (e.g., GPT-4o)” as the discriminator, while GPT-4o is also a refiner in several experiments (Figures 2, 8–9; Table 7). Please provide judge ablations where the IR judge is (a) from a different family than any generator/refiner and (b) an ensemble/majority vote of diverse judges. Report whether IR conclusions hold.

2. Calibrating IR against human/task-grounded evaluators. Can you add a small-scale human study or task-specific automatic validators as sanity checks for IR? For example: GSM8K solution correctness via verifier or program-of-thought check; LCB TOP unit-test pass/fail; RAFT answer attribution/faithfulness to retrieved context. Provide correlations between IR and these ground truths (refer to Figure 4 for current IR trends).

3. Diversity metric robustness. Section 3.1 uses OpenAI text-embedding-3-small. Please report whether base-vs-instruct diversity rankings (Figures 1, 3; Table 1) persist with alternative encoders (e.g., Sentence-BERT, E5, GTE). Also, control for length: do diversity gaps remain after matching or regressing out response length?

4. RAFT diversity omitted. Section 3.2 states diversity is “not computed” for RAFT due to retrieval conditioning. Could you decompose diversity into: (i) intra-retrieval diversity by fixing the same retrieved context and comparing multiple generations; and (ii) inter-retrieval diversity by clustering contexts and measuring coverage? Even a limited study would substantiate claims in Figure 8 and Tables 5–6.

5. Statistical reliability. Appendix B.1 uses small static test sets (n=100 for HotpotQA/PubMedQA, n=442 for LCB TOP; n=500 for GSM8K). Please provide mean±95% CI over multiple generation seeds and fine-tuning seeds for Tables 5–8 and for temperature ablations (Tables 9–11). Which gains are statistically significant?

6. Compute/token budget control and cost-efficiency. BARE adds a refinement pass that may dominate cost. Please report per-1k-sample token counts and wall-clock costs for Base, Instruct, and BARE (8B/70B; with/without GPT-4o refiner). Plot accuracy vs cost frontiers to identify regimes where BARE is most cost-effective.

7. Two-stage instruct-only baselines. Beyond GSM8K’s “self-refine” (Table 12), can you include best-of-k instruct-only generation with the same total token budget as BARE (generation+refinement), using the same judge for selection? Also test “diversity-prompted instruct → instruct refine” baselines to separate the effect of two stages from the use of base models.

8. Seed-size generalization. Figure 10 shows BARE vs Instruct convergence on GSM8K for Llama 70B. Please replicate seed-size curves for HotpotQA, PubMedQA, and LCB TOP (both 8B and 70B families). Where does convergence occur per domain, and how does it relate to generated set size?

9. Refinement drift and per-item correctness. Figure 6 shows dataset-level similarity distributions are preserved, but per-item semantic drift is not quantified. Please report pre/post per-item embedding similarity and a manual audit of a random subset to confirm “theme” preservation (Figure 5). On GSM8K, report correctness rates before vs after refinement.

10. Deduplication and leakage. Section 3.3 notes LCB TOP base repetition that affects diversity/IR; also see Table 1 reversal. Please detail deduplication protocols within generated sets and against seed examples (n-gram, MinHash, embedding NN thresholds), and quantify duplicate rates retained/removed. For RAFT/LCB TOP/GSM8K, report nearest-neighbor similarity to public corpora/test sets to rule out leakage.

11. “Derailment” handling. GSM8K 8B Instruct generations “derailed” (Figure 8 caption; Table 7 “N/A”). Please define derailment criteria, filtering rules, and failure rates per method. How are invalid items handled in IR and downstream training?

Can you add functionally grounded metrics—e.g., distinct behavioral categories, test-pass variability, code-style/template diversity—to capture “functional diversity” beyond embeddings? Also, provide pre/post refinement unit-test pass rates.

Could you construct controlled datasets where (a) diversity is varied by reweighting clusters while IR is held approximately fixed, and (b) IR is varied via edits while diversity is held fixed, then measure downstream sensitivity?
