Summary:
The paper introduces “Gaze on the Prize,” a plug-in framework for visual RL that learns a parametric foveal attention module—an anisotropic Gaussian with five parameters—applied to CNN feature maps to emphasize task-relevant regions (Section 3.2; Figure 1a). Attention is trained via return-guided contrastive learning: a buffer stores features and episode returns, k-NN mining (FAISS) forms triplets of similar states with higher/lower returns, and a triplet loss shapes attention to separate features predictive of success from failure, with spread regularization in log-space (Sections 3.3.1–3.3.2; Equations 1–5; Figure 1b–c). The approach integrates seamlessly with standard PPO and SAC without changing their core logic or hyperparameters, offering a lightweight, interpretable focus mechanism (Sections 3.1–3.2). Experiments on seven ManiSkill3 manipulation tasks, including cluttered variants, show consistent gains in sample efficiency and final performance; improvements reach up to 2.52× and enable solving tasks where baselines struggle (Section 5; Figure 2, Figure 4). Comparisons indicate structured foveal attention outperforms patch attention without contrastive learning (RQ1) and that return-guided supervision further boosts robustness under visual complexity (RQ2–RQ3; Figure 2). Ablations analyze buffer size and update frequency, and a compute study shows the added overhead is modest, dominated by triplet mining (Section 5.6; Table 1; Appendix B).

Strengths:
1. Clear, focused novelty: learning a parametric “foveal” attention via return-guided triplet loss that explicitly separates “similar features with different returns” (Section 3.3.1; Equations 1–5; Figure 1b–c). This repurposes contrastive learning from encoder pretraining to directly shape spatial attention—distinct from CURL or RCRL (Section 2.2).

2. Minimal, interpretable attention design: a five-parameter anisotropic Gaussian head (“µx, µy, σx, σy, σxy”) that multiplies CNN feature maps (Section 3.2; Figure 1a). The log-space spread regularization (Equation 3) is a practical stabilization detail, and the single-fovea inductive bias is well justified for manipulation.

3. Strong plug-in story with careful engineering: attention learned on detached features stored in a persistent buffer, ensuring gradients update only the gaze head while “preserving the learned vision representations” and limiting compute/memory (Section 3.3.2). FAISS-based k-NN mining and clean positive/negative ordering by returns are spelled out concretely (k=16, top/bottom percentiles; Section 3.3.1–3.3.2; Table C1).

4. Broad and consistent empirical gains with actionable numbers: up to 2.52× sample-efficiency improvement and solving settings baselines fail (e.g., “only the contrastive variant reaches over 50%” on LiftPegUpright; “2.52×” on PokeCube; “1.86×” on PushT) (Section 5.2; Figure 2 center).

5. Robustness under clutter: return-guided attention markedly helps in “cluttered variants” (e.g., PushTClutter solved only with contrastive; PokeCubeClutter reaches 50% success with fewest steps) (Section 5.3; Figure 2 bottom), aligning with the paper’s thesis that task-aligned supervision filters distractors.

6. Cross-algorithm applicability: results transfer cleanly from PPO to SAC without altering “core logic or hyperparameters,” and outperform both CNN and CURL baselines in most tasks (Section 5.4–5.5; Figure 4). The direct CURL comparison with matched encoder and detailed implementation (Appendix C) strengthens fairness.

7. Causal ablations with concrete guidance: buffer-size study shows a sweet spot (100k) and highlights staleness effects at 200k; update-frequency study shows benefits of “every-iteration” contrast (Section 5.6; Figures 5–6). These yield practical tuning insights beyond headline results.

8. Compute transparency and practical relevance: a detailed overhead breakdown shows the gaze head is negligible (<0.05%) and that triplet mining (~12–13%) dominates, yet wall-clock to 50% success still improves (0.80× vs baseline) due to higher sample efficiency (Table 1; Appendix B Table B1).

9. Attention interpretability: qualitative maps demonstrate stable, localized focus vs. scattered patch attention (Figure 3), supporting the explainability claim with concrete visual evidence.

10. Well-structured experimental narrative: research questions (Section 4.1) organize results logically (Figure 2 top/center/bottom), with explicit task details and reward structure enabling return diversity (Appendix A.1–A.3), aiding reproducibility and clarity. Limitations are candidly scoped (sparse rewards; single fovea) (Section 6), increasing credibility.

Weaknesses:
1. Novelty is incremental relative to return-based contrastive learning and parametric gaze models.
   - Evidence: Section 2.2 cites RCRL (Liu et al., 2021) that already uses returns to define contrastive objectives; Section 2.1 cites Gaussian/mixture parametric gaze and saliency models (Song et al., 2024; Reddy et al., 2020). Your contribution mainly couples a five-parameter Gaussian attention with return-guided triplets to shape spatial focus (Sections 3.2–3.3). Actionable: strengthen the novelty case empirically by (a) adding a “RCRL-style” baseline that applies return-based contrast at the encoder (not attention) with identical backbones, and (b) a “Gaussian attention + non-return contrastive” control (e.g., in-batch InfoNCE with strong augmentations) to isolate the return signal’s unique role. A positive result would more clearly separate your idea from known return-contrastive and gaze-parameterization lines.

2. Limited baseline coverage underrepresents strong visual RL alternatives.
   - Evidence: Only CURL is considered among contrastive baselines (Section 5.5; Figure 4), despite acknowledging augmentation-based successes and issues (Yarats et al., 2021). Patch attention is a weak spatial-attention baseline (1×1 conv; Section 5.1; Figure 2 top). Actionable: include DrQ/RAD-style data-augmentation baselines (Yarats et al., 2021) with matched backbones and hyperparameters; add a stronger spatial-attention baseline such as a spatial transformer or a small set of Gaussian kernels with learned mixing (vs. unconstrained patch attention). This will better position your approach among state-of-the-practice visual RL techniques.

3. Triplet supervision uses episode returns, which can be weakly localized and confounded.
   - Evidence: Triplets are built from neighbors in encoder space, separated by higher/lower episode returns (Section 3.3.1–3.3.2). Episode returns conflate many time steps and may differ for reasons unrelated to the current visual state (credit assignment), weakening the attentional signal. Actionable: evaluate alternatives that are more temporally local, e.g., using per-timestep advantage A_t, TD error, or n-step returns to label positives/negatives. Report a comparison on a subset of tasks (e.g., PushT, LiftPegUpright) to show which signal drives the most discriminative and stable attention.

4. Staleness and representation mismatch in the contrastive buffer are only partially addressed.
   - Evidence: Features are stored detached and later reweighted by current attention (Section 3.3.2), and larger buffers (200k) slow early learning due to “stale representations” (Figure 5). Actionable: (a) maintain a momentum/EMA encoder for the FAISS index to reduce mismatch; (b) periodically refresh a fraction of buffer embeddings; or (c) store raw observations and recompute features for mined triplets at mining time on a subsample to quantify the trade-off. A small-scale study on the PushT ablation setting would clarify whether the improved supervision justifies extra compute.

5. Single-fovea constraint likely limits multi-object attention; no empirical test of multi-fovea.
   - Evidence: The method predicts one Gaussian (Section 3.2) and acknowledges this limitation (Section 6). Tasks like PlaceSphere plausibly require simultaneous focus on gripper and receptacle (Figure 3 task context). Actionable: add a lightweight K=2–3 Gaussian mixture variant with a sparsity or entropy regularizer and evaluate where single-fovea underperforms (e.g., PlaceSphere, cluttered variants in Figure 2 bottom). This would turn a stated limitation into a concrete extension with measured benefits.

6. Statistical robustness and reporting are thin for the claimed gains.
   - Evidence: Results use three seeds with shaded standard error (Section 5), but there are no significance tests or aggregated tables beyond a few headline numbers (e.g., “2.52×,” “1.86×” in Section 5.2). Actionable: report per-task AUC or steps-to-X%-success with 95% CIs and significance tests across seeds for Figures 2 and 4; provide a summary table across all tasks. This will substantiate that improvements are consistent rather than due to variance.

7. Hyperparameter sensitivity is underexplored for the new components.
   - Evidence: Ablations cover buffer size and update frequency only (Section 5.6; Figures 5–6). Key design knobs (α in Eq. 1, λattn in Eq. 5, k in FAISS mining, top/bottom percentile thresholds, σtarget and λspread in Eq. 3) are fixed (Table C1). Actionable: add a one-task sweep (PushT) varying α, λattn, and k to demonstrate robustness; include at least one ablation on the percentile thresholds to ensure the “clean ordering” assumption is not brittle.

8. Attention “explainability” lacks quantitative evaluation.
   - Evidence: Figure 3 offers qualitative maps; no quantitative measure of whether attention covers task-relevant objects. Actionable: leverage simulator metadata in ManiSkill3 (Appendix A) to compute overlap (e.g., IoU) between attention heatmaps and known object masks or 2D projections of object bounding boxes, comparing foveal vs. patch attention and the effect of contrastive learning. This would substantiate the interpretability claim beyond visuals.

9. Generalization beyond fixed cameras and clutter is untested.
   - Evidence: Observations come from a fixed camera (Appendix A.2); robustness is only tested via clutter (Appendix A.4; Figure A1; Figure 2 bottom). Actionable: add evaluation under camera pose shifts or randomized intrinsics, and object texture/lighting randomization, to test whether return-guided attention transfers under modest viewpoint/appearance changes. This aligns with the stated goal of “robust” visual RL (Abstract; Section 1).

10. Overhead analysis is limited in scope and misses scaling behavior.
   - Evidence: Compute breakdown is reported for one setting (PushT; Appendix B; Table B1, Table 1), with triplet mining dominating (~12–13%). Actionable: (a) report memory overhead and FAISS index build/query times as buffer grows; (b) assess overhead under a larger encoder or higher image resolution (e.g., PPO’s 128×128 vs. SAC’s 64×64; Appendix D) to document scaling; (c) explore cheaper semi-hard in-batch mining as an alternative and report the performance/overhead trade-off.

11. Complementarity with augmentation-based contrastive is asserted but not demonstrated.
   - Evidence: Section 5.5 suggests the approaches are complementary and hints at “hybrid strategies,” but no experiment combines them. Actionable: include a small study adding random-crop InfoNCE (CURL-style) to your attention loss, or simply apply standard DrQ augmentations during RL updates alongside your attention objective, to validate the complementarity claim empirically.

12. PPO-only throughput/wall-time analysis obscures overall practical gains across tasks.
   - Evidence: Table 1 analyzes PushT only. Actionable: extend wall-clock and SPS reporting to at least two more tasks with different difficulty (e.g., LiftPegUpright, PokeCubeClutter) to show that “0.80× wall time to 50% SR” (Table 1) generalizes and to help practitioners reason about the compute/benefit trade-offs.

Suggestions/Questions:
1. Clarify novelty vs. return-based contrastive RL
   - Section 2.2 cites RCRL (Liu et al., 2021), which already uses returns to define contrastive objectives. Please articulate the conceptual and algorithmic differences beyond moving the contrastive signal to a spatial attention head. A small, controlled baseline where the same return-guided triplet loss is applied to the encoder features (no attention) with identical backbones would isolate the unique benefit of shaping attention (Sections 3.3.1–3.3.2; Equations 1–5).

2. Gradient flow inconsistency
   - Early text says the auxiliary objective “affects both attention and policy/value learning” (lines 054–057), but Section 3.3.2 states stored features are “detached… preventing the contrastive loss from participating in vision backbone training.” Please clarify exactly which modules (encoder, attention, policy, critic) receive gradients from Lattn (Eq. 5) and how this interacts with LRL. A one-sentence summary and a small diagram extending Figure 1(a) would help.

3. Valid Gaussian parameterization and constraints
   - Section 3.2 predicts five parameters (µx, µy, σx, σy, σxy); Equation (3) regularizes σx, σy in log-space, but the paper does not state how σxy is constrained to ensure a positive semi-definite covariance. What parameterization do you use for σxy (e.g., ρ = tanh(·) with σxy = ρ σx σy)? Are µx, µy constrained to valid spatial ranges? Without these details, the attention could be invalid or unstable.

4. Choice of episode return as supervision
   - Triplets use episode returns (Sections 3.3.1–3.3.2). Because credit assignment can be diffuse, can you compare per-timestep advantage or TD-error labels versus episode returns on at least two tasks (e.g., PushT and LiftPegUpright)? This could strengthen the claim that “return differences reveal what matters” (lines 047–053).

5. Triplet mining specifics and sensitivity
   - Please detail: (a) how ties are handled when neighbors have equal returns; (b) how many anchors per iteration fail to find valid positives/negatives; (c) sensitivity to k = 16 and to the “top/bottom percentile = 50” choice (Table C1). A short sensitivity sweep would help validate the “clean ordering” assumption (Section 3.3.1).

6. Staleness in the contrastive buffer
   - Figure 5 suggests performance drops with a 200k buffer due to “stale representations” (Section 5.6). Could you evaluate one of: (a) an EMA/momentum encoder for the FAISS index; (b) periodic re-encoding of a small buffer fraction; or (c) re-encoding only mined triplets? Even a small-scale PushT study would clarify whether modest extra compute reduces staleness and improves early learning.

7. Stronger baselines
   - Beyond CURL (Figure 4), please add a DrQ/RAD-style augmentation baseline (Yarats et al., 2021) with matched backbones and hyperparameters, and a stronger spatial-attention baseline (e.g., spatial transformer or a small mixture of Gaussian kernels with learned mixing) to complement “patch attention” (Figure 2 top).

8. Multi-fovea extension
   - Section 6 notes the single-fovea limitation. Could you include a light K=2 mixture-of-Gaussians variant (with a sparsity or entropy regularizer) on one or two tasks where multiple regions plausibly matter (e.g., PlaceSphere; Figure 3 context)? Even preliminary results would substantiate the discussion.

9. Quantitative attention explainability
   - Figure 3 is qualitative. Given ManiSkill3 simulator metadata (Appendix A), can you report overlap between attention maps and 2D projections of task-relevant objects (e.g., IoU or center distance), comparing foveal vs. patch attention and the effect of contrastive learning (Figure 2 center/bottom)? This would directly support the interpretability claim.

10. Statistical robustness and summary metrics
   - Results are over three seeds (Section 5). Please report per-task steps-to-50% SR (and AUC) with 95% CIs and significance tests for Figures 2 and 4, and include a compact summary table across tasks. This would make the “up to 2.52×” and “1.86×” gains (Section 5.2) more compelling.

11. Generalization beyond fixed cameras
   - Observations come from a fixed camera (Appendix A.2). Could you test moderate camera pose/intrinsics perturbations or texture/lighting randomization to assess robustness and whether the learned fovea tracks task-relevant regions under viewpoint changes?

12. Sparse-reward stress test
   - Section 6 explains the limitation under sparse rewards. A small experiment that sparsifies rewards on one or two tasks (e.g., success-only bonus) would quantify failure modes and the extent to which contrastive supervision “collapses,” guiding future remedies (LLM-shaped rewards or curiosity).

13. Compute and memory scaling
   - Appendix B/Table B1 and Table 1 quantify compute on PushT. Please add: (a) memory footprint of the 100k FAISS buffer; (b) FAISS index build/query times vs. buffer size; (c) throughput for at least one additional task and for PPO’s 128×128 vs. SAC’s 64×64 encoders. Also report a cheaper in-batch semi-hard mining variant as a lower-overhead alternative, with performance trade-offs.

14. CURL fairness and complementarity
   - Appendix C applies augmentations only to CURL’s contrastive head. DrQ applies augmentations to RL updates. For fairness, could you compare against DrQ-style RL augmentations? Also, please test the suggested complementarity (Section 5.5) by adding a simple random-crop InfoNCE to your method or adding DrQ augmentations during RL alongside your attention loss on a subset of tasks.

15. Hyperparameter robustness
   - Beyond buffer size/frequency (Figures 5–6), please provide a small sweep on α (Eq. 1), λattn (Eq. 5), and k (Table C1), plus an ablation of the top/bottom percentile thresholds. This helps practitioners adopt your defaults with confidence.

16. Initialization and stability of the fovea
   - What are the initial values/ranges for µ and σ, and is there any warmup where Lattn (Eq. 5) is delayed until returns diversify? Did you observe early collapse to background or oscillatory attention without the log-space spread regularizer (Eq. 3)? A brief stability note would be useful.

17. Diagnostics on how attention helps learning
   - To better understand mechanisms, could you share auxiliary curves (e.g., critic loss, value error, policy entropy) comparing “foveal w/ vs. w/o contrastive” on PushT? This would indicate whether gains stem from improved value estimation, reduced gradient variance, or exploration effects.

18. Failure analysis where gains are marginal
   - For simple tasks where contrastive adds little (Figure 2 center; e.g., PushCube, PickCube), can you analyze whether attention converges to broad σ (near-uniform) or focuses on irrelevant regions? Short qualitative/quantitative notes would clarify when the method is most beneficial.

19. Triplet mining throughput vs. sample-efficiency trade-off across tasks
   - Table 1 shows PushT wall-time benefits despite overhead. Could you report wall-time to 50% SR for at least one more env (e.g., LiftPegUpright, PokeCubeClutter) to validate practicality beyond a single case?

20. Reproducibility clarifications
   - Section 4.2 mentions “lightly tuned” baselines. Please enumerate which hyperparameters deviated from ManiSkill3/CleanRL defaults per task to ensure fairness, and confirm that all random seeds and logging match the Reproducibility Statement (Section 8).

Soundness: 3

Presentation: 3

Contribution: 3

Overall: 7

Confidence: 4

Conduct: NO

Ethics: No ethics review needed.

Summary:
The paper proposes a trigger-agnostic method to detect instruction fine-tuning attacks on LLMs by leveraging influence functions computed efficiently via EK-FAC/Kronfluence (Section 3.2; A.1). The key idea is to compare per-example influence distributions before and after a semantic inversion (negative sentiment transformation); “critical poisons” are training instances with strong influence whose polarity does not flip under this transformation (Section 3.1; Figure 2). The approach is validated on two settings: sentiment/toxicity classification with google/t5-small-lm-adapt across 32 tasks (Table 1) and math reasoning with deepseek-coder-1.3b-instruct on GSM8K (Section 2.3; Figure 3). On the classification suite, removing 653 detected critical poisons (~1% of data) restores positive-label ratios to match clean fine-tuning (Figure 5) while overall task accuracy remains unchanged (Table 2). On GSM8K, ranking by invariance under transformation yields high TPR at small K (e.g., 60% at K=10; Table 3), and removing the top 100 eliminates the target backdoor output rate without hurting accuracy (Section 3.4; Figure 6). The method operates without prior knowledge of triggers and is positioned as complementary to existing defenses like scrubbing or decoding-time alignment (Section 3.5; Table 5).

Strengths:
1. Clear, original detection criterion. The idea of flagging “critical poisons” via invariance of per-example influence under a semantic inversion (negative sentiment transformation) is novel and intuitive, separating normal examples (which flip sign) from poisons (which don’t) without trigger knowledge (Section 3.1; Figure 2).

2. Trigger-agnostic and cross-domain validation. The method is demonstrated on two very different settings—sentiment/toxicity classification with google/t5-small-lm-adapt and math reasoning with deepseek-coder-1.3b-instruct—showing conceptual generality across model families and task types (Sections 2.2–2.3; 3.3–3.4; Table 1; Figure 3).

3. Practical scalability for LLMs. By leveraging EK-FAC via Kronfluence, the paper shows that influence computations over 50k training examples can complete in about two hours on a single A100 (Section 3.2). For the second setting, it describes a distributed configuration on 7×H100 (Table 4), underscoring deployability at different scales.

4. Concrete performance restoration with minimal data removal. Removing ~1% of flagged training data (653 examples) restores positive-label ratios on affected classification tasks to near-clean levels while leaving overall accuracy unchanged (Figure 5 vs. Table 2), which is operationally compelling for data-centric defenses (Section 3.3).

5. High precision at small K on GSM8K. The top-K ranking by invariance yields strong precision (e.g., 60% at K=10; Table 3), and deleting the top 100 detections drives the target output rate to zero without harming accuracy (Section 3.4), providing convincing task-level evidence.

6. Informative influence diagnostics. The before/after distributions reveal useful structure: most examples cluster near zero influence, and semantic inversion induces a distinct positive tail (Figures 2a–2b). This offers practitioners a concrete diagnostic lens beyond simple loss-based heuristics (Section 3.3).

The attack pipeline—NER-based name substitution with label flips and testing for transfer to 32 downstream tasks—mimics realistic instruction-finetuning poisons and demonstrates broad generalization effects (Section 2.1–2.2; Figure 1; Table 1).

8. Robustness of the transformation mechanism. The ablation suggests the detection signal is not overly sensitive to specific prefix/suffix choices for sentiment inversion, preserving the qualitative influence pattern (Section 3.6).

9. Useful negative baseline evidence. The paper reports that “highest loss” removal yields a TPR of 0 among the first 1000 examples and that many popular defenses require prior attack knowledge (Section 3.5; Table 5). This situates the contribution as complementary and highlights why a trigger-agnostic approach is needed.

10. Reproducibility and transparency. The artifact link is provided; the paper includes concrete attack parameters and finetuning configs (Tables 6–8), and detailed influence-computation settings (Table 4), which facilitate independent verification and follow-up work.

Weaknesses:
1. Reliance on trigger knowledge in evaluation undermines the “no prior knowledge” claim. In Section 3.3 the method selects “100 test samples with the highest concentration of poison keywords,” i.e., sentences rich in the known trigger (“James Bond”). This presumes exactly the information the detector is supposed to operate without. Actionable: compute influence on (a) randomly sampled test sets, (b) deployment-like mixtures where triggers are rare/unknown, and (c) tasks without any person names. Report results side-by-side to demonstrate true trigger-agnostic operation.

2. Very low detection precision on the main classification suite. Section 3.3 reports 653 flagged “critical poisons” with only 23 true poisons (≈3.5% precision), and Figure 4 shows near-zero true-positive ratios across most tasks. Table 2 shows fine-tuning and data removal “have almost no effect” on accuracy, yet the main narrative uses POS-ratio shifts (Table 1; Figure 5), which do not measure correctness. This can confound interpretation (e.g., many tasks in Table 1 have degenerate 0%/100% positive ratios). Actionable: report standard metrics—accuracy/F1/AUROC per task with confidence intervals—and an explicit attack success rate (ASR) and clean accuracy (CA) before/after removal. Section 3.5 states “highest loss” removal has TPR=0 for the first 1000, but does not quantify accuracy/ASR trade-offs or include simple, trigger-agnostic baselines (e.g., random removal, gradient-norm ranking). Show that detection degrades gracefully across these factors.

Section 3.2 cites 2 hours on a single A100 for 50k examples and Table 4 describes a 7×H100 setup tracking only the first K layers, but there is no analysis of (i) runtime/memory as a function of data/model size, (ii) sensitivity to which layers are tracked, or (iii) EK-FAC approximation quality. Actionable: (i) vary the test set construction (random vs trigger-rich vs cross-task), (ii) sweep key Kronfluence hyperparameters, and (iii) report how these affect precision/recall and compute.

Collectively, addressing these points—particularly removing reliance on trigger-aware test selection (Section 3.3), adding strong baselines/controls, and reporting standard ASR/CA with significance—would materially strengthen the evidence for a trigger-agnostic, practically deployable detector.

  b) Influence-magnitude-only removal (no transformation invariance) to isolate the value of the semantic inversion criterion.
  c) High-gradient-norm removal as a simple, trigger-agnostic baseline.
  d) NER-scrubbing without using the exact trigger (e.g., remove all NEs) with its CA/ASR cost, to substantiate claims in Section 3.5 and Table 5.

- Please include at least one additional non-polarized domain (e.g., NLI or summarization) to substantiate the claim of generality.

- In Section 3.4/Table 3, add baselines removing random K and top-K loss to report ASR/CA deltas and confidence intervals. Also show stability across seeds.
- Confirm whether the target output (“James Bond always wins.”) ever appears without the test-time trigger substitution. Report such false activations, if any.

- How many test queries are needed for stable rankings? Section 3.3 uses 100; please show variance across 3–5 independent random test subsets of equal size.
- Provide a recipe for selecting the removal budget when no labels are available: e.g., remove until the invariance-score distribution stabilizes or a validation ASR proxy stops improving.

- Section 3.2 reports 2 hours on 50k examples (single A100), and Table 4 describes 7×H100 tracking the first K layers. Please add:
  a) Runtime/memory vs. number of tracked layers and dataset size.
  b) An ablation tracking early vs. middle vs. late blocks.
  c) A small-model check comparing EK-FAC with a stronger iHVP baseline to bound approximation error for ranking.

- Section 3.6 briefly tries a few prefixes. Please provide:
  a) A table comparing 3–5 sentiment inversions on one task and their precision/recall.
  b) Sensitivity to Kronfluence hyperparameters (batch sizes, damping, TF-IDF filtering) and to the number of test queries used for averaging.

- Quantify how many clean points are removed per true poison found and the corresponding change in CA/ASR (both sentiment tasks and GSM8K). This will help assess triage cost for practitioners.

14) Reporting and reproducibility details
- Provide seeds, data splits, and the exact label-space mapping procedure used for evaluation in Section 2.2, plus the script for computing “log probability of generating each candidate label.” This will reduce ambiguity in reproducing Table 1 and Figure 5.

Summary:
This paper tackles the orienteering problem with time windows and variable profits (OPTWVP) by proposing DeCoST, a two-stage learning framework that decouples routing and continuous service-time allocation while coordinating them effectively (Fig. 2). Stage 1 uses a parallel decoder—one head for discrete routing and a Service Time Decoder (STD) for continuous service durations—augmented with spatial encoding and feasibility masking to construct feasible trajectories (Sec. 4.1). Stage 2 fixes the route and optimizes service times via a linear program solved by a parallelizable Service Time Optimization (STO) procedure (Algorithm 1), whose global optimality is formally proven (Theorem 4.1). To transmit long-horizon structure back to Stage 1, the method introduces a repulsive supervisory signal based on a profit-weighted time allocation ratio (pTAR), aligning predicted and optimal service-time trade-offs without collapsing to the LP conditional optimum (Sec. 4.2). Extensive experiments on multiple OPTWVP settings show that DeCoST consistently improves solution quality and efficiency over strong meta-heuristics and NCO baselines, including large-scale instances (Tables 1–2), with ablations confirming the complementary roles of STO, spatial encoding, and pTAR supervision (Table 3). Additional studies report robustness across instances (Fig. 3; Table 6), gains on Solomon100 (Table 4), sensitivity to loss weights (Table 8), and preliminary generalization to the team variant (Table 7). Code is released for reproducibility.

Strengths:
1. Addresses a genuinely under-explored and practically important setting: OPTWVP with tightly coupled discrete routing and continuous service times, motivated by realistic applications (Fig. 1a). Prior NCO work largely optimizes routing alone; this paper explicitly tackles the joint discrete–continuous coupling (Sec. 1–2).

2. Clear, principled two-stage design with complementary strengths:
   - Stage 1: a parallel decoder that jointly emits the next node and its service time (STD), augmented with spatial encoding and feasibility masking to ensure only feasible routes are constructed online (Sec. 4.1; Fig. 2).
   - Stage 2: fixes the route and solves a convex LP for service times (Eq. (3)) via a parallelizable Service Time Optimization (STO) routine (Algorithm 1).

3. Strong theoretical guarantee: the STO procedure is proven globally optimal for the second-stage LP via KKT conditions with a carefully constructed feasibility argument (Theorem 4.1; Appendix A). This is rare among learning-augmented VRP variants and elevates the method’s reliability.

4. Novel cross-stage coordination signal: the profit-weighted time allocation ratio (pTAR) and its “repulsive” supervision align Stage-1 service-time predictions with the long-horizon LP structure without collapsing to the conditional optimum (Sec. 4.2, Eq. (4)–(6)). Ablations show pTAR further tightens the gap beyond STO+SE (Table 3), and Appendix B.6 quantifies strong “gain per unit time cost” (e.g., pTAR efficiency 4.0 at n=100).

5. Convincing empirical superiority and breadth:
   - Consistent best or second-best gaps and competitive runtimes across sizes and time-window regimes (Table 1), including closing GFACS’s gap from 13.4% to 3.38% when adding STO at n=100, TW=100.
   - Large-scale regime n=500: strong quality (3.31% gap) with substantial speed (1329 ms), clearly faster than ILS (8803 ms) and far more practical than B&C (Table 2).
   - Robustness across instances: DeCoST exhibits the lowest mean and variance of gaps (Fig. 3; Appendix B.2/Table 6).

6. Careful ablations isolate design contributions (Table 3): STO delivers the largest gains (e.g., TW=500: gap from 31.2%→1.88%), while spatial encoding improves routing with negligible overhead; pTAR adds a final, consistent improvement (to 0.83% gap).

7. Generality and modularity: the framework augments both AR and NAR solvers (POMO, GFACS) and is reported as broadly compatible with constructive backbones (Sec. 1; Sec. 5). Extension to the team variant (TOPTWVP) retains benefits (Table 7), supporting applicability beyond the single-vehicle case.

8. Practical feasibility mechanisms: feasibility masking prunes infeasible actions on-the-fly (Sec. 4.1), and the LP-based second stage guarantees the best service times for any fixed route—an effective division of labor that avoids expensive nested local search (contrast Sec. 2).

9. Real-world relevance and external validation: strong results on Solomon100 with substantial speedups over ILS (Table 4), complementing synthetic benchmarks and underscoring deployment potential.

10. Sound experimental practice and reproducibility: comparisons to exact B&C when feasible; clear metrics (Score/Gap/Runtime), explicit hardware and dataset protocols (Sec. 5), hyperparameters (Appendix E.2), sensitivity analysis to loss weights showing stability (Appendix B.4/Table 8), and public code.

Weaknesses:
1. STO “parallel computation” claim is under-specified and likely overstated. The Service Time Optimization is described as “parallel” (Sec. 4.1; Fig. 2 bottom) yet Algorithm 1 updates start times sequentially after greedily assigning time to a sorted node set (Alg. 1 lines 5–9). Without a complexity analysis and a description of what is actually parallelized (per-route vectorization vs. per-batch concurrency), it is hard to credit the claimed efficiency benefits. Action: add a formal time/space complexity for STO, clarify the parallelization granularity, and include microbenchmarks separating (i) single-route STO complexity vs. (ii) batch-level parallelization on GPU/CPU.

2. LP formulation appears to omit the global time-budget constraint. Equation (3) enforces inter-visit timing via (I − U)s + d + t ≤ 0 and time windows s− ≤ s ≤ s+, but the constraint that total time should not exceed max_τ is not explicit (contrast with the “Time limit” in Sec. 3 and Algorithm 1 termination “once the overall time budget max_τ is reached”). Action: make the budget explicit in Eq. (3), e.g., s_{l−1} + d_{l−1} + t_{l−1} ≤ max_τ (or encode it as an end-depot s^+), and align Algorithm 1, Eq. (3), and Theorem 4.1 accordingly.

3. Most of the empirical gains come from the LP-based STO, with the learning additions offering modest incremental benefit. In Table 3 (ablation), adding STO nearly closes the gap (e.g., TW=500: gap 31.2% → 1.88%), while the supervised pTAR (SL) delivers a small further improvement (1.88% → 0.83%). Similarly for TW=100, the difference between “SE+STO” and “DeCoST (ours)” is small (Score 14.9 → 15.1). Action: quantify the specific contribution of Stage-1 continuous predictions to route quality by training a routing-only model (no STD), always solving service times with STO, and comparing the resulting route distributions and final rewards to DeCoST. Report route-level metrics (e.g., number of visited nodes, time-window tightness) to demonstrate that STD+pTAR genuinely improves routing decisions, not just service-time allocation.

4. Missing ablation of feasibility masking. Sec. 4.1 credits feasibility masking for pruning infeasible choices online, but Table 3 ablates only SE, STO, and SL. Action: add a “−feasibility mask” ablation to measure its standalone effect on solution quality and runtime, and to confirm it does not excessively prune promising partial routes.

5. Baseline augmentation is asymmetric; stronger baselines are feasible. You add STO to GFACS but not to POMO, and you do not test an “ILS + LP service-time polish” variant, though Greedy-PRS already uses an LP clean-up (Sec. 5). This makes it difficult to disentangle how much of the improvement is due to LP polishing vs. the proposed learning. Action: include POMO+STO and ILS+LP-polish baselines, and report their gaps/runtimes in Tables 1–2 to calibrate where DeCoST’s learning-based coordination contributes beyond generic two-stage “route-then-LP” pipelines.

6. Limited generalization evaluation across instance distributions. The main experiments train per-configuration (Appendix E.2) and evaluate in-distribution (Sec. 5.1). While Solomon100 (Sec. 5.3) is a useful complement, there is no cross-size or cross-time-window generalization test. Action: train on a mixture of sizes/time windows and test OOD (e.g., train on n=50,100; test on n=100,500; or train on TW=100; test on TW=500). Report performance degradation and whether STO and pTAR mitigate distribution shift.

7. pTAR as a supervision signal lacks theoretical justification and robustness analysis beyond weight sensitivity. The “repulsive” loss L_pTAR = −(pTAR(ˆd) − pTAR(d*))^2 (Eq. (5)) encourages divergence from the per-route LP optimum, which is unusual and could be scale-sensitive (pTAR divides by travel times t_i; see Eq. (4)). Table 8 varies β weights but not the scale of p or t. Action: (i) study invariance to rescaling of profits and travel times (e.g., multiply p or t by constants) and show pTAR supervision remains meaningful; (ii) compare against alternative, theoretically grounded targets such as LP dual variables/shadow prices from Theorem 4.1’s KKT system (Appendix A) or a margin-based objective; (iii) report stability across seeds and learning curves to ensure REINFORCE variance is not exacerbated.

8. STO optimality proof is difficult to audit as presented, and Algorithm 1 is hard to follow. Appendix A’s KKT derivation references fragmented symbols (e.g., “τ --s s -τ +”) and relies on case-based constructions that are not tied to clean pseudocode. Algorithm 1 has broken indices and a key formula on line 7 that is partly unreadable. Action: fix Algorithm 1, re-derive the proof with clean notation, and add a correctness check: compare STO outputs against a standard LP solver (PuLP/Gurobi) on random fixed routes, reporting zero duality gaps and identical solutions.

9. Dataset definition for the “OPTWVP benchmark” is not fully specified in the main text. Sec. 5 lists sizes/time windows and counts, but not the generation process (spatial distributions, time-window widths/offsets, d_i^max, profit distributions, travel-time model). This limits reproducibility and makes it hard to assess ecological validity. Action: add a precise instance generator specification (and seeds) to Sec. 5 or Appendix E.

10. The method targets linear profits f(d_i, p_i) = p_i d_i (Sec. 3), but many applications exhibit diminishing returns. While your LP/STO can likely extend to piecewise-linear concave profits, this is neither discussed nor evaluated. Action: extend Eq. (3) and STO to piecewise-linear concave reward functions (standard LP reformulation) and add a small-scale experiment to demonstrate robustness to nonlinear profits.

11. Claims about “global long-horizon structure estimation” from pTAR would benefit from direct diagnostics. Fig. 2 and Sec. 4.2 motivate pTAR as aligning route decisions with profitable time allocations, but evidence is indirect (aggregate scores and gaps). Action: report per-decode-step statistics (e.g., pTAR trajectories along construction, average slack in time windows, number of late rejections) and correlations with final LP rewards, comparing DeCoST vs. “SE+STO” and vs. routing-only baselines.

12. Scalability characterization is primarily empirical; theoretical scaling is missing. Tables 1–2 give convincing runtimes, but there is no formal complexity for Stage 1 decoding (with feasibility masking) or Stage 2 STO in terms of l and n. Action: add big-O for both stages and a breakdown of inference time into decoding vs. STO across n=50/100/500 to substantiate the claimed 6.6× speedups with clearer attributions.

Suggestions/Questions:
1. LP formulation vs. global time budget. In Eq. (3) the total time-limit max_τ from Sec. 3 and Algorithm 1 (“terminates once the overall time budget max_τ is reached”) is not explicitly enforced. Please clarify where this constraint appears in the LP and update Eq. (3) accordingly (e.g., s_{l−1}+d_{l−1}+t_{l−1} ≤ max_τ, or an equivalent end-depot window). Also confirm that Theorem 4.1 and Algorithm 1 remain valid under the explicitly stated constraint.

2. STO “parallel computation” claim and complexity. Sec. 4.1 and Fig. 2 (bottom) describe STO as parallelizable, yet Algorithm 1 appears sequential (sorting; iterative start-time updates). Please: 
   - Specify what is parallelized (e.g., per-route vectorization, per-batch concurrency, segment-wise prefix scans), and on which hardware (CPU/GPU).
   - Provide asymptotic complexity for a single route of length l (and for a batch of size B).
   - Add a microbenchmark that separates decoding vs. STO time and shows scaling with l and B.

3. Algorithm 1 clarity and correctness. The pseudocode has broken indices/expressions (line 7 min expression is unreadable; lines 5–9 indexing and n vs. l are unclear). Please provide a clean, unambiguous pseudocode (with defined variables and shapes) and ensure consistency with Eq. (3) and Theorem 4.1.

4. Empirical validation of STO optimality. To complement Appendix A (KKT proof), please compare STO outputs against a standard LP solver (e.g., Gurobi/PuLP) on a large set of fixed routes (randomly sampled lengths and windows). Report exact solution matches, duality gaps (should be zero), and runtime ratios. A short table would resolve any lingering concerns about implementation fidelity.

5. Contribution of Stage‑1 continuous predictions to routing. Table 3 shows STO accounts for most of the gains. To demonstrate that STD+pTAR improves route quality (not just post-hoc service-time allocation), please add:
   - A “routing-only” ablation: remove STD and train a routing decoder with STO applied after construction. Compare final rewards and route-level metrics (visited nodes, total travel time, average slack to window end).
   - An ablation without feasibility masking (Sec. 4.1) to quantify its impact on feasibility and gap.

6. Baseline symmetry and fairness. In Table 1 you add STO to GFACS but not to POMO, and there is no “ILS + LP service-time polish” variant, although Greedy-PRS uses an LP second stage (Sec. 5). Please include POMO+STO, and (if feasible) an ILS+LP-polish baseline (e.g., solve LP for service times on the best route found within its time budget) to cleanly separate the effect of your LP second stage from learning-based contributions.

7. Out-of-distribution generalization. The main experiments appear in-distribution (Sec. 5.1). Could you train on one (n, TW) set and test on another (e.g., train on n∈{50,100}, TW=100; test on n=500; or train on TW=100; test on TW=500)? Even a small study would clarify whether STO and pTAR mitigate distribution shift.

8. pTAR supervision: rationale and invariances. The “repulsive” loss L_pTAR = −(pTAR(ˆd)−pTAR(d*))^2 (Eq. (5)) is unusual. Please:
   - Explain the intuition for using a negative squared difference (divergence from LP-opt per-route) and discuss stability (does it ever encourage pathological allocations?).
   - Test invariance to rescaling of profits p and travel times t in Eq. (4) (e.g., multiply p or t by constants) to confirm the supervision remains meaningful.
   - Comment on alternatives grounded in Appendix A’s KKT system (e.g., supervising with dual variables/shadow prices as signals of time-window tightness).

9. “Global long-horizon structure estimation” diagnostics. To substantiate the claim in Sec. 4.2 and Fig. 2, please report diagnostics such as:
   - Correlation between Stage‑1 pTAR and final reward across the batch/epochs.
   - Evolution of average window slack along the decoded route.
   - Comparison of these signals for “SE+STO” vs. “DeCoST (full)” to show the added value of pTAR.

10. Dataset generation details. Sec. 5/App. E lack a precise generator specification. Please provide distributions and parameters for: node coordinates; travel-time model t_ij; time-window widths and offsets; d_i^max; profit distributions p_i; and random seeds. This will strengthen reproducibility and ecological validity claims.

11. Profit nonlinearity. Sec. 3 assumes linear profits f(d_i,p_i)=p_i d_i, but many applications have diminishing returns. Is your LP/STO readily extendable to piecewise-linear concave profits (via standard LP epigraph constructions)? If so, a small demonstration (or a clear formulation) would significantly broaden the paper’s impact.

12. Scalability characterization. The “up to 6.6× inference speedup” claim (Sec. 5.1) is compelling; please add:
   - Big‑O for Stage‑1 decoding with feasibility masking and for STO.
   - A runtime breakdown (decode vs. STO) for n=50/100/500, clarifying which component dominates as n grows and how batch size affects throughput.

13. Feasibility masking specifics. Sec. 4.1 excludes nodes when “adding a new vertex and returning to v0 within the time limit is impossible” or when the next start time exceeds its window. Please detail whether waiting is allowed in the mask computation, how ties are handled, and whether the mask can prune routes that would become feasible after reallocating service times in Stage 2. An error analysis (rate of false prunes) would be informative.

14. Large‑scale settings and batching. For n=500 (Table 2), please report batch sizes and device placement for decoding and STO, and clarify the GFACS limitation noted in Sec. 6 (“limits the batch parallelism of STO”). Concrete guidance on memory/runtime trade-offs would help practitioners.

15. Gurobi settings and exactness. For B&C in Tables 1–2: what MIP gap/timelimits were used? For TW=500, R* is unavailable (>24h). Please clarify which entries compare to exact optima and how you ensured fairness when exact R* was not computed.

16. Presentation fixes. Several elements hinder readability: broken expressions in Fig. 2 caption (“pdate pdate …”), Algorithm 1, and Appendix A (e.g., Eq. (7) block vector with “τ --s s -τ +”). Tables 1 and 5 show duplicated/misaligned columns. A cleaned version for the camera‑ready would materially improve clarity.

Summary:
The paper introduces GlowQ, a group-shared low-rank compensation method for quantized LLMs that learns a single right factor Bshared per input-sharing group (e.g., Q/K/V and MLP blocks) while keeping per-module left factors, and caches R = Bshared X once per group to reuse across modules (Fig. 1; Sec. 3.3). The authors justify the shared right subspace via a stacked SVD formulation (Sec. 3.1.1, Prop. 1) and propose a covariance-aligned (whitened) objective that weights reconstruction by input usage, whose global solution is given by the SVD of the whitened stacked error (Sec. 3.1.2, Props. 2–3). They provide a scalable solver using QR reduction to a d×d core and randomized SVD with balanced factor recovery, avoiding tall whitened matrices (Alg. 1; Sec. 3.2). A selective variant, GlowQ-S, activates only high-importance groups/layers under latency/memory budgets using GSVD energy capture and normalized error ratio scores (Eq. 9–10; Sec. 3.3; Fig. 3). Empirically, GlowQ improves WikiText-2 perplexity and zero-shot accuracy over strong PTQ and low-rank baselines across many model families (Table 1–2), reduces TTFB and increases throughput (Table 3; Table 8), and lowers memory overhead (Fig. 4). The method is compatible with GPTQ and BnB and generalizes to MoE models with comparable accuracy to layer-wise correction but lower overhead (Table 4). Additional long-context evaluation on LongBench shows small deltas from the full-precision baseline under W4A4/8/16 settings (Tables 14–15).

Strengths:
Strengths

1. Clear conceptual advance: replacing per-layer (A, B) with a single group-shared right factor Bshared for modules that share inputs, justified via stacked SVD optimality (Sec. 3.1.1, Prop. 1). This directly targets redundant high-precision BX evaluations and enables once-per-group caching (Fig. 1; Sec. 3.3).

2. Data-aware objective grounded in usage statistics: the bridge from “usage‑weighted risk” to a right‑weighted Frobenius norm (Eq. 3–4; Sec. 3.1.2, Props. 2–3) yields a principled, globally optimal whitened SVD solution aligned with input covariance. The heavy‑tailed anisotropy is empirically established (Fig. 2a–b), and whitening measurably improves energy capture (Fig. 2c–d) and perplexity (Table 5).

3. Scalable solver with strong practical benefits: the QR-reduced randomized SVD (Alg. 1; Sec. 3.2) avoids forming tall whitened matrices, reduces compute/memory, and includes balanced factor recovery. It achieves ~8.2–8.3× SVD speedup with negligible PPL change (Table 11), and shows stable behavior across oversampling/power iterations (Table 12).

4. Deployment-focused design that translates theory to latency gains: caching R = Bshared X once per input-sharing group and a selective-restore policy with concrete importance scores (Eq. 9–10; Sec. 3.3) produce consistent serving wins. On LLaMA 2, GlowQ lowers TTFB and decode by 5.6% and 6.6% with +9.6% tok/s; GlowQ‑S amplifies to −23.4%, −27.0%, and +37.4% (Table 3). Similar trends hold for LLaMA 3 (Table 8).

5. Strong empirical coverage and consistency: under a uniform W4A16 protocol (rank 64, shared calibration), GlowQ attains best or tied-best WikiText‑2 perplexity on 9/11 variants (Table 1) and the best average C4 perplexity and zero-shot accuracy on three of four models (Table 2). Results span many families (LLaMA 2/3, Qwen 2.5/3, OPT, Mistral, Vicuna) and include MoE.

6. Memory–accuracy trade-off is carefully quantified: GlowQ reduces additional GPU memory versus layer-wise restoration at fixed rank and achieves lower perplexity at equal memory (Fig. 4). The full GlowQ matches layer-wise accuracy while using fewer resident correction parameters (Table 7).

7. Compatibility and plug-and-play nature: GlowQ provides additive gains on top of GPTQ and BitsAndBytes (Table 4, top), underscoring orthogonality to PTQ choices. It also generalizes to an MoE model with near layer-wise accuracy but much lower low-rank parameter footprint, supported by covariance-aligned subspace alignment heatmaps (Sec. 4.5; Fig. 7–9).

8. Robustness and ablations that isolate design choices: whitening beats unweighted stacked SVD (Table 5); performance is stable across small calibration sizes and shrinkage levels (Table 9; Fig. 10), and across rank sweeps (Table 10). Randomized SVD hyperparameters are explored with clear guidance (Table 11–12).

9. Family-aware selective restoration policy: the paper characterizes restoration curves and chooses operating points per family (knee vs. gradual) with evidence (Fig. 3; Fig. 13), and compares multiple ranking metrics to select effective ones (Fig. 12).

10. Breadth across datatypes and contexts: GlowQ improves perplexity across integer (INT2/3/4) and microscaled FP formats (MXFP4/6, NVFP4) (Table 13) and maintains small deltas from FP16 on LongBench at 4K/8K contexts (Tables 14–15).

11. Clarity and reproducibility: precise statements and proofs (Appendix A; e.g., core equivalence in A.3 and RSVD guarantees in A.4), a compact notation table (Table 6), and an operational runtime description (anchor policy in Sec. 3.3) make the method easy to implement and verify.

Weaknesses:
Weaknesses and actionable suggestions

1. Latency evaluation scope and baselines
- Evidence: Sec. 4.3 (Table 3) and App. C (Table 8) compare only against a “Layerwise” AB baseline using identical custom W4A16 CUDA kernels on RTX 4090, with calibration on A100.
- Issue: The speedups are demonstrated relative to a single, internal baseline rather than against state-of-practice PTQ+LoRC inference stacks. It remains unclear whether the gains persist under different hardware and batching regimes.
- Suggestions:
  - Add end-to-end latency and throughput evaluations on datacenter accelerators (A100/H100) and across batch sizes (e.g., 1, 4, 16) and context lengths; report both prefill and decode scaling. Reproduce Table 3/8 on A100/H100.
  - Include runtime comparisons against at least one optimized low-rank correction baseline that uses its own best-known inference path (not just perplexity, as in Table 1–2), to show that caching, not just kernel idiosyncrasies, drives the improvements.

2. Per-model metric selection for GlowQ-S risks tuning to validation
- Evidence: “we adopt a model-specific scoring rule” and “per model, adopt the metric that yields the stronger outcome” (Sec. 4.6; Fig. 12–13; Sec. 3.3 Eq. 9–10).
- Issue: Choosing between g_ec and g_ner per model introduces extra selection overhead and a risk of cherry-picking. The procedure and its cost are not quantified, and robustness to a mis-specified metric is not evaluated.
- Suggestions:
  - Fix a single default metric per family (derived from Fig. 13’s shapes) and report performance without per-model metric switching; add a sensitivity study where the “wrong” metric is used.
  - Report the validation compute/time used to select the metric and to choose the restoration fraction (the “elbow” point for LLaMA), so total deployment cost is transparent.

3. Calibration/data-shift robustness insufficiently explored
- Evidence: Calibration uses 64 sequences of length 2048 (Sec. 4.1); stability is shown when varying N and shrinkage α (App. D.1–D.1.1; Table 9; Fig. 10). The whitened objective depends on Σx (Sec. 3.1.2; Eq. 3–4).
- Issue: The shared right subspace Bshared is tuned to the calibration distribution. No experiments test distribution shift (e.g., calibrate on one corpus, evaluate on another), so robustness of covariance alignment under shift is unknown.
- Suggestions:
  - Cross-calibration experiments: calibrate on one dataset and evaluate perplexity/accuracy on others (you already report C4 and WikiText‑2; mix them for calibration vs. evaluation).
  - Evaluate stability over domains (code, math, conversation) and report how often re-calibration is required; quantify the degradation if Σx is stale.

4. Practical memory footprint on very large models not demonstrated
- Evidence: App. D.1.2 (Fig. 11) profiles OPT up to 30B; main memory load comes from error and covariance tensors on CPU; “can be streamed/sharded” is proposed but not realized.
- Issue: For current 70B+ dense and large MoE models, the stacked-error and covariance collection may exceed practical CPU RAM or I/O budgets; the proposed mitigations are not validated.
- Suggestions:
  - Implement and benchmark streaming/sharded accumulation of Ecat and Σx (I/O time, peak RAM) on a 70B dense model; report wall-clock and memory versus N.
  - Provide a recipe for diagonal/low-rank Σx approximations with explicit trade-offs (accuracy vs. memory), including an ablation of full vs. diagonal Σx in Table 5’s “white vs. no-white” comparison.

5. Theoretical novelty is modest relative to the mathematical tools used
- Evidence: Core results rely on established formulations: stacked SVD/Eckart–Young–Mirsky (Sec. 3.1.1; Prop. 1), covariance weighting/whitening (Sec. 3.1.2; Props. 2–3), and QR-reduced RSVD (Sec. 3.2; Alg. 1, App. A.3–A.4).
- Issue: The theory specialized to the quantized-LLM setting does not go beyond optimality characterizations for low-rank approximation. There are no bounds that link the shared-B approximation to end-task degradation under quantization anisotropy.
- Suggestions:
  - Provide conditions under which shared B achieves near-layerwise error (e.g., a bound in terms of subspace angles between per-module right subspaces and the stacked/whitened subspace; relate to Fig. 5–6).
  - Add a sample-complexity result for estimating Σx (calibration N vs. recovery error for row(B⋆)), justifying the observed saturation at N≈32–64 (Fig. 10).

6. Limited MoE evidence and no MoE runtime results
- Evidence: Only Qwen1.5‑MoE‑A2.7B is evaluated (Table 4; Fig. 7–9), showing near-equality in perplexity to layerwise with memory savings.
- Issue: The generality to large, contemporary MoE stacks is not established; there is no latency/throughput measurement for MoE inference where shared B across experts might alter compute/memory traffic patterns.
- Suggestions:
  - Add MoE latency/throughput on at least one larger MoE (e.g., more experts/routers), and report expert-parameter memory savings and end-to-end TTFB/tok/s analogous to Table 3/8.
  - Evaluate whether selective restore interacts with expert routing (e.g., restore only the most frequently chosen experts) and quantify accuracy-latency trade-offs.

7. Accuracy gains are small on some models and settings; failure cases underexplored
- Evidence: Average gains are modest (e.g., “reducing perplexity on WikiText‑2 by 0.17% and increasing downstream accuracy by 0.42 pp” in Abstract); some models favor PTQ alone (OPT‑6.7B in Table 1).
- Issue: The paper does not analyze when GlowQ underperforms or provides negligible benefit, nor give guidance to disable it automatically.
- Suggestions:
  - Provide a diagnostic using g_ec/g_ner or the cross-basis alignment (Fig. 5–6) to predict when group-shared B will not help (e.g., small captured energy or poor alignment), and show an auto‑off policy that falls back to PTQ.

8. Deployment-side memory/traffic analysis is high-level
- Evidence: Fig. 4 shows additional GPU memory percentages versus rank and equal-memory perplexity; caching stores Rℓ = XB⊤shared once per group (Sec. 3.3; Eq. 7–8).
- Issue: Activations lifetime and memory traffic implications of caching are not profiled; it is unclear how gains scale with sequence length and batch.
- Suggestions:
  - Add a roofline-style or profiler-based analysis (bytes moved, tensor-lifetimes, GEMM counts) showing how caching reduces high-precision matmuls and DRAM traffic; sweep sequence length and batch to expose scaling limits.

Suggestions/Questions:
1. Latency baselines and profiling
- Can you provide end-to-end latency/throughput on datacenter GPUs (A100/H100) and across batch sizes and context lengths, mirroring Table 3 and App. C Table 8? This would help establish whether BX caching (Sec. 3.3; Eq. 7–8) generalizes beyond the single-RTX 4090 setup.
- Please include a runtime comparison against at least one optimized low‑rank correction baseline using its best-known inference path (not only accuracy as in Table 1–2). A kernel‑level profile (GEMM counts, bytes moved) or a roofline-style analysis quantifying how many high-precision BX matmuls are eliminated by caching would clarify where the TTFB/Dec gains in Table 3/8 come from.

2. Clarify the covariance estimator and its cost
- In practice, do you use the full Σx, a diagonal approximation, or a shrunk variant in all main experiments? Section A.2 mentions shrinkage and diagonal options; Table 5 shows large gains from “White” vs. “No‑White.” Please specify which estimator is used for each result table and the exact regularization (α) used.
- What is the wall-clock/time and memory impact of building Σx and Ecat on larger models (beyond the OPT-30B profile in Fig. 11)? A concrete recipe for streaming/sharded accumulation with measured peak RAM and I/O time on a ≥70B model would strengthen the practicality claim in Sec. D.1.2.

3. Robustness to calibration shift
- Since the objective is Σx-weighted (Sec. 3.1.2; Eq. 3–4), how robust is GlowQ when calibration data differ from the deployment domain? Please report cross-calibration experiments (e.g., calibrate on C4 and evaluate on WikiText‑2, and vice versa; or across domains such as code/math/chat). A small table akin to Table 5 would suffice.
- If Σx becomes stale, what is the degradation over time? A sensitivity analysis where Σx is replaced by an older estimator or a mismatched domain would help users decide when re‑calibration is needed.

4. Selective restoration policy (GlowQ‑S)
- Sec. 4.6 adopts per‑model metric selection between g_ec (Eq. 9) and g_ner (Eq. 10). Could you present results with a single default metric per family (as suggested by Fig. 13) and quantify the loss relative to per‑model switching? This would address concerns about selection overhead and robustness.
- What is the computational/engineering cost to find the “elbow” point for LLaMA (Fig. 3) or to choose the 50% budget on Qwen? Please report the validation tokens/FLOPs/time involved, so the total deployment overhead is transparent.

5. Theoretical characterization of shared-B vs. layerwise-B
- Beyond Prop. 1–3, can you provide a bound relating the error of shared B to the collection of per-module subspaces (e.g., via principal angles between the module-wise right subspaces and the stacked/whitened subspace)? Even a simple worst‑case or perturbation bound would help explain why Table 7 shows near parity with layerwise across models.
- Given the heavy‑tailed spectra in Fig. 2a–b, can you give a sample‑complexity statement for estimating row(B⋆) from N calibration sequences (consistent with the saturation at N≈32–64 in Fig. 10 and Table 9)?

6. MoE generality and runtime
- Sec. 4.5 reports perplexity on Qwen1.5‑MoE‑A2.7B (Table 4) and strong alignment heatmaps (Fig. 7–9). Could you add MoE latency/throughput analogous to Table 3/8 and quantify expert-parameter memory savings end‑to‑end?
- Does GlowQ‑S interact with routing? For instance, if only a subset of experts are frequently selected, can selective restore prioritize those experts and improve latency with minimal accuracy loss?

7. Anchor policy and grouping details
- Sec. 3.3 mentions an “anchor policy” (q anchors k,v; gate anchors up). Please specify exact tensor lifetimes and reuse patterns: where is Rℓ (Eq. 7) materialized/freed in a standard decoder block schedule, and how many times is it consumed in attention vs. MLP? A small schematic with tensor sizes would clarify memory traffic.
- For solo modules (e.g., o_proj, down_proj), have you quantified their relative cost and whether grouping variants (e.g., sharing across adjacent modules) provide additional wins?

8. Rank and budget selection
- You fix r=64 (Sec. 4.1), and Table 10 shows diminishing returns beyond r∈{32,64}. Could you provide a practical rule to select r per family or per group using the GSVD energy-capture curve (Sec. 3.3; Fig. 2c–d)? An automatic rank selection heuristic would make deployment less manual.
- In Table 1, GlowQ‑S restores 51% of layers for LLaMA‑3.2‑3B while others use 50%. Please confirm this small mismatch does not materially affect conclusions and, if needed, report exactly‑matched budgets.

9. Compatibility with PTQ pipelines and datatypes
- Table 4 shows additive gains on GPTQ and BnB; Table 13 covers multiple integer and microscaled FP datatypes. Are there any interactions with channel‑wise rescaling (e.g., AWQ) that change g_ner (Eq. 10) or the construction of Ecat? Please state whether Wg in g_ner is pre‑ or post‑rescaling and how that choice affects ranking.
- Do you foresee using GlowQ to partially correct activation quantization (W4A4, Table 1 lower block)? Any evidence that targeting activation-induced error (e.g., via a similar stacked/whitened objective) would further reduce the W4A4 gap?

10. Long-context and task-level stability
- LongBench results (Tables 14–15) show small deltas, but a few tasks degrade more (e.g., RepoBench‑P). Can you comment on where GlowQ underperforms and whether cross-basis alignment (Fig. 5–6) or g_ec/g_ner values could predict such cases? A simple diagnostic to “auto‑off” GlowQ when it offers negligible benefit (e.g., OPT‑6.7B in Table 1) would be very useful.

11. RSVD defaults and reproducibility
- Alg. 1 and Tables 11–12 suggest q=1–2 and modest p suffice. Please state the exact (p, q) defaults used in all main tables and whether they are model‑dependent. Also, list seeds, calibration corpus identity (Sec. 4.1 uses 64×2048 sequences), and any deviations per model family to ease reproduction.

12. Code release and integration
- Given the deployment‑oriented nature (Sec. 3.3), will you release kernels or integration guides for popular inference stacks? A brief note on how to integrate caching and selective restore into standard transformer runtimes (e.g., hooks for computing and reusing Rℓ) would materially increase impact.

Soundness: 4

Presentation: 3

Contribution: 4

Overall: 8

Confidence: 4

Conduct: NO

Ethics: No ethics review needed.

Summary:
This paper studies the training–inference mismatch in masked diffusion language models (DLMs) that arises when inference uses planner-guided denoising orders rather than the uniform unmasking assumed by standard training. Using a path-wise KL view of Markov chains, the authors prove that common planners (e.g., greedy ancestral) violate the standard DLM ELBO (§3.2; Proposition 3.1), and derive a general planner-aware ELBO (P-ELBO) that explicitly incorporates planner-based reverse dynamics (§3.3). The framework recovers the uniform ELBO as a special case and subsumes popular heuristics such as MaskGIT-style greedy and P2-style planning (§A.2, §A.4). Building on P-ELBO, they propose Planner-Aware Path Learning (PAPL), an efficient training objective that reweights the masked cross-entropy by planner-derived confidences via a soft-greedy planner with temperature, implemented as a one-line change (Algorithm 1; Figure 1; §3.4). Empirically, PAPL improves protein generation (e.g., +40% relative foldability with better pTM/pAE; Table 1; Figure 3), text generation on OWT (up to 4× MAUVE and substantially lower generative perplexity; Table 2), and code generation (HumanEval pass@1: 18.5→20.8; pass@10: 31.1→38.4; plus infilling gains; Tables 3–4). Ablations show faster convergence, stronger performance across sampling budgets, and robustness to temperature (Figure 2), with sensitivity to the planner temperature τ and weight α (Figure 4). Theoretical derivations and CTMC-based alternatives supporting the P-ELBO are provided in Appendix A.

Strengths:
Strengths
1. Precise diagnosis of the training–inference mismatch with a formal counterexample. Proposition 3.1 (§3.2; §A.1.7) rigorously shows that greedy ancestral sampling can violate the vanilla DLM ELBO, using an explicit L=2 construction. This directly challenges the common practice of planning-only-at-inference and motivates the rest of the paper.

2. Unifying, planner-aware ELBO with dual derivations. Proposition 3.2 (§3.3) provides a general P-ELBO that (i) reduces to the standard ELBO for uniform planners (Eθ,ϕ2 vanishes), and (ii) admits both discrete-time and CTMC proofs (§A.1.4, §A.3), strengthening correctness and situating the result within existing DLM theory.

3. Coverage of multiple planners in one framework. The paper specializes P-ELBO to concrete planners—uniform, greedy (Corollary A.9), soft-greedy (Corollary A.10), and P2-style planners with remasking (Proposition A.14; Corollary A.15; §A.4)—including derivations of the planned transition probabilities (Eq. 4; §A.1.6). This turns a collection of heuristics into principled instances of a single objective.

4. A practical training recipe that is minimally invasive and efficient. Planner-Aware Path Learning (PAPL) (Algorithm 1; §3.4) becomes a “one-line” modification of the masked cross-entropy by replacing uniform weights with planner-derived weights (Eq. 7), while reusing uniform masking to avoid path simulation. The stabilization via interpolation (α) is motivated and empirically supported (Figure 5; §C.1–C.2).

5. Strong, cross-domain empirical validation under matched configurations. 
   - Proteins: 40% relative foldability improvement (59.40% vs. 42.43%) with better pTM (0.72→0.65) and much lower pAE (8.97→12.00) at the same 150M scale, while preserving entropy/diversity (Table 1; Figure 3).
   - Text: consistent MAUVE gains up to 0.067 at T=128 and markedly lower Gen PPL across T (Table 2), with planner comparisons confirming P2-Self superiority (Table 5).
   - Code: consistent improvements on HumanEval/MBPP (e.g., 18.5→20.8 pass@1; 31.1→38.4 pass@10) and better infilling (Tables 3–4).

6. Robustness and optimization benefits quantified. Figure 2 shows faster convergence, stronger performance across sampling steps, and greater resilience to temperature, both from-scratch and fine-tuning. Hyperparameter sweeps (τ, α) reveal actionable guidance (Figure 4), with sharper planners (lower τ) and moderate α improving outcomes.

7. Analytical insights beyond the main bound. The paper characterizes the form of the optimal planner for a fixed denoiser (Proposition A.8), clarifying how planner mass should align with path likelihoods under the current denoiser. This offers a theoretically grounded target for future planner learning.

8. Methodological transparency via ablations of approximations. The impact of detaching the planner and reusing uniform-masked states is explicitly measured (Table 7), and instability of the pure PAPL loss is documented (Figure 5). This candor clarifies why the final recipe diverges from the exact ELBO while still yielding consistent gains.

9. Thorough experimental and evaluation detail enabling reproducibility. Appendix B provides concrete dataset, training, and evaluation protocols—e.g., precise protein foldability criterion combining pLDDT, pTM, and pAE (B.1), OWT setup and metrics (B.2.1), and code benchmarks/protocols (B.3.1)—facilitating independent verification.

Weaknesses:
Weaknesses and actionable suggestions

1. Theory–practice gap in the deployed objective
   - The practical loss departs materially from the derived P-ELBO: it (i) reuses uniformly masked xk rather than planner-driven states, and (ii) drops the Eθ,ϕ2 correction by detaching gradients through the planner (§3.4; §A.2.3). Table 7 quantifies loss-level effects but does not show sample-quality consequences.
   - Action: Evaluate tighter approximations to the P-ELBO: (a) truncated planned rollouts that simulate j planned steps to form xk (small j), with importance weighting to control variance; (b) a stop-grad schedule that keeps gradients for E2 early and detaches late; (c) k-step “greedy-unroll” on toy lengths where the exact greedy ELBO (Cor. A.9) is tractable, reporting both loss and generation quality.

2. Training–inference planner mismatch remains in experiments
   - Models are trained with soft-greedy self-planning but evaluated with P2 at inference (§4.1), while the P2-aware ELBO is only analyzed (not used) due to computational cost (§A.4, last paragraph).
   - Action: Add at least one planner-matched setting: train with a P2-style approximation (e.g., P2-TopK with small k or low η) and decode with the same P2; report a 2×2 matrix (train-planner × test-planner) to confirm alignment benefits beyond soft-greedy→P2 transfer (cf. Table 5).

3. Unclear impact of planner weighting on rare/hard tokens
   - PAPL emphasizes high-confidence positions (Eq. 7; Fig. 1). While entropy/diversity are reported, they do not reveal long-tail behavior (Table 1; Table 2).
   - Action: Report token-level (or n-gram) accuracy stratified by frequency bins for text/code, amino-acid usage drift for proteins, and rare-token perplexity to ensure the weighting does not erode recall on infrequent symbols.

4. Instability and lack of stabilization ablations beyond proteins
   - Pure PAPL is unstable (Figure 5), and stabilization uses interpolation with the vanilla loss (α) and a soft-greedy temperature τ (§3.4; §C.1–C.2). The only hyperparameter sweeps are on protein foldability (Figure 4).
   - Action: Provide τ and α sweeps and training curves on text and code to establish robustness across domains; consider weight clipping/normalization for wi, or curricula that increase α over training.

5. Statistical rigor and novelty checks in protein evaluation
   - Only 100 sequences per length are generated (§4.1 Setup), and results are reported without uncertainty; novelty vs. training data is not assessed.
   - Action: Report confidence intervals via bootstrap per length and on the aggregated “foldability.” Add homology filtering/nearest-neighbor identity to UniRef50 to quantify novelty. Provide per-length distributions of pLDDT/pTM/pAE to rule out length-specific artifacts.

6. Planner-aware evaluation is not isolated from planner quality
   - Gains are reported under P2 inference (Tables 1–2, 4), which itself is strong (Table 5), making it hard to attribute improvements purely to planner-aware training.
   - Action: Evaluate under multiple inference planners (uniform ancestral, greedy, probability margin, P2) for the same denoisers, showing whether PAPL consistently improves each decoding rule (beyond the text-only Table 5).

7. Baseline comparability and reporting for code and text
   - Text: “All checkpoints are reused from prior work” (B.2.1), and AR results are not trained under the same recipe. Code: DLM (0.5B) is compared to AR and edit-flow models at 1.3B with different data/training (Table 4).
   - Action: Include matched-size AR and diffusion baselines trained under the same corpus/recipe (e.g., a 0.5B AR on FineCode, and a 0.5B MDLM without PAPL). Report decoding budgets (samples per prompt for pass@10), and wall-clock/compute to contextualize pass@k gains.

8. Efficiency claims lack quantitative support
   - PAPL is claimed to be a “one-line code change” with “no additional computational overhead” (§3.4; §6), but no throughput or memory numbers are provided.
   - Action: Report training speed (tokens/sec), GPU memory, and step time versus MDLM across domains. If overhead is negligible, numbers will substantiate the claim.

9. Limited validation of P2-style extensions
   - The P2 generalization is developed theoretically (Proposition A.14; Corollary A.15) but not instantiated due to perceived cost (§A.4).
   - Action: Implement a lightweight P2-aware training variant (e.g., TopK with small K or stochastic subsetting) and evaluate how much additional alignment it buys over soft-greedy PAPL, especially under high-remasking regimes (vary η as in §A.4).

10. Oracle settings in code infilling can be misleading
   - Table 3 includes “DLM (0.5B) + PAPL (Oracle length)” with very large gains, which is an unrealistic setting for deployment.
   - Action: Move oracle results to the appendix and add non-oracle length-control baselines (e.g., learned length predictors or P2-based length heuristics) to quantify practical benefits.

   - Action: On synthetic small-L tasks, compare ELBO-tight training (exact or near-exact) against PAPL, reporting likelihood along the planned path and generation quality, to validate that the approximations preserve benefits.

   - Only unconditional OWT is considered; MAUVE gains (Table 2) are still far from AR and may not translate to conditional tasks.
   - Action: Add at least one conditional text task (e.g., short-form continuation or summarization) to demonstrate that planner-aware training helps when conditioning constrains the path, or clarify limits to unconditional generation.

Since PAPL upweights high-confidence positions (Eq. 7), can you report token- (or n-gram-) level accuracy split by frequency bins for text/code, and amino-acid usage drift for proteins? This would allay concerns that planner weighting harms rare/hard symbols despite similar entropy/diversity (Tables 1–2).

7. Protein evaluation rigor. In §4.1 you generate 100 sequences per length without uncertainty estimates. Please add CIs (bootstrap) per-length and on the aggregate “foldability,” and a novelty analysis (e.g., nearest-neighbor sequence identity to UniRef50) to confirm gains are not due to memorization. Also show distributions of pLDDT/pTM/pAE by length.
