Summary:
The paper introduces EarthMind, a unified multimodal LLM for Earth Observation that natively handles single-sensor and cross-sensor (optical + SAR) inputs and supports image-, region-, and pixel-level tasks, producing both text and segmentation outputs (Sec. 3.1, Fig. 2). Its core contribution is Hierarchical Cross-modal Attention (HCA), a two-stage fusion mechanism—cross-sensor attention followed by text-guided attention—that adaptively balances modality contributions and mitigates optical bias, as quantified by the proposed Modality Attention Score (Sec. 3.2; Fig. 4). The authors curate FusionEO, a 30K paired optical–SAR instruction-tuning corpus generated via a three-stage pipeline (metadata, RoI-based summarization, and self-instruct VQA) to support cross-sensor learning (Sec. 3.3; Fig. C). They also release EarthMind-Bench, a 2,841-pair benchmark spanning 10 perception and reasoning tasks with optical-only, SAR-only, and fused settings, combining multiple-choice, GPT-scored open-ended, and mIoU-based segmentation evaluations (Sec. 4; Fig. 3). Empirically, EarthMind (4B) achieves state-of-the-art results on EarthMind-Bench across all modalities (Tab. 1), surpasses prior EO MLLMs and proprietary baselines on diverse public image-, region-, and pixel-level benchmarks (Tab. 2–3), and demonstrates clear gains from HCA over naive fusion strategies (Tab. 4) alongside ablations validating multi-granular and multi-sensor co-training (Tabs. D–E).

Strengths:
Strengths

1. Clear, well-motivated problem framing: The paper isolates a concrete limitation of current EO MLLMs—single-sensor reliance—and argues for cross-sensor fusion with specific modality trade-offs (optical vs. SAR) (Sec. 1; Fig. 1). Related Work explicitly notes that “none explicitly assess MLLM performance under multi-sensor scenarios” (Sec. 2), sharpening the contribution’s significance.

2. Technically novel and targeted fusion design: The Hierarchical Cross-modal Attention (HCA) couples (i) bidirectional cross-sensor attention with spatial alignment and (ii) text-guided attention to derive query-relevant fusion weights (Sec. 3.2; Fig. 2, bottom). This architecture is lightweight, reduces sequence length by producing fused N×D tokens instead of concatenation (Sec. 3.2), and is tailored to mitigate the observed optical bias.

3. Diagnostic metric for modality imbalance: The Modality Attention Score (MAS) provides a concrete layer-wise measure of optical vs. SAR attention share (Sec. 3.2; Tab. 4 right, “gap from MAS using Eq. 1”), enabling principled analysis of fusion behavior beyond end metrics.

4. Strong empirical validation of HCA: Compared to single-modality and naive fusion (concatenate/average/native attention), HCA yields clear gains on challenging tasks that most benefit from cross-sensor cues—Object Counting (+2.6 over best naive) and Spatial Relationship (+21.0) while also improving Referring Segmentation (+1.6 mIoU) (Tab. 4 left). The modality attention gap is substantially reduced across layers (Tab. 4 right), and visualizations show query- and region-specific modality weighting (Fig. 4a–b).

5. Unified multi-granular capability, including pixel-level grounding: The system integrates an LLM with global and grounding encoders plus a mask decoder triggered by a special <SEG> token (Sec. 3.1; Appendix D). This enables end-to-end text and mask outputs across image/region/pixel tasks in a single model (Fig. 2).

6. Practical non-RGB handling via video-like formatting: Treating SAR and multispectral inputs as video-like sequences enables reuse of shared encoders while exploiting spectral “temporal-like” dependencies (Sec. 3.1). Ablations quantify practical preprocessing choices for SAR and multispectral bands (Appendix H, Tab. C).

7. Substantive dataset contribution (FusionEO): A 30K paired optical–SAR corpus created via a three-stage automated pipeline—metadata, RoI-based summarization that overlays masks, and self-instruct VQA—directly supports cross-sensor instruction tuning (Sec. 3.3; Fig. C). Scaling curves show consistent gains and that RoI injection adds fine-grained supervision (Fig. 4c).

8. First benchmark to systematically evaluate fused multi-sensor MLLMs with multi-granular tasks: EarthMind-Bench (2,841 pairs) spans 10 tasks across perception and reasoning with optical-only, SAR-only, and optical+SAR modes, mixing multiple-choice, GPT-scored open-ended, and mIoU segmentation (Sec. 4; Fig. 3). Expert-driven annotation guidelines and cross-validation increase reliability (Appendix E). The comparison table further situates novelty versus prior benchmarks (Appendix C, Tab. A).

9. Broad, consistent SOTA across modalities and granularities: On EarthMind-Bench, EarthMind (4B) leads in all three settings; in the fused mode it attains M-Avg 70.0 and O-Avg 3.02, surpassing GPT-4o (61.1 and 2.28) notably on fine-grained tasks like Spatial Relationship (59.7 vs. 43.5) and Object Counting (52.4 vs. 31.6) (Tab. 1). It also delivers strong single-sensor results, including SAR-only (M-Avg 61.3; Tab. 1). On public datasets it achieves 428.2 CIDEr on DIOR-RSVG and 82.2/62.6 mIoU on RRSIS-D/RefSegRS, outperforming specialized segmentation methods (Tab. 2).

10. Demonstrated cross-sensor and cross-granularity co-training benefits: Joint training across granularities improves both region and pixel tasks (e.g., RSVG 428.2 and RRSIS-D 82.2 vs. single-granularity baselines; Appendix Tab. D). Joint multi-sensor training improves both RGB and SAR evaluation, and especially their fusion (70.6 vs. ≤69.0; Appendix Tab. E).

11. Sensible curriculum and efficient adaptation: A three-stage curriculum (general image-language → EO RGB → multi-sensor) materially improves performance across all granularities (Appendix Tabs. F–G). Despite strong results, the model remains relatively compact (4B) with LoRA training and 8×A100 setup (Sec. 5.1), strengthening practical significance.

12. Clarity through concrete figures and task definitions: The architecture schematic (Fig. 2), benchmark task wheel and examples (Fig. 3), attention visualizations and dataset scaling (Fig. 4), and detailed annotation guidelines (Appendix E) make the approach and evaluation interpretable and reproducible.

Weaknesses:
Weaknesses and actionable suggestions

1. Incomplete mathematical specification of the core method
- Evidence: multiple “formula-not-decoded” placeholders in Sec. 3.1–3.2 where MAS, cross-sensor attention, text-guided attention, and fusion equations should appear.
- Why it matters: hampers reproducibility and makes it difficult to assess what is learned vs. hard-coded (e.g., normalization, temperatures, pooling/alignments, how λ is trained).
- Action: restore all missing equations; specify shapes, normalization (softmax temperature, layernorm), positional encodings, the pooling scheme for spatial alignment, how λ is initialized/optimized, and where HCA layers are inserted relative to the LLM stack.

2. Fusion baselines are too weak to substantiate HCA’s advantage
- Evidence: Tab. 4 compares against Concatenation, Element-wise Average, and a “Naive Attention” (cosine-sim) baseline.
- Why it matters: These do not reflect standard, stronger fusion alternatives.
- Action: include (i) modality-gated concatenation (learnable scalar gates per modality), (ii) co-attention blocks between optical/SAR (cross-attention with learned queries/keys), (iii) FiLM/adapter-based conditioning, and (iv) a radar–optical feature-fusion front-end such as CROMA (Fuller et al., 2023) or MCANet (Li et al., 2022) plugged before the LLM. Report accuracy/mIoU and efficiency vs. HCA.

3. Attention “gap” analysis is not apples-to-apples
- Evidence: Tab. 4 (right) uses MAS from LLM self-attention for “Concatenation” but uses “learned fusion weights” for HCA.
- Why it matters: fusion weights are not the same object as downstream LLM attention; conclusions about balancing at the LLM level may be confounded.
- Action: compute MAS after HCA as well (on the LLM’s self-attention over fused tokens traced back to source modality contributions); report both and correlate “gap” with performance across tasks/samples.

4. Evaluation bias via GPT-based judging combined with GPT-generated training data
- Evidence: FusionEO is synthesized with GPT-4o (Sec. 3.3; Fig. C); open-ended tasks on EarthMind-Bench use GPT-based scoring (Sec. 4; Fig. B).
- Why it matters: style alignment with the judge can inflate scores.
- Action: add a human evaluation on a stratified subset; report inter-rater agreement. Also report robustness to alternative judges/prompts (e.g., two GPT prompts) and complementary automatic metrics for captioning (CIDEr/SPICE). Provide results using only multiple-choice/mIoU to show conclusions do not hinge on the judge.

5. Fairness of multispectral comparisons and fused prompting for proprietary baselines
- Evidence: Sec. 5.3 notes baselines use RGB while EarthMind exploits full spectra; Tab. 1 fused-mode rows for GPT-4V/4o use a naïve multi-image interface.
- Why it matters: architectural advantage and prompting may confound claimed fusion gains.
- Action: (i) add a control where EarthMind is restricted to RGB on multispectral benchmarks (Tab. 3); (ii) provide carefully engineered multi-image prompts for GPT-4V/4o (e.g., per-image analysis + synthesis) and report whether performance improves; (iii) include an EarthMind variant that uses concatenation without HCA but identical training to isolate HCA’s effect in the fused setting.

6. Missing efficiency evidence despite efficiency claims
- Evidence: Sec. 3.2 states HCA “reduces sequence length,” but no runtime/memory/throughput comparisons are reported.
- Why it matters: practical value hinges on latency/VRAM, especially with video-like formatting for multispectral inputs (Sec. 3.1).
- Action: report tokens, FLOPs, VRAM, and latency for single-sensor, concatenation, and HCA across band/frame counts; include a speed–accuracy tradeoff with different N and pooling factors.

7. Limited robustness analysis to misregistration and adverse conditions
- Evidence: Stage 1 of HCA assumes pooled alignment (Sec. 3.2), but robustness to cross-sensor spatial shifts, speckle, and cloud cover is not quantified; Fig. 4(a) offers only anecdotal cases.
- Action: evaluate on synthetic misregistration (e.g., pixel shifts/affine jitter), speckle augmentation for SAR, and cloud-obscured optical subsets. Plot performance vs. shift magnitude and noise level.

8. Missing component ablations within HCA
- Evidence: Sec. 3.2 introduces two stages (cross-sensor and text-guided), but there is no study isolating their contributions or λ sensitivity.
- Action: ablate “Stage 1 only,” “Stage 2 only,” and vary λ; report per-task effects and visualize how per-task modality weights (Fig. 4b) change.

9. Generalization to multispectral is not uniformly superior and underexplored
- Evidence: On SoSAT-LCZ42, EarthMind (58.3) underperforms EarthDial (60.7) in Tab. 3; Appendix H Tab. C shows single-band grouping is slightly better but more costly.
- Action: analyze failure modes on SoSAT-LCZ42; test token-reduction with single-band grouping to close the gap; include per-class results to identify spectra-sensitive categories.

10. Statistical reliability and variance
- Evidence: No confidence intervals or multi-seed results are provided for key metrics (Tab. 1–3; Tab. 4).
- Action: report mean±std over ≥3 seeds for EarthMind-Bench M-Avg/O-Avg and core external benchmarks (RSVG, RRSIS-D), and conduct paired significance tests for HCA vs. best baseline.

11. Benchmark transparency details could be strengthened
- Evidence: Sec. 4 and Appendix E describe expert verification but lack geographic/source composition breakdowns and inter-annotator agreement.
- Action: publish per-source dataset proportions, geographic coverage, and task-wise agreement statistics; release strict data cards and licenses.

Suggestions/Questions:
Questions and suggestions for the rebuttal

1. Missing equations and precise HCA specification
- Sec. 3.1–3.2 contain “formula-not-decoded” placeholders (e.g., MAS, cross-sensor attention, text-guided attention, adaptive fusion). Please provide the exact formulas, shapes, normalization (softmax temperature, layer/layernorm use), positional encodings, and the spatial pooling/alignment used to obtain N×D tokens for SAR/optical before HCA. How is λ initialized and optimized? Where is HCA inserted relative to the VLP/LLM stack in Fig. 2?

2. Modality Attention Score comparability
- In Tab. 4 (right), the “Concatenate Gap” is computed from MAS (Eq. 1), while the HCA gap is “derived from the learned fusion weights.” Could you recompute MAS on the LLM’s self-attention after HCA (tracing fused tokens back to source-modality contributions) so the gaps are comparable? Correlating that gap with task performance across samples would strengthen the causal story (Sec. 3.2; Fig. 4b).

3. HCA component ablations
- Please ablate Stage 1 (cross-sensor attention) vs. Stage 2 (text-guided attention) and report the sensitivity to λ on the six EarthMind-Bench subtasks listed in Tab. 4 (left). Per-task trends would clarify where text guidance matters most.

4. Stronger fusion baselines
- Beyond Concatenation/Element-wise/Naive Attention (Tab. 4), can you add: (i) learnable modality gates on concatenated tokens; (ii) symmetric cross-attention (“co-attention” blocks) between modalities; (iii) FiLM/adapter-style conditioning; and (iv) a radar–optical fusion front-end (e.g., CROMA; MCANet) before the VLP? Reporting both accuracy/mIoU and compute would more rigorously position HCA.

5. Efficiency evidence
- Sec. 3.2 claims HCA “reduces sequence length.” Please provide token counts, FLOPs, peak VRAM, and latency on A100-80G for single-sensor, concatenation, and HCA across representative band/frame counts. Where does HCA sit on the speed–accuracy tradeoff?

6. Robustness to misregistration and noise
- HCA relies on “adaptive pooling to align optical features with SAR dimensions” (Sec. 3.2). How robust is EarthMind to cross-sensor misalignment or SAR speckle? Please report performance vs. synthetic pixel/affine shifts and speckle levels; include a cloud-obscured optical subset analysis.

7. Clarify dataset size inconsistency for FusionEO
- The Abstract and Appendix G say “30K,” Sec. 3.3 says “30K,” while Sec. 6 states “20K paired instruction-tuning dataset.” Please reconcile the numbers, and specify train/val splits.

8. Clarify LLM-use disclosure inconsistency
- Appendix B states “no Large Language Models were used,” but Sec. 3.3/Appendix G explicitly use GPT-4o for caption/VQA generation. Please correct the disclosure and discuss any implications.

9. Benchmark leakage safeguards
- EarthMind-Bench is built from test sets of several datasets (Sec. 4), and FusionEO samples training splits of the same sources (Appendix G). Please confirm no geographic tile overlap or near-duplicate pairs across train (FusionEO) and test (EarthMind-Bench), and detail your duplicate-removal criteria.

10. Open-ended evaluation bias
- Since FusionEO uses GPT-4o and EarthMind-Bench open-ended tasks are GPT-scored (Sec. 4; Fig. B), could you provide a human evaluation on a stratified subset with inter-annotator agreement, plus robustness to alternative judges/prompts? Also add caption metrics (CIDEr/SPICE) and report EarthMind-Bench results restricted to MC+mIoU only.

11. Fairness of multispectral comparisons
- Sec. 5.3 notes baselines use RGB while EarthMind uses full MS bands. Please add a control where EarthMind is restricted to RGB on BigEarthNet/SoSAT-LCZ42 (Tab. 3) to quantify pure architecture/training gains.

12. GPT-4 baseline prompting for fused inputs
- For GPT-4V/4o in the fused setting (Tab. 1), what multi-image prompt design was used? Provide the exact prompts and an ablation with a stronger chain-of-analysis-and-synthesis prompt per image before fusion. Does their performance improve materially?

13. Encoder training/freeze details
- Sec. 5.1: you “train only the projector, the LLM via LoRA, and the mask decoder.” Are the visual and grounding encoders (InternVL2, SAM2; Sec. 5.1) fully frozen? Any adapter tuning? Clarify visual token counts per frame and final token budget fed to the LLM.

14. Pixel-level grounding behavior
- Appendix D: if “[SEG] is not generated,” you treat it as “not present.” How often does this occur on Referring Segmentation in EarthMind-Bench? Do you enforce decoding constraints to ensure [SEG] emission when a mask is expected?

15. Multispectral “video-like” formatting
- Sec. 3.1: bands are “grouped in triplets” into multi-frame sequences. Which band orderings are used for Sentinel-2 (or other MS sensors)? Are groupings fixed per sensor or learned? Could you share an ablation on EarthMind-Bench tasks (not just classification in Tab. C) comparing three-band vs. single-band grouping with token-reduction?

16. Statistical reliability
- Please report mean±std over at least 3 seeds for key EarthMind-Bench metrics (M-Avg, O-Avg, Referring Seg.) and for DIOR-RSVG/RRSIS-D (Tab. 2), and provide significance tests for HCA vs. the best non-HCA baseline.

17. Per-task error analysis
- Fig. 4b suggests modality weighting varies by task. Could you provide error breakdowns (e.g., confusion for Object Counting and Spatial Relationship) stratified by optical quality (clouds, shadow) and SAR SNR to demonstrate when SAR helps most?

Summary:
This paper addresses text spotting in complex artistic images by fine-tuning multimodal LLMs with a joint SFT+RL approach. It introduces SupGRPO, which integrates GRPO with a matching-based online SFT applied only to coordinate tokens, mitigating GRPO’s reward sparsity for localization and SFT’s instance-order dependency (Fig. 1b, Sec. 3.3). The GRPO side uses four rule-based rewards—format, word-level text F1, IoU precision, and IoU recall—to align training with non-differentiable evaluation metrics (Sec. 3.2, Fig. 2). Matching for SFT supervises coordinates only when predicted and ground-truth text match and IoU > 0, and the combined loss is given in Eq. (10). The authors also curate ATS, an artistic text spotting dataset with 6.5k training and 2.5k test images, annotated with word-level quadrilateral boxes and transcriptions (Sec. 4.1, Fig. 3). Experiments on Qwen2.5-VL (3B/7B) and Qwen3-VL-8B show that SupGRPO improves both recognition and detection over SFT-only, GRPO-only, and a two-stage SFT→GRPO baseline across Total-Text, ICDAR15, CTW1500, and ATS (Tabs. 1–3), with ablations confirming complementary effects of SFT (detection) and GRPO (recognition) (Sec. 4.4, Tabs. 5–8).

Strengths:
1. Clear, original training paradigm that couples RL with targeted SFT. SupGRPO integrates GRPO with a matching-based online SFT applied only to coordinate tokens (Sec. 3.3, Eq. (9)–(10), Fig. 2), directly addressing two concrete issues: GRPO’s reward sparsity for localization and standard SFT’s instance order dependency (Fig. 1b).

2. Task-aligned reward design. The four rewards—format, word-level content F1, IoU precision, IoU recall—are carefully motivated to match non-differentiable evaluation metrics (Sec. 3.2). The rationale for choosing word-level F1 over soft metrics (ANLS/Edit Distance) and the multiset handling of duplicates to penalize hallucinated repeats are thoughtful and practically important (Eq. (6)).

3. Evidence-backed decomposition of detection vs. recognition gains. The paper establishes a non-trivial empirical insight—“SFT yields more significant improvements in text detection… whereas GRPO provides a more substantial boost to text recognition” (Sec. 4.4, Tab. 5)—and then capitalizes on it with a joint objective (Eq. (10)) that materially improves both.

4. Strong, consistent, and broad empirical improvements. SupGRPO outperforms SFT-only, GRPO-only, and two-stage SFT→GRPO across four datasets and multiple base models (Tabs. 1–3). Notably large gains on ATS recognition and detection (Tab. 1, Tab. 2), validating the approach in the intended hard regime.

5. Thorough ablations that isolate design choices. The paper dissects token-level supervision (all/text/location tokens) and shows that supervising only location tokens with matching is best for joint performance (Sec. 4.4, Tab. 6–7). It also demonstrates that separating precision and recall rewards is superior to a single F1 reward for detection (Tab. 8).

6. Effective matching criterion for online SFT. The combined text+IoU matching used to supervise coordinates outperforms IoU-only and text-only alternatives (Sec. 4.4, Tab. 7), providing concrete evidence that the matching strategy is crucial rather than incidental.

7. Training stability improvements are quantified. SupGRPO yields higher and smoother reward curves and lower, more stable loss than vanilla GRPO (App. Fig. 5), supporting the claim that online SFT regularizes exploration updates.

8. Practical engineering that improves parseability and evaluation. The format reward (Sec. 3.2) ensures outputs are structurally valid JSON-like lists, which is a pragmatic and often overlooked necessity for RL fine-tuning of MLLMs on structured tasks.

9. Demonstrated scalability and generality. The method works across Qwen2.5-VL 3B/7B and Qwen3-VL-8B (Sec. 4.2; Tabs. 1–3), and scaling to 8B narrows the detection gap to specialized spotters (e.g., ATS 86.2 vs. ABCNet v2 87.5 in Tab. 2; Total-Text/IC15 in Tab. 3).

10. New, targeted benchmark with clear characterization. ATS specifically targets artistic text, is non-trivial in size (6.5k/2.5k), and is well described with qualitative exemplars (Fig. 3) and distribution statistics (App. Fig. 4). It fills a gap not captured by standard scene-text sets (Sec. 4.1).

11. Reproducibility-oriented presentation. The method is specified with concrete equations (Sec. 3.1–3.3), explicit hyperparameters (Sec. 4.2: LoRA, batch size, G=8 samples, β=0.04, λ=1e-4), training data composition (~30k samples), and open-source training frameworks (Open-R1/VLM-R1), facilitating reimplementation.

12. Compelling qualitative behaviors. Visuals show better localization than MLLMs and broader recognition coverage than specialized spotters, including multilingual spotting and plausible completion under occlusion (App. Fig. 6), reinforcing the quantitative claims.

Weaknesses:
1. Recognition comparisons mix incompatible protocols, conflating conclusions. In Sec. 4.3 and Tab. 1, specialized spotters are scored only when detection is correct (detection-coupled), while MLLMs are scored on recognition from the whole image “even if the specific localization … is less precise.” This favors MLLMs and makes cross-family rankings hard to interpret. Actionable: add an end-to-end spotting metric that requires joint box+text correctness for all methods (e.g., IoU ≥ 0.5 and exact text match via bipartite matching), and report both detection-free recognition and detection-coupled recognition for MLLMs.

2. Reward decomposition is misaligned with true end-to-end objectives. Sec. 3.2 optimizes text F1 over a bag-of-words and detection precision/recall over IoU matches independently. This allows progress on boxes without correct text (and vice versa), whereas standard end-to-end spotting requires a joint match. Actionable: introduce an instance-level, bipartite-matched spotting reward that scores a pair only when both IoU and text are correct (e.g., per-pair reward of 1 if IoU ≥ τ and text exact match, else 0), or a weighted version that combines IoU and exact/near-exact text. Compare against the current “Text + P + R” reward in Tab. 8.

3. Missing permutation-invariant SFT baselines. The central argument against standard SFT is “instance order dependency” (Fig. 1b, Sec. 3.3). However, the paper does not test order-agnostic SFT trained with matching (Hungarian) over predicted/GT instances—common in DETR-style models (Carion et al., 2020; TESTR, Zhang et al., 2022). Actionable: implement a permutation-invariant SFT baseline that supervises both text and coordinates after bipartite matching, and compare it against SupGRPO to establish the necessity of RL.

4. No sensitivity analysis of key couplings/thresholds. The combined loss weight λ in Eq. (10) is fixed to 1e-4; β (KL in Eq. (1)) is 0.04; GRPO uses G=8 samples (Sec. 4.2). The matching IoU threshold is inconsistent—“IoU > 0” in Sec. 3.3 versus 0.3 in Sec. 4.4/Tab. 7. Actionable: (a) report performance vs. λ, β, G, and the matching IoU threshold; (b) standardize and justify the chosen IoU threshold; (c) consider curriculum/schedules for λ to reduce interference between RL and SFT.

5. Coordinate-only SFT leaves recognition to sparse RL signals. Ablations (Tab. 7) show “+ Text Tokens SFT” boosts recognition (84.1) but hurts detection (60.8). The current choice avoids text SFT altogether, likely underutilizing supervised signals for hard texts. Actionable: devise a permutation-invariant text SFT (via matching) and explore gated/coordinated weighting so text-token SFT does not suppress detection (e.g., alternate updates, uncertainty-aware weights, or text-SFT only on high-IoU matches). Report the accuracy/efficiency trade-off.

6. Limited reporting on computational efficiency and stability beyond curves. While App. Fig. 5 shows smoother rewards/losses for SupGRPO, there is no wall-clock, GPU-hours, or throughput comparison against SFT-only and GRPO-only, nor sample-efficiency metrics. Actionable: report training time, GPU budget, and inference latency for TS-VL-3B/7B/8B; include convergence speed (steps to target F1) to substantiate claims that SupGRPO is “more stable and efficient.”

7. ATS dataset documentation is insufficient for assessing quality and potential bias. Sec. 4.1 and App. Fig. 4 give distributions, but there is no annotation protocol, inter-annotator agreement, de-duplication across train/test, or license/source attributions for re-use from TextSeg/WAS. Actionable: add (a) QA procedures and spot-check error rates; (b) near-duplicate analysis across splits; (c) guidelines for text normalization (case, punctuation); (d) licensing and ethical sourcing; and (e) style/category tags to enable stratified evaluation.

8. Generalization to unseen artistic styles is not stress-tested. Tab. 4 shows that adding ATS to training improves ATS test performance, but does not quantify robustness to new artistic distributions. Actionable: perform leave-one-style-out evaluations within ATS, or train without ATS and test on ATS subsets grouped by style/complexity (Fig. 3 categories), to measure true cross-domain robustness.

9. Ambiguity in detection metrics and thresholds undermines reproducibility and comparability. Tabs. 2–3 report a single “Detection” score without specifying IoU threshold(s), matching (one-to-one/greedy), or whether transcription correctness is required (Sec. 4.3 implies not). Actionable: (a) specify detection metric details; (b) add PR curves or AP at multiple IoUs; (c) report an end-to-end detection+recognition score on the same protocol.

10. Two-stage baselines are narrow. Only SFT→GRPO is tested (Tabs. 1–3), but not GRPO→SFT or alternating schedules that might preserve SFT’s localization while leveraging GRPO’s recognition gains. Actionable: add GRPO→SFT and interleaved schedules; report where they fail/succeed relative to SupGRPO to strengthen the joint-training claim.

11. Reward design for text may still encourage undesirable behaviors. Although Sec. 3.2 uses multisets to penalize hallucinated duplicates, bag-of-words F1 disregards word order and grouping, which are crucial in artistic compositions (Sec. 4.1). Actionable: augment text rewards with instance-level correctness via matching, or incorporate phrase-level rewards (e.g., bigram F1) to discourage shuffling/hallucination while keeping non-differentiability aligned with evaluation.

Suggestions/Questions:
1. Evaluation protocol for recognition (Sec. 4.3; Tab. 1).  
   - Can you add an end-to-end spotting metric for all methods that requires joint correctness (IoU ≥ τ plus exact text via bipartite matching) so specialized spotters and MLLMs are directly comparable? Please report both the current “recognition from the full image” and a detection-coupled recognition for MLLMs. This could change the interpretation of Tab. 1.

2. Reward alignment with end-to-end objectives (Sec. 3.2; Eq. (6)–(8)).  
   - Your rewards decompose text (bag-of-words F1) and detection (IoU precision/recall). Did you try an instance-level, bipartite-matched reward that grants credit only when both IoU ≥ τ and text match exactly? A comparison against “Text & P & R” in Tab. 8 would clarify whether joint scoring improves policy learning.

3. Permutation-invariant SFT baseline (Sec. 3.3; Fig. 1b).  
   - The order-dependency critique of standard SFT is central. Could you include a DETR-style, permutation-invariant SFT baseline that supervises both text and coordinates after Hungarian matching between predicted and GT instances? If this narrows the gap to SupGRPO, it would calibrate the necessity of RL.

4. Matching threshold inconsistency (Sec. 3.3 vs. Sec. 4.4/Tab. 7).  
   - Sec. 3.3 states “IoU > 0” for matches used in L_SFT-coord (Eq. (9)), while Tab. 7 uses 0.3 for IoU-based matching. What threshold is used in SupGRPO training? Please standardize and provide sensitivity to the threshold.

5. Sensitivity of key hyperparameters (Eq. (10); Sec. 4.2).  
   - Please report performance vs λ (set to 1e-4), β in Eq. (1) (0.04), the GRPO group size G (8), and decoding parameters during sampling. Also clarify which π_ref you use (Fig. 2) and whether β is fixed or adaptive. This will increase confidence in robustness.

6. Coordinate-only SFT choice (Sec. 3.3; Tab. 7).  
   - “+ Text Tokens SFT” improves recognition but hurts detection. Have you tried text-token SFT after matching (i.e., supervise text only for high-IoU matches), alternating updates (e.g., text-SFT every k steps), or uncertainty/gating to avoid suppressing detection? A small study here could reveal a better recognition–detection trade-off.

7. Detection metric details (Tabs. 2–3).  
   - Please specify IoU thresholds, one-to-one vs. greedy matching, and whether transcription is ignored for detection scoring. Adding PR curves or AP at multiple IoUs (e.g., 0.5/0.75) would make comparisons clearer and aid reproducibility.

8. ATS dataset documentation (Sec. 4.1; Fig. 3; App. Fig. 4).  
   - Can you detail the annotation protocol, QA (spot-check error rates, inter-annotator agreement), de-duplication across train/test, text normalization (case, punctuation), language coverage, and licensing/source attributions from TextSeg and WAS? This is critical for assessing bias and reusability.

9. Generalization to unseen styles (Sec. 4.1; Fig. 3).  
   - Beyond Tab. 4’s “with/without ATS,” could you provide stratified results by ATS categories (overlap, irregular arrangement, complex scenes) or a leave-one-style-out evaluation? This would test the claim that MLLM reasoning helps on novel artistic layouts.

10. Two-stage and interleaved schedules (Sec. 4.3; Tabs. 1–3).  
    - You evaluate SFT → GRPO. What about GRPO → SFT or interleaving (e.g., alternating epochs)? If these underperform SupGRPO, brief evidence would strengthen the joint-training argument.

11. Credit assignment granularity in GRPO (Sec. 3.1; Eq. (2)).  
    - Advantages are sequence-level and applied uniformly to all tokens. Did you explore per-instance or per-span weighting (e.g., higher weight on coordinate tokens or on matched instances) to tighten credit assignment? Any preliminary findings would clarify whether finer-grained shaping helps.

12. Handling unmatched predictions in online SFT (Sec. 3.3; Eq. (9)).  
    - Unmatched predicted boxes seem to receive no SFT signal. Did you consider “no-object” negatives or contrastive penalties for unmatched coordinate tokens to discourage spurious boxes?

13. Text reward normalization and multilingual cases (Eq. (6); App. Fig. 6).  
    - How are case, punctuation, Unicode normalization, and tokenization handled for word-level F1, especially for non-space-delimited scripts (e.g., Chinese in Fig. 6)? A precise definition will help others reproduce your scores.

14. Computational budget and efficiency (Sec. 4.2; App. Fig. 5).  
    - Please report wall-clock training time, GPU-hours, and convergence steps for SFT-only, GRPO-only, and SupGRPO on 3B/7B/8B, plus inference latency/memory. This would substantiate the “more stable and efficient” learning claim suggested by Fig. 5.

15. Format reward ablation and parseability (Sec. 3.2; Fig. 2).  
    - How often do generated sequences violate the required structure over training, and how much does the format reward contribute to final metrics? A small ablation or a plot of parse success rate would clarify its necessity.

16. Catastrophic forgetting (Sec. D).  
    - Could you quantify the reported “slight degradation” on standard multimodal benchmarks and show whether LoRA rank/target layers modulate this trade-off? A table with before/after scores would make the limitation more concrete.

17. Reproducibility details (Sec. 4.2).  
    - Please provide LoRA config (rank/alpha/target modules), seeds, prompt templates, coordinate tokenization/quantization scheme (e.g., range, precision, rounding), and decoding settings used during GRPO sampling and evaluation. These specifics can materially affect results.

18. Release plan.  
    - Confirm that ATS (with licenses/attributions) and code will be released upon acceptance, and whether evaluation scripts for rewards and metrics will be included to ensure comparability.

Summary:
The paper addresses pervasive artifacts in LLM-agent benchmarks by proposing a component-wise taxonomy of issues across User, Environment, Evaluation System, and Ground Truth (Sec. 3.2; Table 3), covering problems such as ambiguous instructions, incorrect tool responses, brittle scoring, and erroneous ground-truth calls. Building on this taxonomy, the authors introduce AgentBenchCleaner, a three-stage automated pipeline: (1) rule-based filters for deterministic defects, (2) an LLM-as-a-judge for nuanced issues, and (3) an optional difficulty-based curation to increase challenge (Sec. 4; Figure 2). Applying Stages 1–2 yields an issue-cleaned benchmark; adding Stage 3 produces AgentHard-Bench, a harder derivative with standardized evaluation protocols (Sec. 4.3). Across six representative benchmarks (BFCL V3, ACEBench, DrafterBench, τ-Bench, τ2-Bench, CFB), the pipeline aligns well with expert judgments (F1 0.759–0.880; Table 4), removes large fractions of flawed or saturated tasks (e.g., 32.1% via issue filtering and 56.1% after the full pipeline; Sec. 5.3, Figure 5), and improves benchmark quality by reducing model agreement and increasing confidence-separation while preserving diversity (Table 4; Figure 4). The method also leads to clearer and more stable leaderboards—for example, τ-Bench rankings shift for 75% of models with widened top-model gaps (Table 5; Table 9). The authors will release the taxonomy, pipeline, and AgentHard-Bench to support robust and reproducible agent evaluation.

Strengths:
1. Actionable, component-wise taxonomy. The four-component breakdown (User, Environment, Evaluation System, Ground Truth) is precise and operational (Sec. 3.2; Table 3), not merely descriptive. It pinpoints concrete, automatable failure modes such as “user role confusion,” “misleading tool design,” and “malformed tool calls,” with quantitative evidence on prevalence (e.g., τ-Bench shares in Table 2).

2. Taxonomy-to-pipeline mapping. The paper goes beyond auditing: it encodes the taxonomy into a practical three-stage pipeline that cleanly separates deterministic rule checks from semantic LLM judging and a final difficulty curation (Sec. 4.2; Figure 2). This modularity increases scalability and maintainability.

3. Carefully engineered judge prompting. The LLM-as-a-judge design is unusually thorough and transparent, including a generalizable template and a crucial “Actively Reconstruct the Conversation” rule to avoid false positives when milestone-only trajectories are provided (Appendix A.4). This is a notable methodological contribution for agent evaluation.

4. Strong, multi-pronged validation of issue detection. Human alignment is measured with both balanced subset labeling and full post-hoc verification (Sec. 5.2.1), achieving F1 0.759–0.880 (Table 4) and high end-to-end accuracy (Figure 3). This dual protocol convincingly supports the LLM-judge’s utility at scale.

5. Stage-wise ablations across six benchmarks. The paper quantifies each stage’s contribution to agreement, CI non-overlap, diversity, and compression (Tables 10–15), making the causal impact of rule filters, LLM judging, and difficulty-based curation clear rather than relying on end-to-end gains alone.

6. Cross-model robustness of the LLM judge. The judge works consistently across strong proprietary and open models (Gemini/Claude/DeepSeek), with comparable precision/recall per benchmark (Table 6). This reduces dependence on any single vendor and strengthens generality claims.

7. Measurable benchmark-quality improvements. After cleaning, separability improves in multiple ways—model agreement drops (e.g., ACEBench −0.138; τ-Bench −0.040) and CI non-overlap increases (e.g., ACEBench +0.181; τ2-Bench +0.050), while diversity is preserved or slightly improved (Table 4; Figure 4). The improvements are clearly contextualized against random-task baselines.

8. Practical leaderboard impact. The cleaned and harder versions materially change and clarify rankings (Table 5; Table 9; Figure 6): on τ-Bench, 75% of models shift, the top-2 swap, and the top gap widens from 0.018 to 0.045, demonstrating that artifact removal meaningfully affects conclusions practitioners would draw.

9. Compression with capability coverage safeguards. The pipeline achieves substantial compression (e.g., final 56.1% in Sec. 5.3; Figure 5) without hollowing out skills: embedding-based diversity remains stable (Table 4), subtask retention is analyzed in detail, and a 10% per-subtask floor protects breadth (A.7; Figures 7–8).

10. Breadth and depth of evidence across diverse benchmarks. The study spans six heterogeneous suites (Table 1), and the case studies cover all four components with concrete, real errors (Appendix A.1/Table 7)—e.g., τ-Bench “do-nothing” pass rate (38%), CFB mis-resolving “Melbourne,” DrafterBench’s incorrect system prompt—demonstrating the taxonomy’s wide applicability.

11. Support for dataset repair, not just filtering. The pipeline’s structured reasoning traces pinpoint minimal fixes (Appendix A.3), e.g., filename correction in BFCL V3 or enum mismatch in ACEBench, offering a practical path for benchmark maintainers beyond binary removal.

12. Clear scoping and usage guidance. The paper is explicit about when to use the issue-filtered set versus the difficulty-curated AgentHard-Bench and the dependence of Stage 3 on reference models (Sec. 6), which helps ensure fair downstream use.

13. Standardized evaluation protocol for the harder suite. AgentHard-Bench is positioned with “standardized evaluation protocols and explicit quality criteria” (Sec. 4.3), helping normalize practices across agent evaluations rather than proposing yet another idiosyncratic testbed.

Weaknesses:
1. Residual error and brittleness of the LLM-as-a-judge undermines cleaning precision
- Evidence: F1 ranges 0.759–0.880 across suites (Table 4); post-hoc end-to-end accuracy is “at least about 77%” (Fig. 3). Failure modes include false positives from partial trajectories and “misjudgment of redundancy,” and false negatives on malformed/incorrect calls and incorrect tool responses (Sec. 5.5; App. A.2/Table 8).
- Why it matters: Systematic FP/FN directly affect which tasks are removed, potentially biasing the cleaned benchmark and downstream rankings.
- Actionable: (a) Report per-category precision/recall for the judge (e.g., by Table 3 categories) to identify weak spots. (b) Use judge ensembles with disagreement-based adjudication and calibrated thresholds to cap FP rates; measure cross-judge agreement (Cohen’s κ) beyond Table 6. (c) Add targeted counterfactual prompts for failure categories in App. A.2, especially “partial trajectory” and “redundancy” cases, and show error reductions. (d) Introduce light human-in-the-loop spot checks on high-uncertainty items to bound FP in the final release.

2. Rule-based filtering is assumed “perfectly aligned” without independent precision auditing
- Evidence: “Rule-based filtering is deterministic by construction and thus achieves perfect alignment” (Sec. 5.1). Fig. 3 reports proportions of rule-based TPs but does not quantify potential FPs.
- Why it matters: Determinism ≠ correctness; schema and policy rules can be over- or mis-specified, causing silent over-pruning.
- Actionable: Add a stratified human audit (by issue type and benchmark) of a random sample flagged by Stage 1; report precision with CIs. Publish the exact rule catalog mapping each taxonomy item (Table 3) to deterministic checks to enable external validation.

3. Difficulty-based curation (Stage 3) is under-specified and model-panel–dependent
- Evidence: Stage 3 is a “simple heuristic” that filters tasks “that nearly all models can solve” (Sec. 4.2), and its dependence on reference models is acknowledged as a limitation (Sec. 6). Thresholds and selection criteria are not fully detailed.
- Why it matters: Results and “hardness” may shift as model panels evolve, confounding longitudinal comparability and fairness across labs.
- Actionable: (a) Specify exact thresholds (e.g., pass-rate quantiles) and tie them to a fixed, versioned reference panel. (b) Provide sensitivity analyses showing how AgentHard-Bench composition and separability change under alternative panels. (c) Release a frozen “v1 reference panel” and a re-computation script so future users can reproduce/compare versions.

4. “More stable rankings” are not rigorously established
- Evidence: Stability is argued via lower agreement and higher CI non-overlap (Table 4; Fig. 4), while Table 5/9 emphasize ranking changes rather than test–retest stability.
- Why it matters: Stability should reflect robustness of ranks under resampling/noise, not just larger inter-model gaps.
- Actionable: Add bootstrap-based reliability: Kendall τ/Spearman ρ of rankings across many resampled task subsets (before vs after cleaning), plus Rank-Biased Overlap for top-k. Report indistinguishability counts with CIs (Table 9) and show reductions are statistically significant.

- Evidence: Diversity uses Qwen3-Embedding-8B cosine distance (Sec. 5.1) and shows small drops on τ-Bench/τ2-Bench/DrafterBench (Table 4). Subtask retention plots (A.7, Figs. 7–8) are qualitative.
- Why it matters: Embedding distance may not reflect capability coverage; modest declines could accumulate with future updates.

(b) Quantify distribution shift (e.g., Hellinger distance) between original and cleaned sets per subtask and per component (User/Env/Eval/GT). (c) Report statistical tests to demonstrate that diversity losses are negligible.

- Evidence: “Evaluation System” issues appear in Table 3 (too lenient/too strict), yet the LLM-judge prompt omits evaluation issues “irrelevant to flaws in individual samples” (App. A.4), and Stage 1 examples focus on schemas/ground truth.

- Actionable: Implement harness-level detectors: (a) run standardized baselines (no-op, echo, random) to measure pass rates and flag tasks with inflated baseline success; (b) enforce semantic, execution-based equivalence instead of brittle string-match, and auto-flag high string/semantic mismatch rates; (c) publish per-benchmark evaluation-quality reports alongside cleaned tasks.

- Evidence: Related work contrasts MixEval/SMART/Arena-Hard conceptually (Sec. 2), but no side-by-side empirical comparison is shown.

- Actionable: Reproduce MixEval/SMART-style filtering on the same base suites and compare: human alignment (Table 4 protocols), separability, diversity, and compression. Include a combined (“ours + SMART”) setting to demonstrate complementarity.

8. Limited reporting on scalability and cost
- Evidence: The pipeline claims scalability, but there is no accounting of cost/latency (Sec. 4–5). Judge robustness is shown (Table 6), not throughput.
- Why it matters: Adoption depends on predictable cost-quality trade-offs, especially for large suites (e.g., CFB 1,000 tasks; Table 11).
- Actionable: Provide end-to-end runtime and cost per 1k tasks for Stages 1–2, plus cost–quality curves (precision/recall vs budget via dynamic stopping or adaptive re-judging on uncertain cases).

9. Repair is demonstrated but not quantified or productized
- Evidence: App. A.3 gives three repairable cases and argues detectors “aid human-in-the-loop repair,” but no estimate of salvageable fraction or time-to-fix is provided.
- Why it matters: Filtering discards data; repair could recover coverage and diversity at modest cost.
- Actionable: Quantify a “salvage rate” by sampling pipeline-flagged items, estimating minimal-edit repairs and annotator time. Consider releasing a parallel “Repaired” subset with provenance tags.

- Evidence: The taxonomy is “easily applicable to unseen benchmarks” (Sec. 6), but experiments exclude large interactive suites like WebArena/OSWorld mentioned in Sec. 2.
- Why it matters: External validity strengthens claims of broad utility.
- Actionable: Add a small-scale pilot on one environment-rich suite (e.g., a subset of WebArena), reporting the same metrics (Table 4) to demonstrate portability.

11. Reproducibility gaps in pipeline specification
- Evidence: A representative judge prompt is provided (App. A.4), but complete rule sets, thresholds for Stage 3, and per-benchmark prompt variants are not fully enumerated.
- Why it matters: Without exact detectors and thresholds, reproducing Table 4–15 results is difficult.
- Actionable: Release (or include in the paper) the full mapping from taxonomy (Table 3) to rule detectors, all prompts per benchmark, and the precise Stage-3 thresholds/panel, along with seeds and evaluation harness configurations.

Suggestions/Questions:
1. LLM-as-a-judge error analysis and mitigation
- Table 4 and Figure 3 show nontrivial judge errors (F1 0.759–0.880; end-to-end accuracy “at least about 77%”). Could you report per-category precision/recall aligned to the taxonomy in Table 3 (e.g., “Malformed tool calls” vs “Incorrect tool responses”) to localize weak spots?
- Appendix A.2/Table 8 lists recurrent FP/FN modes (“partial trajectory”, “misjudgment of redundancy”). Did you try prompt variants targeted at these modes? Please provide an ablation showing error reductions from such targeted instructions (citing Appendix A.4).
- Beyond Table 6, have you explored judge ensembles with disagreement-aware adjudication or calibrated thresholds to cap FPs? Reporting cross-judge agreement (e.g., Cohen’s κ) and the final decision rule would strengthen confidence.

2. Rule-based filtering validation
- Sec. 5.1 states “Rule-based filtering is deterministic … and thus achieves perfect alignment.” Determinism is not sufficient for correctness. Please add a stratified human audit of a random sample flagged by Stage 1 (by taxonomy category and benchmark) and report precision with confidence intervals. Also, could you publish the exact Stage-1 rule catalog mapping each Table 3 issue to concrete checks?

3. Stage 3 difficulty curation: thresholds, panel dependence, and sensitivity
- Sec. 4.2 (Stage 3) and Sec. 6 acknowledge dependence on the reference panel. What exact threshold defines “nearly all models can solve” (e.g., pass-rate ≥ p across the panel, required margin)? Please specify the versioned panel used.
- Provide sensitivity: how do AgentHard-Bench composition and separability (Table 4 metrics) change under alternative panels and thresholds? A small grid or bootstrap over model subsets would clarify robustness.
- Would you release a frozen “v1 reference panel” and script to re-compute curation for longitudinal comparability?

4. Ranking stability vs separability
- Claims of “more stable model rankings” (Abstract; Sec. 5.2.2) rely on agreement and CI non-overlap (Table 4) plus ranking changes (Table 5/Table 9; Fig. 6). Could you add bootstrap-based rank reliability (Kendall τ/Spearman ρ over many resampled task subsets) and top-k Rank-Biased Overlap before/after cleaning, with CIs, to directly quantify stability gains?

5. Diversity measurement and capability coverage
- Diversity uses Qwen3-Embedding-8B cosine distance (Sec. 5.1). To ensure capability coverage, could you add capability-aware metrics: subtask entropy, API/schema/type coverage, argument-shape diversity, and tool-graph structure diversity? Complement A.7 (Figs. 7–8) with quantitative distribution-shift measures (e.g., Hellinger distance) per subtask.
- Are the diversity findings robust to the choice of embedding model? A parallel analysis with a second embedding model would help.

6. Evaluation-harness issues: detection and remediation
- Table 3 includes “Too lenient/Too strict,” and τ-Bench’s “do-nothing” success (38%) is noted in Appendix A.1. Yet Appendix A.4 says evaluation issues were omitted from the judge prompt. Can you add harness-level detectors: (i) standardized baseline probes (no-op/echo/random) to flag inflated pass rates, (ii) semantic/execution-based equivalence metrics to identify brittle string matches, and (iii) per-benchmark evaluation-quality reports accompanying the cleaned sets?

7. Human labeling protocol details
- For the balanced subset validation (Sec. 5.1): how many experts annotated each benchmark, what were the instructions, and what was inter-annotator agreement? How were disagreements resolved? Please add CIs to the precision/recall in Table 4.

8. Exact definitions and computations of separability metrics
- Sec. 5.1 references “model agreement rates (Gupta et al., 2025)” and “CI non-overlap,” and Table 4 reports CI non-overlap “relative to baseline.” Please define the precise agreement formula (pairwise vs across-all), CI construction, number of random baselines, and the non-overlap computation. Sharing code would avoid ambiguity.

9. Comparison to prior filtering pipelines
- Sec. 2 argues conceptual complementarity to MixEval/SMART/Arena-Hard. Could you include side-by-side empirical comparisons on overlapping inputs: human alignment (Table 4 protocol), separability/diversity (Table 4), compression, and a combined (“ours + SMART”) setting to show additive gains?

10. Scalability and cost
- For adoption, please provide end-to-end runtime and cost per 1k tasks for Stages 1–2, broken down by benchmark size (e.g., CFB 1,000 tasks; Table 11). Include cost–quality trade-offs (precision/recall vs budget) via: (i) adaptive re-judging for high-uncertainty items, (ii) judge selection (Table 6) under a fixed budget.

11. Repairability and salvage rate
- Appendix A.3 shows three “minimal-fix” cases. Could you estimate a salvage rate by sampling pipeline-flagged items and reporting the fraction amenable to minimal edits, plus median annotator time? Would you release a parallel “Repaired” subset with provenance tags to balance compression with coverage?

12. Generalization beyond the six suites
- Sec. 2 mentions environment-rich suites (WebArena/OSWorld). A small pilot on one such suite—reporting the same Table 4 metrics—would strengthen claims that the taxonomy and pipeline generalize across interaction modalities.

13. Standardized protocol for AgentHard-Bench
- Sec. 4.3 claims “standardized evaluation protocols and explicit quality criteria.” Please enumerate these concretely: pass/fail semantics (tool-call vs final-state), allowed variances, and how they supersede inconsistent original harnesses. A compact “Eval Card” per benchmark would be valuable.

14. Reproducibility package
- Appendix A.4 provides a representative judge prompt for τ2-Bench. For full reproducibility, can you release: (i) all per-benchmark prompts, (ii) the Stage-1 rule library, (iii) Stage-3 thresholds and the exact model panel, (iv) seeds and harness configurations, and (v) scripts to compute metrics in Tables 4 and 10–15?

15. Retention safeguard and potential skew
- Sec. 5.3/A.7 use a 10% per-subtask retention floor. Why 10%? Please provide sensitivity showing how separability, diversity, and leaderboard conclusions change for 5%/15% floors, and whether the floor inadvertently preserves low-value subtasks.

16. Post-hoc validation specifics
- Figure 3 aggregates manual verification of pipeline-flagged tasks. Could you report per-benchmark and per-stage (Stage 1 vs Stage 2) FP rates with 95% CIs, and provide a confusion breakdown by Table 3 categories?

17. Clarify agent model panel and settings
- Table 5 lists many models with “thinking-on/off” variants. Were agent prompts, tool-calling scaffolds, and temperature identical across models? Did “thinking” modes change tool-use tendencies and thus Stage-3 curation? A short protocol table would help ensure comparability.

18. Quantify significance of heatmap improvements
- Figure 4 visually suggests reduced agreement for ACEBench post-cleaning. Please add quantitative tests (e.g., paired bootstrap on agreement statistics) to assess significance of changes beyond visual inspection.

Presentation: 3

Contribution: 3

Overall: 7

Confidence: 4

Summary:
The paper tackles dataset distillation under long‑tailed class imbalance by redesigning the distribution‑matching metric itself. It introduces Class‑Aware Spectral Distribution Matching (CSDM), which replaces linear‑kernel “MSE/MMD” with a principled Spectral Distribution Distance (SDD) derived from universal, shift‑invariant kernels via Bochner’s theorem, yielding an exact spectral form of MMD that matches full distributions and is estimated with linear complexity O(LND) (Section 4.2.2; Theorem 3; Figure 2). CSDM further decomposes SDD into amplitude and phase terms and applies class‑specific weights α(c) to emphasize diversity for head classes and realism for tail classes, while preserving metric discriminativity (Section 4.2.4; Proposition 1; Eq. (17)). Extensive experiments on CIFAR‑10/100‑LT and long‑tailed ImageNet subsets show consistent gains over prior DD methods, with the strongest margins at low IPC and high imbalance (Table 2, Table 3), along with strong cross‑architecture transfer (Table 4). Ablations validate the importance of universal kernels and scale selection (Figure 3) and the head/tail amplitude‑phase weighting (Figure 4). The abstract reports that on CIFAR‑10‑LT with 10 IPC, CSDM improves over prior state of the art by 14.0% and remains stable as tail images drop from 500 to 25 (Abstract).

Strengths:
Strengths

1. Principled, theoretically grounded metric redesign. The paper moves beyond linear-kernel “MSE/MMD” by deriving Spectral Distribution Distance (SDD) as the exact spectral form of universal‑kernel MMD via Bochner’s theorem (Section 4.2.2; Theorem 3). This re-establishes metricity and identifiability (Theorem 1) and directly targets “Problem 1: Inadequate Alignment of Distributions” in the Introduction.

2. Clear decomposition that addresses long‑tailed imbalance. The amplitude–phase split of the CF discrepancy with class‑aware weights α(c) (Section 4.2.4; Eq. (17)) operationalizes the head/tail needs—diversity vs. realism—and is not just heuristic: discriminativity of the overall distance is formally preserved for any α(c) ∈ (0,1) (Proposition 1).

3. Computational efficiency with linear scaling. SDD admits a Monte‑Carlo estimator with O(LND) complexity (Section 4.2.2), replacing the quadratic cost typical of kernel-matrix MMD. In practice, CSDM stays fast and memory‑lean across IPC settings (Table 6: 0.30–0.35 s/iter; 3.43–3.45 GB), while DATM/DC/MTT encounter OOM at higher IPC.

4. Resolves pervasive misconceptions in DD/DM. The paper precisely diagnoses the “Misnomer of Mean Square Error in DM” (Section 3) and shows why linear‑kernel MMD only matches means (Eq. (4)). Appendix A.2 (Theorem 6) gives a concrete moment‑expansion of Gaussian‑kernel MMD, demonstrating “all‑order” sensitivity; Appendix A.3 clarifies the relationship between SDD and CFD and why kernel‑anchoring provides metric guarantees absent in ad‑hoc CF weightings.

5. Sound kernel design guidance with practical robustness. The paper delineates which kernels are both universal and shift‑invariant (Table 1), and ties the RBF spectral measure to Gaussian sampling. The ablation in Figure 3 links performance to the scale γ and shows that feature normalization enables a single γ = 2 across datasets, improving robustness versus prior MMD uses that underutilized universality through poor scale choices.

6. Strong, targeted gains on long‑tailed benchmarks. On CIFAR‑10‑LT and CIFAR‑100‑LT, CSDM is consistently best across IPC and imbalance factors (Table 2). Concrete margins over strong baselines are sizable, e.g., CIFAR‑10‑LT at IPC=50: 76.5 ± 0.2 (CSDM) vs. 75.6 ± 0.2 (NCFM) and 70.5 ± 0.4 (LAD); CIFAR‑100‑LT at IPC=50: 50.0 ± 0.3 (CSDM) vs. 48.0 ± 0.3 (NCFM) and 40.0 ± 0.1 (LAD). The narrative highlights stability under severe imbalance (β=200) with large deltas over DC/IDM/LAD (Section 5.2).

7. Robustness on high‑resolution, long‑tailed ImageNet subsets. CSDM markedly outperforms prior DD on ImageNette/ImageWoof/ImageMeow/ImageSquawk (Table 3). For instance, ImageNette (β=5, IPC=10): 29.5 ± 0.9 (CSDM) vs. 25.2 ± 1.9 (RDED) and 17.2 ± 0.5 (Random), confirming that the class‑aware spectral design scales beyond CIFAR.

8. Cross‑architecture transferability. Synthetic sets distilled with a small ConvNet transfer well to AlexNet/VGG‑11/ResNet‑18 (Table 4), e.g., VGG‑11: 69.8 (CSDM) vs. 55.5 (LAD), and ResNet‑18: 65.9 (CSDM) vs. 60.0 (LAD), indicating the metric-centric approach generalizes beyond the distillation architecture.

9. Careful experimental validation of design choices. The head/tail weighting ablation (Figure 4) empirically supports the intuition “emphasize diversity (amplitude) for head, realism (phase) for tail,” with peak accuracy around αhead ≈ 0.7–0.9 at high imbalance. Together with Figure 3, these ablations link theory to practice in a measurable way.

10. Conceptual unification and positioning. Section 6 and Appendix B systematically relate CSDM to IID/DSDM (low‑order cumulant matching; Theorem 7), to M3D (kernel scale pitfalls), and to NCFM/CFD (lack of metric guarantees and min‑max misalignment). This framing is valuable for the community because it reframes “MMD is only mean‑matching” as a kernel‑choice issue and offers SDD as a principled, efficient anchor for future spectral/neural frequency samplers.

11. Clarity of pipeline and assumptions. Figure 2 cleanly separates feature extraction, kernel embedding, and class‑aware spectral matching, and Section 4.2.4 explicitly states the assumption of shared class priors in distillation, making the theoretical guarantees (Proposition 1) transparent in scope.

Weaknesses:
Weaknesses and actionable suggestions

1. Incremental novelty of the core metric
   - SDD is the spectral form of universal-kernel MMD via Bochner’s theorem (Section 4.2.2; Theorem 3), and the “all-order” sensitivity is a standard property of characteristic/universal kernels (Theorem 1; Appendix A.2/Theorem 6; Gretton et al., 2008). The amplitude–phase decomposition is also classical (Section 4.2.4; Oppenheim & Lim, 1981; Mandic & Constantinides, 2009).
   - Suggestion: Emphasize distinct technical advances beyond re-expression of known MMD results—e.g., (i) a principled, provably optimal choice or learning of the spectral measure within the class of universal, shift-invariant kernels; (ii) generalization bounds that connect SDD minimization to downstream risk under class imbalance; (iii) theoretical analysis of the class-aware objective’s optimization landscape and its effect on tail-class error.

2. Incomplete operationalization of class-aware weights α(c)
   - The method hinges on α(c) (Section 4.2.4), yet experiments mostly tune an “αhead” and use 1−αhead for tails (Figure 4) with a few fixed settings (Appendix E.1 mentions α=0.11 or 0.7 by IPC). There is no principled mapping from class frequency to α(c) or learning rule beyond manual choices.
   - Suggestion: Specify and justify a monotone schedule α(c)=g(nc) (e.g., via effective sample size) and add sensitivity analyses across datasets. Since Proposition 1 holds for any α(c)∈(0,1), consider learning α(c) jointly with S under constraints (e.g., box or Lipschitz on g) and report stability.

3. Missing baselines where they matter most
   - Long-tailed ImageNet subsets (Table 3) omit strong recent DD competitors included elsewhere (e.g., NCFM, LAD), and Wasserstein-based DD discussed in Section B.4 is not compared on LT settings. This weakens the central claim of robustness on high-resolution LT data.
   - Suggestion: Add NCFM/LAD/Wasserstein-DD results to Table 3 under identical protocols, or explain reproducibility barriers. Also include a “universal-kernel MMD (kernel-matrix)” baseline to disentangle the benefits of spectral estimation from amplitude–phase weighting.

4. Lack of analysis of the Monte-Carlo estimator (L) and its accuracy/speed trade-off
   - Section 4.2.2 asserts O(LND) complexity but provides no guidance on choosing L and no variance/convergence analysis. There is no ablation of accuracy vs. L or wall-clock vs. L.
   - Suggestion: Add an L-sweep (error bars) on at least CIFAR-10-LT and one ImageNet subset, report the variance of SDD estimates, and plot accuracy/time vs. L. Provide bounds or empirical calibration for L as a function of feature dimension d and sample size N.

5. Limited diagnosis of when CSDM’s gains over strong baselines are modest
   - On several CIFAR-10/100-LT settings the gains over NCFM are small (e.g., Table 2: +0.8–2.0 points in some cases), and on balanced CIFAR (Appendix Table 5) CSDM is sometimes only slightly ahead or slightly behind NCFM/FreD at certain IPCs.
   - Suggestion: Provide per-class accuracy breakdowns (head/mid/tail) and ablate amplitude-only vs. phase-only vs. class-aware on the same splits to clarify where improvements originate. Include spectral residual visualizations (per-class amplitude/phase gaps) to show that α(c) choices close the right discrepancy.

6. Kernel/scale selection remains heuristic
   - Figure 3 shows sensitivity to γ and suggests γ=2 after feature normalization, but there is no principled, data-dependent scheme. Only RBF/Laplace are explored in a single LT configuration.
   - Suggestion: Add a median-heuristic-style calibration or a cross-validated scheme on features, and report its cross-dataset robustness. Include Laplace-SDD ablations mirroring Figure 3 and show that conclusions are not RBF-specific.

7. Theory–practice gap in assumptions
   - Theorem 1 assumes compact X; Section 5.3.1 notes feature normalization but does not formally connect it to the theorem’s conditions or to characteristicness in non-compact Rd. Similarly, Proposition 1 assumes equal class priors.
   - Suggestion: State the exact normalization/compactness assumptions used in practice (range, norms) and whether characteristicness still holds under the employed kernels. Discuss robustness when synthetic class priors deviate from the real ones during optimization (and whether the result extends to prior shift).

8. Limited evidence that “amplitude = diversity, phase = realism” holds in feature space
   - The interpretation draws from classical image Fourier results (Section C) and Figure 6 shows qualitative effects at α extremes on CIFAR-10; however, quantitative validation in learned feature space is sparse.
   - Suggestion: Report intra-class dispersion and mode coverage metrics for head classes (e.g., mean pairwise feature distance, number of discovered modes) and nearest-neighbor realism/precision-style scores for tail classes, alongside accuracy, under amplitude-only, phase-only, and class-aware settings.

9. Fairness and protocol details in efficiency claims
   - Table 6 shows large speed/memory advantages, but it is unclear whether batch sizes, augmentations (A(·,ω)), and hardware utilization are matched across methods.
   - Suggestion: Provide a standardized profiling protocol and per-method configs; add scaling curves (time/memory vs. IPC and vs. N) to substantiate the claimed O(LND) advantage empirically.

10. Scope limitations: feature extractor dependence
   - The optimization objective averages over fϑ and A(·,ω) (Eq. (2)), but experiments do not ablate the choice of feature network used during distillation (only downstream evaluation is cross-architecture; Table 4).
   - Suggestion: Distill with different feature extractors (depth/normalization) and report SDD’s sensitivity to fϑ, or show that the same α(c) schedule transfers across feature networks.

Addressing these points—especially principled α(c), estimator analysis (L), stronger LT baselines on ImageNet subsets, and quantitative validation of amplitude/phase roles in feature space—would substantially strengthen the paper’s claim of a “principled, class-aware” metric for long-tailed dataset distillation.

Suggestions/Questions:
Questions and suggestions for the rebuttal

1. Class-aware weighting α(c): specification and learning
   - Section 4.2.4 and Figure 4 vary “αhead” but do not give a principled mapping from class frequency to α(c). Can you provide a concrete schedule α(c)=g(nc) (e.g., via effective number of samples) used in Tables 2–3? Please include sensitivity results across datasets/imbalance factors.
   - Proposition 1 requires α(c)∈(0,1). In practice you sometimes use αhead≈0.9–0.99 (Figure 4). Do you ever take α(c)=0 or 1? If so, does discriminativity break, and empirically what fails? If not, please clarify bounds enforced during training.
   - Have you tried learning α(c) jointly with S under box constraints, or learning a monotone function g(nc) with a few parameters? A brief study could strengthen the “class-aware” claim.

2. Monte-Carlo estimator details for SDD
   - Section 4.2.2 states O(LND) complexity but does not specify L or how it scales with d and N. What L values are used in Tables 2–3, and are they fixed across datasets? Please add an accuracy/time vs. L sweep (with error bars) on CIFAR‑10‑LT and one ImageNet subset.
   - What is the variance of the SDD estimator as a function of L and d? Any stabilization (e.g., antithetic sampling) used? Guidance for choosing L would help reproducibility.

3. Relation to Random Fourier Features (RFF)
   - The SDD estimator via sampling t∼p(t) (RBF: N(0,2γI)) resembles RFF‑based MMD approximations. Can you explicitly connect your estimator to RFF MMD, and compare (i) kernel‑matrix MMD; (ii) RFF‑MMD; and (iii) SDD with amplitude‑phase reweighting on CIFAR‑10‑LT, keeping L comparable?

4. Kernel choice and scale parameter γ
   - Figure 3 shows strong γ sensitivity and mentions normalizing FT and FS to a “unified scale.” Please specify the exact normalization (per‑class or global; mean/variance or norm constraints) and justify why a single γ=2 works across datasets. A small ablation for Laplace‑SDD mirroring Figure 3 would test RBF‑specificity.
   - Table 1 lists Laplace as universal and shift‑invariant. Could you add a brief citation/justification for Laplace universality in Rd and comment on any practical differences you observed relative to RBF under LT settings?

5. Assumptions in Proposition 1 and robustness to prior shift
   - Proposition 1 assumes “the class prior over labels is the same.” During optimization, can synthetic priors drift before convergence? If so, does your objective remain discriminative, and are there practical mechanisms to enforce priors? Any evidence on robustness if priors are slightly mismatched?

6. Amplitude = diversity, phase = realism (feature‑space validation)
   - Section 4.2.4 and Appendix C argue this decomposition; Figure 6 shows pixel‑space effects. Could you add quantitative feature‑space evidence (e.g., intra‑class dispersion/mode coverage for heads; k‑NN precision/realism or overfitting proxies for tails) comparing α=1, α=0, and class‑aware on CIFAR‑10‑LT?

7. Per‑class performance and where gains arise
   - To substantiate the head/tail benefits, please report per‑group accuracies (head/mid/tail) on CIFAR‑10‑LT/100‑LT and one ImageNet subset, and ablate amplitude‑only vs. phase‑only vs. class‑aware under the same settings. Spectral residual plots (per‑class amplitude/phase gaps before/after) would be illuminating.

8. Frequency sampling strategy across classes
   - Are the sampled frequencies {ti} shared across all classes or drawn per class? If shared, did you test class‑conditional sampling (same p(t), different draws) and does it affect stability or performance under severe imbalance?

9. Numerical stability of phase term
   - The phase discrepancy includes |ϕFT||ϕFS|(1−cos(Δθ)). For frequencies where amplitudes are very small, is the phase term noisy? Do you threshold amplitudes or regularize the argument of the empirical CF to avoid instability? Implementation details would help (Section 4.2.4).

10. Stronger baselines on long‑tailed ImageNet subsets
   - Table 3 omits several strong contenders compared elsewhere (e.g., NCFM, LAD; Wasserstein‑based DD discussed in Appendix B.4). Can you add these under the same protocol, or explain reproducibility constraints? This comparison is particularly important to support robustness at higher resolution.

   - To separate benefits of (i) universal kernel; (ii) spectral estimator; and (iii) class‑aware weighting, please include a baseline that minimizes Gaussian‑kernel MMD via kernel matrices (or RFF with large L), and another that uses SDD without class‑aware reweighting.

12. Efficiency and fairness of profiling
   - Table 6 shows large speed/memory gains. Please detail the profiling protocol (same batch size, augmentation A(·,ω), and optimizer/hardware settings across methods). A scaling plot of time/memory vs. IPC (and vs. N) would empirically demonstrate the O(LND) advantage.

13. Feature extractor and augmentation dependence
   - Eq. (2) averages over fϑ and A(·,ω), but experiments fix a specific ConvNet and DSA‑style augmentations. How sensitive is CSDM to the choice of feature backbone used during distillation? An ablation with an alternative feature network or augmentation strength (especially for tails) would clarify robustness.

14. Clarifying abstract claims with plots
   - The abstract claims “only a 5.7% performance drop when the number of images in tail classes decreases from 500 to 25.” Please point to the exact setting and add a plot of accuracy vs. tail sample count (fixed IPC) to make this evidence visible.

15. Cross‑architecture evaluation protocol
   - Table 4 evaluates AlexNet/VGG‑11/ResNet‑18 using data distilled with a 3‑layer ConvNet. Were training schedules and hparams re‑tuned per architecture or fixed? Please clarify to ensure a fair cross‑arch comparison.

A small diagnostic (e.g., learned frequency distributions vs. pRBF(t)) on LT CIFAR‑10 could clarify why your fixed µ helps.

17. Theory–practice alignment of “compactness” assumptions
   - Theorem 1 assumes a compact X. You normalize features (Figure 3 caption), but can you state the exact condition that ensures effective compactness in your pipeline? A short remark connecting the practical normalization to the theorem’s setup would close the loop.

18. Table formatting and “Full Dataset” references
   - Table 2/3 contain duplicated/misaligned headers and some “Full Dataset” entries that appear inconsistent (e.g., CIFAR‑100‑LT). Please clarify what “Full Dataset” denotes under LT settings and ensure these numbers are directly comparable within each block.

19. Practical guidance for users
