Summary:
The paper proposes HELM, an equivariant GNN that predicts both Hamiltonian matrices and total energies from atomic structures, enabling transfer from electronic-structure supervision to downstream energy prediction (Section 3; Fig. 1). To train and evaluate at realistic scales, the authors curate OMol CSH 58k, a Hamiltonian dataset with 56,657 molecules spanning 58 elements, up to 150 atoms, long-range interactions, and a large def2-TZVPD basis, with two test splits (“OMol all 5k” and “OMol common 1k”) (Section 3.1; Fig. 2; Table 1). HELM incorporates SO(2) convolutions, gated irreps, node-parity constraints, and element-referenced l=0 scaling, and uses a root-MSE+MSE loss to stabilize learning across sizes and elements (Section 3; Section B.3; Table 9). On Hamiltonian prediction, HELM achieves state-of-the-art errors on MD17/QM7 and ∇²DFT, e.g., ~3.6–9.3 µEh for small molecules and ~57–60 µEh on ∇²DFT (Section 4.1; Table 2). The authors introduce “Hamiltonian pretraining,” where the HELM backbone is first trained on H and then used (frozen or finetuned) for energy prediction, yielding up to ~2× lower test MAE in low-data regimes on ∇²DFT and OMol CSH 58k compared to direct energy training (Section 4.2; Fig. 3; Tables 3–4). Embedding analyses show that pretraining learns fine-grained, element-resolving descriptors (UMAP in Fig. 4), and additional studies demonstrate accurate recovery of eigenvalues and electron densities from predicted H (Figs. 12–13) and the importance of parity-expansion and l=0 scaling (Table 9). Overall, the work provides a scalable architecture, a large diverse Hamiltonian dataset, and a pretraining recipe that leverages electronic-structure supervision to improve data efficiency in energy prediction.

Strengths:
Strengths
1. Clear, impactful idea: leveraging the routinely available but underused Hamiltonian matrices for representation learning and transfer to energy prediction. The “Hamiltonian pretraining” setup is executed cleanly and yields substantial and consistent gains in low-data regimes (up to ~2× test MAE reduction) with careful controls on parameter counts and schedules (Section 4.2; Fig. 3; Tables 3–4; Table 10).

2. Scalable and thoughtfully engineered architecture: HELM combines SO(2) convolutions and gated irreps with two targeted innovations that specifically address known bottlenecks in large, diverse electronic-structure learning:
   - Node-parity expansion for diagonal H blocks, improving high-magnitude intra-atomic predictions (Section 3, “Hamiltonian output head”).
   - l=0 element-referenced normalization that homogenizes per-element scale and stabilizes optimization across 58 elements (Section B.3 “Normalizing scalar node block irreps”).
   These choices are ablated and shown to dramatically reduce both H_err and derived energy errors (Table 9).

3. Strong empirical performance and breadth: HELM achieves new state of the art on both small-molecule and chemically diverse benchmarks, improving matrix-element MAE by 3–5× over prior best on ∇²DFT and outperforming strong baselines on MD17/QM7 (Section 4.1; Table 2). The ability to reproduce total energies from predicted H to within tens of meV for small molecules further validates the fidelity of the learned electronic structure (Table 2).

4. High-value dataset contribution aligned with the paper’s goals: OMol CSH 58k is carefully curated to maximize informative coverage over elements, orbital interactions, and distances, while matching realistic MLIP scales (58 elements, up to 150 atoms, long-range interactions, def2‑TZVPD; Section 3.1; Fig. 2; Table 1). The inclusion of two test splits (“OMol all 5k” and “OMol common 1k”) supports both universal and community-comparable evaluation.

5. Practical scalability-oriented design choices: The backbone’s one-way node→edge dependency allows omission of edge updates for the energy head (Section 3, Eq. (2) and “Energy output head”), improving reuse and fine-tuning efficiency. Distance trimming to 12 Å based on quantified decay (Section B.2; Fig. 6) and edge-binning for balanced large-batch distributed training (Section C.2) demonstrate rare attention to the systems aspects required for 100+ atom molecules and high-l_max bases.

6. Rigorous scientific diagnostics beyond aggregate metrics: The paper connects matrix errors to eigenvalue/energy sensitivity and resolves occupation instabilities with overlap filtering (Section D.1; Fig. 10), analyzes distance- and angular-degree–resolved errors (Fig. 11), visualizes near-indistinguishable electron densities from predicted H (Fig. 13), and shows that pretraining learns element- and irrep-structured embeddings (UMAP in Fig. 4; extended in Figs. 14–15). These provide convincing, mechanistic evidence for the claimed data-efficiency and generalization benefits.

7. Reproducibility and clarity: Architecture, hyperparameters, parameter counts, and training setups are specified in detail (Fig. 1; Tables 5–8; Section C.2), and the ablations isolate exactly which components drive the gains (Table 9). The dataset statistics and visuals (Fig. 2; Table 1) are particularly informative for future benchmarking.

Weaknesses:
Weaknesses (with actionable suggestions)

1. Limited baselines for the central “Hamiltonian pretraining” claim
   - Evidence: Energy transfer is only compared against the same backbone trained “direct,” “pretrained-frozen,” and “finetuned” (Section 4.2; Fig. 3; Tables 3–4, 10). There is no comparison to competing pretraining signals or multitask schemes that also leverage electronic information (e.g., eigenvalues, densities, multipoles) or to strong energy-only/equivariant MLIP baselines in identical low-data regimes.
   - Why it matters: The core claim is that H-supervision yields better representations than alternatives. Without such baselines, it is unclear if H is uniquely effective.
   - Suggestions: (i) Add controlled pretraining on alternative labels available “for free” from SCF—occupied eigenvalues and/or density on a reduced grid—and report the same downstream energy evaluation; (ii) Add a simple multitask variant that jointly fits H and energy; (iii) Include at least one strong energy-only equivariant baseline trained under the same data budget and scheduler to quantify the practical advantage of H-pretraining.

2. Practicality gap for energy accuracy and missing force/MD evaluation
   - Evidence: On OMol, downstream energy MAEs remain very large (e.g., 2.1–3.9 eV for test splits in Table 4), and even on ∇²DFT the meV-per-atom numbers (Table 10) are promising but not yet sufficient to argue for MLIP readiness. No forces or MD stability results are reported. The paper notes this as “the next step” (end of Section 4.2).
   - Why it matters: The stated goal is to improve MLIPs; forces and MD stability are central.
   - Suggestions: (i) Report force errors and short MD stability tests after energy finetuning for at least ∇²DFT (e.g., force MAE, drift, temperature/energy conservation); (ii) Provide learning curves vs. energy data size to demonstrate convergence towards practically usable accuracy; (iii) Report per-atom energy MAE alongside per-molecule MAE for all tables to ease comparability.

3. Finetuning often hurts generalization on OMol; regularization/adapter strategies are undeveloped
   - Evidence: On “OMol common 1k” and “OMol all 5k,” the pretrained-frozen model generalizes better than finetuning (Table 4). Validation curves show clear overfitting during finetuning (Fig. 3c).
   - Why it matters: The claimed recipe should scale to larger and more diverse settings; current finetuning degrades test accuracy where diversity is highest.
   - Suggestions: (i) Use layer-wise learning-rate decay and early stopping; (ii) Add lightweight adapters or low-rank updates to retain pretrained structure; (iii) Stronger regularization (weight decay, stochastic depth, SWA) and element-stratified sampling during finetuning; (iv) Try partial-freezing (early layers) and compare.

4. No per-element or compositionally out-of-distribution analysis
   - Evidence: OMol “all 5k” has substantially higher H_err than “common 1k” (Table 4), indicating heavier elements are harder, but there is no per-element breakdown. The dataset deliberately excludes first-row transition metals and lanthanides (Section 3.1), and no element holdout experiments are reported.
   - Why it matters: The universal claim hinges on element diversity and rare-element robustness.
   - Suggestions: (i) Report H_err and downstream energy MAE stratified by element and element-pair distance; (ii) Add element-holdout evaluations (zero-shot transfer to specific heavy elements); (iii) Quantify how performance scales with per-element sample counts.

5. Loss design favors large diagonal blocks; long-range and spectrally critical terms may be underweighted
   - Evidence: The node-parity expansion plus l=0 scaling (Table 9) dramatically reduce errors dominated by diagonal blocks, but Fig. 11 shows the highest relative errors at long range where magnitudes are small; Fig. 10 shows large total-energy outliers from spectral/occupation instabilities.
   - Why it matters: Long-range couplings and spectral fidelity underpin polarization/dispersion and stable electron occupations.
   - Suggestions: (i) Add distance-aware or magnitude-normalized weighting to emphasize small-magnitude, long-range H_ij; (ii) Include a cheap spectral term (e.g., sub-sampled block eigenvalue loss or Low-rank Hutchinson-style spectral matching) to improve occupied eigenvalue stability without assembling full H; (iii) Report eigenvalue MAE after such modifications.

6. Cutoff justification for diffuse bases is not empirically stress-tested
   - Evidence: Inter-atomic H_ij are clipped beyond 12 Å based on a 10^-5 Eh threshold (Section B.2; Fig. 6), but no sensitivity study shows the effect of this truncation on learned H or downstream energy.
   - Why it matters: Def2‑TZVPD includes diffuse functions; small long-range couplings can matter cumulatively and for excited-state–sensitive properties.
   - Suggestions: Provide an ablation varying the cutoff (e.g., 10/12/15 Å) and show impact on H_err, eigenvalue MAE, and downstream energy.

7. Transfer across basis sets and functionals is untested
   - Evidence: HELM is trained/evaluated on def2‑SVP (MD17/∇²DFT) and def2‑TZVPD (OMol) separately, but no cross-basis or cross-functional transfer is reported.
   - Why it matters: A key promise of pretraining is reusability across computational settings.
   - Suggestions: (i) Pretrain on def2‑SVP H, finetune energy on def2‑TZVPD (and vice versa); (ii) Pretrain on one functional’s H (e.g., ωB97X‑D from ∇²DFT) and finetune energies with another; (iii) Quantify degradation vs. in-domain pretraining.

8. Potential leakage/transfer fragility in l=0 element-referenced normalization
   - Evidence: The l=0 scaling uses element-wise means/variances “averaged over the structures in the dataset” (Section B.3; Fig. 7). It is not explicit that statistics are fit on training data only, and the approach may be brittle for under-sampled heavy elements and cross-dataset transfer.
   - Why it matters: Such normalization can inadvertently encode dataset priors and harm OOD behavior.
   - Suggestions: (i) Fit statistics strictly on train splits and report effect; (ii) Explore robust/quantile scaling or per-block (shell-resolved) normalization to reduce element prior leakage; (iii) Test portability of learned scalings when transferring across datasets (e.g., ∇²DFT → OMol).

9. Heavy compute/memory costs without quantitative scaling or efficiency analysis
   - Evidence: Param counts are large (e.g., 84.5M backbone for l_max=6; Table 6); training used up to 1,536 GPU hours on ∇²DFT and 64 processes on OMol (Section C.2), but no throughput/VRAM/runtime vs. molecule size or l_max curves are reported.
   - Why it matters: A stated goal is scalability; practitioners need concrete cost–accuracy tradeoffs.
   - Suggestions: (i) Report wall-clock, memory, and tokens/sec vs. N atoms and l_max, and compare to prior H-predictors on ∇²DFT; (ii) Investigate block-sparse/low-rank parameterizations of TC and irreps; (iii) Explore mixed precision, edge subsampling, hierarchical (atom→shell→AO) message passing, or dynamic l_max per element.

10. Reliance on external QM tools at inference time (S and XC grid) limits end-to-end utility
   - Evidence: Overlap S is “rapidly obtained with PySCF” and used to compute energies and densities from predicted H (Section A.2; Table 2 caption; Fig. 13). Spectral instabilities are mitigated by filtering S (Fig. 10).
   - Why it matters: For broad deployment, one would like to avoid dependence on external SCF components or at least quantify the added cost/fragility.
   - Suggestions: (i) Train a lightweight S-prediction head with symmetry/positivity constraints and report end-to-end energy from predicted (H, S); (ii) Use entropy-smearing (finite‑T occupations) during post-processing to reduce occupation flips; (iii) Quantify added wall-clock for PySCF post-processing relative to model inference.

Collectively, addressing these points—especially stronger baselines for the pretraining claim, element- and distance-resolved analyses, force/MD evaluations, and efficiency/scaling studies—would make the case for HELM as a practical, general recipe for improving MLIPs via electronic-structure supervision substantially more convincing.

Suggestions/Questions:
1. l=0 element-referenced scaling: Section B.3 computes µZ, σZ “averaged over the structures in the dataset.” Were these statistics fit strictly on the training split for each benchmark (MD17, ∇²DFT, OMol CSH 58k), with no test leakage? Please report an ablation where µZ, σZ are fit on train-only vs. all data, and quantify any change in H_err and downstream E_err (cf. Table 9). Also, how portable are these statistics across datasets (e.g., trained on ∇²DFT, applied to OMol)?

2. Distance cutoff sensitivity with diffuse basis: You trim inter-atomic H_ij beyond 12 Å based on the 10^-5 Eh threshold (Section B.2; Fig. 6). Could you provide a small ablation (e.g., 10/12/15 Å) on OMol CSH 58k showing impacts on H_err, occupied-eigenvalue MAE, and downstream E_err? This would reassure that the cut does not underweight long-range couplings in def2‑TZVPD.

3. Pretraining alternatives and multitask: The pretraining baseline uses H only (Section 4.2). Can you add a controlled comparison where the backbone is pretrained on (i) occupied eigenvalues, (ii) a coarse electron-density grid, or (iii) simple multipoles, and then finetuned on energy, under identical data/compute budgets? A lightweight multitask (H + E) on ∇²DFT Train‑2k would also help establish H’s unique value.

4. Forces and MD stability: Since the motivation is to improve MLIPs (Introduction), could you report force MAE after energy finetuning and a brief MD stability check (e.g., short NVE on ∇²DFT test conformers), even if preliminary? This would ground the claim in practical use.

5. Finetuning regularization on OMol: Fig. 3c shows overfitting; in Table 4 the pretrained‑frozen variant generalizes better than finetuning on OMol splits. Can you try partial freezing (e.g., freeze early layers), layer-wise LR decay, or adapter/LoRA-style updates, and report test E_err? Element-balanced sampling during finetuning may also help given Fig. 2c–d.

6. Per-element and composition analysis: Please provide H_err and E_err broken down by element and by element-pair distance bins on OMol (Fig. 2d), and an element-holdout evaluation (zero-shot on a small set of heavy elements). This would clarify which chemistries drive the gap between “OMol common 1k” and “OMol all 5k” (Table 4).

7. Efficiency/scaling characterization: Table 6 and Section C.2 imply high parameter counts and significant GPU time. Could you add plots of VRAM, wall-clock per step, and throughput vs. N atoms and l_max, and compare to a prior H-predictor on ∇²DFT? Also quantify the speedup from omitting edge updates for the energy head (Section 3, Eq. (2)).

8. Spectral stability and losses: Section D.1 (Fig. 10) shows occupation flips. Have you tried entropy-smearing (finite‑T occupations) during post-processing, or a cheap spectral term (e.g., sub-sampled block eigenvalue loss or stochastic trace/Hutchinson estimates) to stabilize the occupied spectrum without assembling full H? A small ∇²DFT ablation would be persuasive.

9. Loss weighting for long-range, small-magnitude couplings: Fig. 11 shows higher relative errors at long range. Would a magnitude-normalized or distance-aware weighting in the root-MSE+MSE loss reduce these relative errors, and does this improve eigenvalue/E_err stability?

10. Cross-basis and cross-functional transfer: Since HELM targets universal use, can you pretrain on def2‑SVP H (∇²DFT) and finetune energy on def2‑TZVPD (OMol), and vice versa? Similarly, pretrain on ωB97X‑D (∇²DFT) and finetune on the OMol25 functional. Quantifying the degradation vs. in-domain would strengthen the generality claim.

11. OMol CSH 58k curation details: Section 3.1 says the subset “efficiently samples” elements, orbital interactions, and distances. Please detail the selection algorithm/heuristics and show that sampling doesn’t bias toward specific chemistries (e.g., charge, functional groups). Confirm that “OMol all 5k” and “OMol common 1k” (Table 1) are compositionally disjoint from train, with hash-level dedup.

12. Precision/noise floor in H labels: Section B.2 notes values to six decimal places and truncation error. Can you estimate a label noise floor and, if non-negligible, assess whether a noise-aware (heteroscedastic) objective helps, especially for long-range, small-magnitude elements?

13. Energy head design: The energy head applies one node-conv and a linear readout over l=0 (Section 3, “Energy output head”). Do higher-l channels contribute through the added node-conv, and would a deeper head or inclusion of selected l>0 features help? An ablation comparing shallow vs. deeper heads would clarify the representational bottleneck.

14. Edge omission in the energy path: Section 3 emphasizes that omitting edge updates enables reuse for energy prediction. Can you report an ablation where the energy head also consumes edge embeddings to test the trade-off between complexity and accuracy?

15. Electron density evaluation: Fig. 13 is qualitative. Could you report quantitative density errors (e.g., L2 on a grid) and derived properties (dipole, quadrupole) computed from predicted vs. reference H for a small test set? This would connect to physically meaningful observables.

16. UMAP embeddings quantification: Fig. 4 and Section D.4 show clearer clustering after pretraining. Can you quantify this with a simple kNN element-classification accuracy or silhouette scores by element and by angular degree l, and correlate with per-element H_err?

17. External QM components at inference: Appendix A.2 requires S and XC-grid evaluation via PySCF. What is the wall-clock overhead relative to model inference, and could a small S‑prediction head (SPD-constrained) reduce this dependence? Even a rough estimate would contextualize end-to-end practicality.

18. ECP variability: Section B.3 notes ECP-induced shifts for heavy elements. Are ECP types encoded in inputs, or do you rely on the model to infer them from patterns in H? If ECPs differ across datasets, how robust is the l=0 scaling and the model’s transfer?

19. Open-shell/extensible settings: OMol CSH is closed shell (Section 3.1). What changes are needed for open-shell (UKS) systems—e.g., spin blocks in H, parity constraints—and do you foresee any bottlenecks with the current TC layout (Section B.1)?

20. Reproducibility artifacts: To facilitate exact replication once released (Reproducibility Statement), please confirm you will share: train/val/test indices, per-element l=0 µZ, σZ used in training (train-only), node-parity masks, Wigner-3j settings, and PySCF options (basis grids, thresholds) used to compute energies/eigenvalues from predicted H.

Summary:
The paper proposes Structured Policy Initialization (SPIN), a two-stage framework for offline RL in large discrete, combinatorial action spaces. In Stage 1, an Action Structure Model (ASM) is pre-trained with a masked conditional modeling objective to learn a state-conditioned representation in which coherent joint actions concentrate on a low-dimensional manifold (Section 4.1; Algorithm 1). In Stage 2, the ASM is frozen and lightweight policy heads (with learnable queries) are trained over this representation, retaining cross-dimensional dependencies via shared attention while keeping control tractable (Section 4.2; Algorithm 2). SPIN is broadly compatible with actor updates expressed as weighted log-likelihoods (e.g., IQL, AWAC, BCQ). Empirically, SPIN achieves state-of-the-art performance and substantially faster convergence on discretized DM Control across dataset qualities, with up to 39% higher return and up to 12.8× faster time-to-target (Table 1; Figure 1), and scales favorably with action cardinality in dog-trot (Table 2). Analyses show performance improves with ASM pre-training (Figure 2), the learned representation captures cross-joint structure via linear probes (Section 6.2), and a distilled, attention-free student retains most of the gains, underscoring the value of the representation itself (Table 3–4).

Strengths:
1. Clear, original problem decomposition. The paper reframes offline RL in combinatorial action spaces as “learn structure first, then control,” separating action-structure learning from policy optimization (Section 4; Algorithms 1–2). This decoupling is a concrete, creative way to remove instability and slowness observed when learning both jointly (Section 2; SAINT comparison).

2. Principled and tractable architecture design. The ASM uses a permutation-equivariant Transformer with masked conditional modeling over sub-actions, conditioned on state (Section 4.1; Algorithm 1). This directly targets the compositional nature of joint actions while avoiding enumeration, and preserves cross-dimensional dependencies without imposing an arbitrary ordering.

3. Strong, consistent empirical gains with careful accounting. SPIN achieves the best overall average return and the lowest time-to-target across diverse datasets (Table 1), including a large 13% gain on the most heterogeneous random-medium-expert suite (499.2 vs. 438.9 for SAINT). Wall-clock comparisons include ASM pre-training and use a principled 95% target to normalize across methods (Section 5.1; Appendix B Table 5).

4. Scaling to extreme combinatorial growth. As action cardinality increases in dog-trot (38D; up to 30 bins/dim ≈ 1.35×10^56 actions), SPIN’s advantage widens in both return and runtime stability (Table 2; Appendix B Table 6). This is compelling evidence that the representation-first approach mitigates exponential search.

5. Careful, controlled head-to-heads. The main comparison against SAINT holds the policy class fixed and varies only the training paradigm (joint vs. two-stage), isolating where the benefit comes from (Section 5). All core results use the same IQL objective to remove confounding from algorithmic differences.

6. Convincing causal analysis of where the gains come from. Performance increases monotonically with ASM pre-training epochs and saturates quickly (Figure 2), indicating that “representation quality” is the key driver rather than mere warm-starting.

7. Direct measurement of learned structure (not just return). Linear probes quantify that the pre-trained ASM encodes cross-joint coordination beyond independence baselines (tuple accuracy 4.52% vs. 0.10% random ASM and >2× the independence expectation 0.90^38 ≈ 1.83%; Section 6.2). This is a rare, rigorous diagnostic in RL representation work.

8. Architecture-agnostic strength of the representation. SPIN-Distill replaces attention with an MLP and retains nearly all asymptotic returns while further reducing time-to-target (Table 3–4). This isolates the representation as the core asset and demonstrates practical deployability with lighter heads.

9. Robustness across offline RL objectives and domains. The framework works with IQL, AWAC, and BCQ, consistently improving returns and substantially cutting time-to-target (Appendix D; Tables 9–12). It also shows competitive generalization to a qualitatively different Maze domain, maintaining a clear efficiency edge (Appendix E; Tables 13–14).

10. Sound efficiency story, backed by numbers. The paper quantifies that ASM pre-training is a tiny fraction of wall-clock (1.4–5.6%) and highlights rapid early adaptation (≥90% target performance after only 10k steps in many settings; Section 6.4; Table 4). This aligns the proposed training decomposition with tangible compute savings.

11. Strong contrast to trajectory-centric pre-training. Against REPREM, SPIN attains much higher returns while being >200× faster, attributing the gap to horizon-independent, action-centric masking (Appendix F; Table 15). This sharpens the paper’s claim that modeling action composition is the right inductive bias for combinatorial spaces.

12. Clear scope and boundaries. The paper explicitly delineates compatibility with weighted log-likelihood actor updates and explains why global, joint-action objectives like CQL are out-of-scope given tractability and structural goals (Section 4.2). This clarity avoids over-claiming and guides future extensions.

Weaknesses:
1. Claims about “coherent/valid joint actions” are not directly evaluated. While the motivation stresses avoiding incoherent/invalid combinations, all core experiments are on discretized DM Control where any bin combination is technically valid (Section 5). There is no metric of action coherence or constraint satisfaction. Actionable: add tasks with hard combinatorial constraints (e.g., k-of-n, mutual exclusion) and report invalid-action rate, joint-constraint satisfaction, or off-manifold distance of produced tuples. Within current benchmarks, quantify “coherence” via dataset-NN distance in ASM space, joint PMI across sub-actions, or a joint-Q synergy score to show SPIN reduces incoherent combinations.

2. Evaluation breadth is narrow relative to the stated application scope. The paper motivates routing, resource allocation, and healthcare (Introduction; Section 2), but results are limited to discretized locomotion and a near-saturated Maze (Tables 1–2; Tables 13–14). Actionable: include at least one domain with explicit combinatorial structure (e.g., the cited routing/resource-allocation families) under an offline protocol, or release offline datasets derived from those simulators; alternatively, add constrained combinatorial control tasks where structure matters and Maze is not ceilinged at ~99% for all methods.

3. Time-to-target metric may favor methods surpassing the target baseline and does not separate sample- from wall-clock efficiency. Using “95% of F-IQL’s asymptote” (Section 5.1; Appendix B, Table 5) normalizes across methods with different ceilings but can advantage approaches that learn quickly to a moderate return (or that ultimately exceed F-IQL). Actionable: report (i) area-under-learning-curve, (ii) gradient steps to reach 95% of each method’s own asymptote, and (iii) steps-to-fixed absolute returns. Also provide throughput (env-steps/sec, updates/sec) and parameter counts to complement wall-clock numbers (Appendix B Tables 5–6).

4. Incremental conceptual novelty. The policy architecture is SAINT (frozen) and the pre-training is BERT-style masked modeling over sub-actions (Section 4.1–4.2), so the primary novelty is the two-stage training schedule and freezing. The paper partially addresses this via comparisons to VAM/CAM and REPREM (Appendix C, F), but the conceptual leap remains modest. Actionable: add a principled analysis linking masked conditional modeling of action tuples to improved offline policy optimization (e.g., bounds on support preservation or bias in advantage-weighted updates when acting on the ASM manifold), or demonstrate unique properties vs. generic denoising (e.g., failures of token-dropout or permutation-breaking variants).

5. Lack of cross-dataset/task transfer to validate “representation-first” reuse. All pre-training uses the same dataset distribution as downstream control (Section 5; Figure 2). Summary:
The paper proposes LAYS (Line-Aligning Yaw Scoring), a cross-view yaw estimator that isolates yaw as a 1-DoF problem under location uncertainty by aligning ground-image columns with radial lines in a BEV image. The method extracts column-wise ground features with relative yaw (Sec. 3.2), matches each BEV pixel to a representative ground column via cosine similarity and confidence weighting (Sec. 3.3), and performs pair-wise yaw voting into discrete yaw bins for every candidate 2D pose (Sec. 3.4; Fig. 1–2), avoiding assumptions about ground height. A multi-resolution scoring scheme and a BEV-based pose plausibility prior further stabilize estimation (Sec. 3.4; Alg. 1; Sec. C.3–C.4). Across Mapillary Geo-Localization, Ford Multi-AV, KITTI, and VIGOR, LAYS achieves state-of-the-art sub-degree accuracy, e.g., on MGL improving <1° accuracy from 32.67% to 72.10% under ±45° noise and from 6.55% to 34.81% under ±180° (Table 1), with large gains also on Ford (Table 2), KITTI (Table 3), and VIGOR (Table 4). Ablations validate key design choices, including column aggregation and train-time probabilistic selection (Table 5). Finally, fixing yaw with LAYS benefits downstream 3-DoF localization, reducing FG2’s mean error and showing advantages of decoupling yaw from translation (Table 6).

Strengths:
1. Clear and original problem reformulation. The paper isolates yaw as a 1-DoF line-alignment problem under location uncertainty, avoiding the usual entanglement with translation and height assumptions. This is crisply articulated and operationalized: “one line correspondence … is sufficient to estimate yaw” (Sec. 1; Fig. 1), and the method “does not assume ground-truth position or ground height” (Sec. 3.1).

2. Principled “relative-yaw” decomposition. The use of column-wise ground features that encode relative yaw, combined with absolute angles from candidate BEV poses, yields a simple, geometry-aware estimate θest = θabs − Mr(u,v) (Eq. (6)–(7); Fig. 1b). This elegantly removes dependence on ground height or explicit projection.

3. Effective BEV–ground matching design. Matching each BEV pixel to a representative ground column via cosine similarity with confidence weighting (Eq. (2)–(5); Sec. 3.3) is a compact mechanism that extracts consistent line evidence without 3D reconstruction. The train-time probabilistic selection avoids domination by a single feature (Eq. (3)) and is validated empirically (Table 5).

4. Scalable pair-wise yaw voting with line consensus. The score accumulation into yaw bins per 2D pose (Eq. (8)–(9); Alg. 1; Fig. 2) operationalizes the key insight that pixels aligned along a linear structure (e.g., a road) agree on yaw across all poses on that line (Fig. 1c). Visualizations substantiate this behavior (Fig. 3; Sec. 4.4.1; Figs. 4–9).

5. Removal of a major prior limitation. By avoiding projection and height hypotheses, LAYS directly addresses “radial location uncertainty” that impedes projection-based cross-view methods (Intro; Sec. 3.1), a practical obstacle in sloped or cluttered scenes.

6. Strong, consistent SOTA gains under severe yaw noise. Across four datasets, LAYS substantially improves sub-degree accuracy, especially where baselines collapse at ±180°: MGL <1° 34.81% vs. 6.55% (Table 1), KITTI cross-area <1° 45.51% vs. 3.14% (Table 3), and VIGOR cross-area <1° 23.67% vs. 12.39% (Table 4). Under ±45°, gains are also large (e.g., Ford <1° 67.05% vs. next best 41.36%; Table 2).

7. Broad generalization and relevance. The evaluation spans diverse settings—crowd-sourced urban imagery with non front-aligned views (MGL; Sec. 4.3), highway driving (Ford), classic benchmarks (KITTI same/cross area), and panoramic scenes (VIGOR)—demonstrating robustness beyond vehicle-centric, flat-ground assumptions.

8. Component-level validation. The ablation study is informative and specific: line-based yaw scoring outperforms exhaustive 3-DoF projection (Point-to-Point Match 13.19% vs. Ours 34.81% <1°; Table 5); weighted column aggregation beats keypoint features and MLP-only aggregation; and train-time stochastic selection improves over greedy/test-time weighting.

9. Downstream impact via modularity. Fixing yaw with LAYS improves a fully integrated 3-DoF localizer (FG2), and explicitly reducing the search to 2-DoF yields further gains (mean error 5.10 vs. 5.95; Table 6). This demonstrates practical utility as a reusable module, not merely a standalone metric.

10. Robustness to non-ideal gravity alignment. The method retains strong performance with injected ±10° pitch/roll during rectification (Table 7), aligning with the design choice to rely on per-column relative yaw rather than absolute gravity cues (Sec. 3.2).

11. Concrete, reproducible formulation. The paper provides end-to-end implementable details—closed-form equations (Sec. 3.2–3.4), explicit discretization and distance constraints (Sec. C.2), multi-resolution scheme (Sec. C.4), loss (Eq. (18)), and pseudocode (Alg. 1)—which enhances clarity and reusability despite formatting glitches elsewhere.

12. Insightful qualitative analysis. The PCA-based feature visualizations tie the mechanism to observed behavior, showing consistent focus on roads, trees, and building edges that drive line-consensus voting (Fig. 3; Figs. 4–9), strengthening the causal link between design and outcomes.

Weaknesses:
1. Identifiability and theory behind “one line is sufficient.”
   - The paper asserts that “one line correspondence … is sufficient to estimate yaw” under location uncertainty (Sec. 1; Fig. 1), operationalized via θest = θabs − Mr(u,v) (Eq. (6)–(7)). However, there is no analysis of when this is unique or stable. Degenerate cases (parallel lines, near-radial alignment w.r.t. pose, symmetric façades/lanes) can yield ambiguous or low-curvature objectives in S(θ,(x,y)) (Sec. 3.4; Alg. 1).
   - Actionable: State sufficient conditions for identifiability (e.g., non-parallel multi-line configurations or texture diversity across columns), and provide empirical stress tests that vary the number/geometry of lines (e.g., synthetic grids, multi-lane highways, intersections) to quantify ambiguity rates and error vs. line geometry.

2. Computational scalability of 3D voting not characterized.
   - The core estimator accumulates scores over S ∈ R|Θ|×|X|×|Y| (Sec. 3.1; Eq. (8); Alg. 1), with discretization detailed in Sec. C.2. There is no profiling of runtime, memory, or how costs scale with noise ranges (±45° vs ±180°) and BEV resolution.
   - Actionable: Report GPU memory, latency, and throughput per dataset/noise regime; show how |Θ|, ∆x/∆y, and R impact complexity and accuracy. Provide an engineering recipe (e.g., coarse-to-fine on |Θ| and (x,y), Hough-like accumulators, sparse/top-k BEV pixels) to keep inference real-time.

3. Sensitivity to discretization and distance constraint R is missing.
   - The method relies on hard binning (“1-degree angle bin” in the multi-level scheme; lines 270–282) and a fixed distance radius R (Sec. C.2 sets R = 36.32 px or 1/4 BEV side). Eq. (8) uses an equality indicator, which can be brittle near bin edges and sensitive to ∆θ and R, but no sweep is reported.
   - Actionable: Add controlled sweeps over ∆θ ∈ {0.5°,1°,2°}, grid stride ∆x/∆y, and R, reporting accuracy vs. runtime. Replace I(θ=[θest]) by circular kernel/smoothing (e.g., von Mises or triangular weights with wrap-around) and ablate its effect.

4. Influence and potential bias of the BEV-only plausibility prior S_P is unevaluated.
   - S_P is added to votes (Eq. (9)) and is learned from BEV features only (Sec. C.3). It could dominate S in structured areas (roads) irrespective of ground–BEV matches, effectively injecting a BEV pose prior.
   - Actionable: Provide an ablation without S_P across all datasets; quantify its contribution (Δaccuracy, Δconfidence). Stress-test S_P with OOD BEV textures and scenes with atypical layouts. Consider regularizing S_P (entropy penalty, temperature scaling) so M_s-driven evidence remains primary.

5. Robustness beyond mild gravity misalignment and calibration errors is underexplored.
   - The method assumes gravity-aligned ground images (Sec. 3.1) and tests ±10° pitch/roll (Table 7). Real-world AR/robotics can see larger roll/pitch transients, intrinsics/FOV changes, and rectification inaccuracies.
   - Actionable: Evaluate with larger mis-rectification (±20°), focal length errors, lens distortion residuals, and varying camera heights/FOVs. Report how column-relative yaw encoding (Sec. 3.2) degrades and whether simple pre-corrections (e.g., horizon/vanishing line cues) recover performance.

6. Baseline parity and comparability issues.
   - KITTI: CCVPE’s unknown-orientation numbers are approximated as upper bounds for <2°/<4° (Table 3), weakening the comparison. VIGOR: using open-sourced weights “unless noted as re-trained” (Sec. 4.2) may not match this paper’s noise/setup. MGL/Ford: baselines are retrained, but per-method hyperparameters for the ±180° regime are not detailed.
   - Actionable: Retrain CCVPE under the exact KITTI ±180° protocol; ensure all VIGOR baselines are retrained with the stated noise and unknown yaw. Provide a per-baseline hyperparameter table and training details to eliminate confounds.

7. Claims on VIGOR are overstated relative to Table 4.
   - The text says “our method performs best on this dataset” (Sec. 4.3.1), but in Same Area <4° FG2 (two-stage) achieves 62.11% vs 59.32% for LAYS (Table 4). The advantage is pronounced in Cross Area, but not uniform.
   - Actionable: Temper the claim and give a nuanced summary (Same vs Cross Area, thresholds). If possible, adopt the same two-stage protocol with LAYS as the first stage to test whether the FG2 two-stage gain can be matched or exceeded.

8. Limited coverage and failure-mode analysis across datasets.
   - Ford results are only on Log1 highway (Table 2). The method relies on line consensus (Fig. 1c; Fig. 3), but its behavior where linear structures are scarce or highly curved is not analyzed (Sec. 4.4.1 acknowledges location errors along the primary line).
   - Actionable: Report per-scene/category breakdowns (highway/urban/suburban; sparse/curvilinear/occluded lines); evaluate on additional Ford logs; include failure cases and diagnostics (e.g., when parallel lanes yield identical yaw, or intersections with conflicting lines).

9. Handling of multi-line/parallel-line ambiguities is not explicit.
   - When several parallel lines are present (multi-lane highways, grid-like cities), many (u,v) matches can vote the same yaw for different (x,y), risking spurious peaks driven by S_P (Sec. 3.4). The current design picks a single best column per BEV pixel (Eq. (3)–(5)), which may under-utilize diversity.
   - Actionable: Explore top-k column matches with soft weighting at test-time; penalize redundant votes from highly collinear sets; introduce diversity-aware aggregation (e.g., discourage identical Mr from adjacent columns) and quantify gains in ambiguous layouts.

10. Metrics and calibration are narrow.
    - Results emphasize thresholded accuracy (<1°, <2°, <4°; Tables 1–4). There is no report of mean/median absolute error, CDFs, or confidence calibration of yaw (useful for downstream fusion).
    - Actionable: Add MAE/median/CDFs and calibration metrics (e.g., ECE) for the argmax-bin confidence; consider fitting a circular distribution over bins to output a mean yaw and uncertainty.

11. Evidence for “no ground-height assumption” advantage is indirect.
    - While MGL is argued to have height ambiguities and time changes, there is no controlled study isolating height variability as the causal factor for LAYS’ advantage over projection-based methods (Intro; Sec. 4.3.1).
    - Actionable: Create controlled perturbations (synthetic height shifts, slopes, overpasses) and compare LAYS to homography/projection-based baselines (e.g., Wang et al., 2023b; Song et al., 2023) to quantify robustness specifically to height errors.

12. Reproducibility details for the multi-resolution scheme and voting are incomplete in the main text.
    - The “Multi Level Score” description is garbled (lines 270–282), and the voting uses a hard equality in Eq. (8) without a clear circular wrap-around policy in the main section.
    - Actionable: Provide a clean, self-contained algorithmic description of multi-resolution accumulation and a circular voting kernel in the main paper, with all hyperparameters and schedules, so others can reproduce without relying on appendices.

Suggestions/Questions:
1. Identifiability of “one line is sufficient”
   - You claim that “one line correspondence … is sufficient to estimate yaw” (Sec. 1; Fig. 1). Please formalize sufficient conditions for identifiability and stability (e.g., non-parallelism to the pose radial, absence of bilateral symmetry). Can you provide synthetic stress tests varying line geometry (parallel lanes, intersections, near-radial alignments) that quantify when S(θ,(x,y)) (Sec. 3.4; Alg. 1) becomes ambiguous?

2. Voting discretization and circularity
   - Eq. (8) uses a hard equality I(θ=[θest]) with 1° bins at the finest level (Sec. 3.4; “Multi Level Score”). Do you handle angular wrap-around explicitly? Have you tried circular smoothing kernels (e.g., von Mises/triangular) around θest to reduce bin-edge brittleness? Please include accuracy/runtime sweeps over Δθ ∈ {0.5°, 1°, 2°} and report the best practice.

3. Distance constraint R sensitivity
   - Sec. C.2 sets R = 36.32 px for MGL/Ford and 1/4 BEV side for VIGOR. What is the rationale and sensitivity of performance to R? Please add an ablation over R and discuss failure modes when R is too small/large (e.g., spurious local consensus vs. diluted votes).

4. Runtime and memory profile
   - The 3D accumulator S ∈ R|Θ|×|X|×|Y| (Sec. 3.1; Eq. (8); Alg. 1) could be heavy under ±180° noise and high BEV resolution. Please report GPU memory, latency (per query), and throughput per dataset and noise regime, and how they scale with |Θ|, grid stride (Δx,Δy), and R. Any engineering tricks (sparse/top-k BEV pixels, Hough-like accumulators, coarse-to-fine over (x,y,θ)) that make this practical?

   - S_P is added to votes (Eq. (9)) and learned from BEV features only (Sec. C.3). Could it dominate S and bias yaw toward common road poses? Please provide ablations “w/o S_P” across Tables 1–4, quantify its contribution, and discuss regularization (e.g., temperature scaling, entropy) to ensure M_s-driven evidence remains primary.

   - Table 3 uses CCVPE’s unknown-orientation numbers as upper bounds for <2°/<4°. Can you retrain CCVPE (and other baselines) under your exact ±180° KITTI protocol? Summary:
This paper explains why soft-label regularizers (label smoothing, Mixup, CutMix) simultaneously improve calibration and adversarial robustness by analyzing the geometry of the representation space (penultimate-layer features). It shows that decision regions are effectively cone-shaped around the origin in high dimensions even with classifier biases (Section 3.1; Table 5, Table 6), and introduces confidence contours and loss-gradient directions that radiate from minimum-loss points (Fig. 2). The authors define class centers as minimum-loss points and demonstrate that feature alignment to these centers correlates best with confidence across architectures on ImageNet (Table 1). They prove and empirically verify that soft labels shrink feature norms (RMS) and increase alignment to class centers (Theorem 1; Figs. 4–6; Table 2), which reduces overconfidence in a way akin to temperature scaling (Section 4.3; Fig. 25). The analysis further links higher alignment to improved robustness against gradient-based attacks (FGSM, PGD, AutoAttack) and transfer-based black-box attacks (Section 4.4; Fig. 3 middle; Table 2; Table 4), and documents broader gains under natural corruptions (Table 3). The paper also clarifies why robustness gains taper under strong iterative attacks via trajectory analysis in the representation space (Appendix N; Fig. 13).

Strengths:
1. Clear, original definition of class centers via minimum-loss points and strong validation. The paper argues that alignment should be measured to “the point where the classification loss is the lowest” rather than to the class mean or weight vector (Section 4.1). This choice is quantitatively justified: minimum-loss centers have the highest correlation with confidence across multiple architectures on ImageNet (Table 1), and the estimates are robust to optimization hyperparameters (Appendix I; Table 9). The 2D illustration makes the distinctions concrete (Fig. 2d).

2. Nontrivial geometric finding that cone-shaped decision regions persist in high dimensions even with classifier biases. Contrary to prior visualizations that omit bias, the authors provide a scalable verification method: linearly sweep features toward the origin and measure the first misclassification index (Appendix C). The indices are ≳99/100 across datasets and models (Table 5), and bias-dependence ratios n′c/nc are near zero (Table 6), supporting the claim in Section 3.1 without relying on 2D projections.

3. Introduction of confidence contours and gradient-direction fields in representation space that “radiate outward from the minimal-loss points,” exposing convex structure (Section 3.2). The visual analyses (Fig. 2a–c; Fig. 5) are novel, actionable, and directly connect feature norm and angular alignment to both calibration and adversarial gradients.

4. Theoretical grounding of the soft-label effect on feature norms. Theorem 1 (Appendix J) proves that soft-label training yields a finite optimal feature norm while hard-label training pushes norms to infinity. This theoretical claim is empirically borne out across architectures (Table 2; Figs. 4–6), providing a rare theory–practice bridge in representation geometry.

5. Unified mechanism linking calibration improvements to norm shrinkage, with a precise operational analogy to temperature scaling. Section 4.3 demonstrates that reducing feature RMS scales logits similarly to temperature scaling and improves calibration without changing accuracy; this is verified by manual feature scaling (Appendix L; Fig. 25) and reliability diagrams (Fig. 3 bottom).

6. Mechanistic and quantitative link from alignment to robustness across attack families. The paper shows bin-wise that higher cosine similarity to class centers lowers attack success for FGSM, PGD, and AutoAttack under weak and strong settings (Fig. 3 middle; Figs. 19–22; Table 2). The analysis extends beyond white-box settings to natural corruptions (ImageNet-C; Table 3) and transfer-based black-box attacks (Table 4), increasing practical significance.

7. Resolution of a subtle contradiction with an insightful, testable argument. Section 5 reconciles “closer to decision boundaries due to smaller RMS” with “more robust” by showing that (i) perturbation directions become inward for well-aligned features (Fig. 5a) and (ii) perturbation scale in representation space grows with feature RMS (positive correlation in Fig. 7). This is a crisp, empirically supported explanation rather than a heuristic claim.

8. Methodological contributions for high-dimensional verification. Besides the origin-sweep index (Appendix C), the paper introduces a simple bias-dependence diagnostic and reports small |bc| and n′c/nc in real high-D models (Appendix D; Table 6). These tools make otherwise hard-to-verify geometric claims reproducible without bespoke visualization tricks.

The main claims are tested on ResNet50, Swin-T, MobileNetV2, ConvNeXt-T, and ViT-B/16, with multiple soft-label regularizers (Label Smoothing, Mixup, CutMix) and even pretrained variants (Table 2; Table 8; Appendices K, E). The repeated observation—RMS↓ and cosine similarity↑—bolsters generality.

10. Transparent analysis of limitations with an explanatory trajectory view. The paper does not overclaim; it shows why gains diminish under stronger iterative attacks by visualizing how PGD trajectories turn outward after initial inward steps (Appendix N; Fig. 13). This candid, mechanistic account increases credibility.

11. Clarifying discussion on CNN vs. Transformer robustness/calibration under matched recipes. The controlled comparison suggests that, absent soft-label regularization, Swin-T is “as overconfident” and often more attack-susceptible than ResNet50 (Section A Discussion; Table 2), challenging a common narrative and attributing perceived advantages to training choices.

The narrative is easy to follow, with strong figure support (e.g., Fig. 1–2, 4–6) and a clear 2D/3D visualization pipeline (Appendix H). Could you (i) measure decision changes along angular sweeps at fixed radii around w_c to directly test cone behavior, (ii) report per-class failure rates, and (iii) correlate deviations with |b_c| and inter-class angles (Appendix D; Table 6)? This would clarify when/why non-cone deviations arise in high-D.

Adding a post-hoc temperature-scaling baseline would help disentangle the norm-shrinkage mechanism from generic logit scaling.

Please also report whether the 2D-bottleneck models retain similar accuracy and ECE to their high-D counterparts to rule out learning artifacts.

- Table 2 evaluates PGD with 7 steps and AutoAttack at two ε. For a fuller picture, could you provide: (i) robust accuracy vs ε curves; (ii) PGD-50/100 and CW-L2 (or Square Attack) results; (iii) gradient-obfuscation checks (e.g., loss landscape smoothness, BPDA/EOT if any non-differentiabilities)? - Please report the partial correlation between perturbation RMS and feature RMS when controlling for input gradient norm and class. Also show results at multiple ε and with PGD to confirm the relation is not attack-specific. Confidence intervals or bootstraps for correlation coefficients would make effect sizes clearer.

9. Minimum-loss center estimation: compute and surrogates
- Section 4.1 and Appendix I do not quantify the computational cost of estimating centers on ImageNet. Please report runtime/compute and propose practical surrogates (e.g., optimizing along w_c only, or convex combinations of weight vector and class mean). How close do these surrogates get to the Table 1 correlations?

10. Sensitivity to soft-label hyperparameters and convergence issues
- Appendix G.2 fixes LS=0.1 and α=1.0 for Mixup/CutMix on ImageNet, and Table 1 notes a CutMix failure to converge for ConvNeXt-T. Could you provide sensitivity curves over LS ε and α for each architecture, reporting RMS, cosine, ECE, and robust accuracy, and diagnose the ConvNeXt-T/CutMix failure (e.g., learning rate, mix probability, label mixing strategy)?

12. Pretrained weight anomalies and calibration metrics
- In Table 8, stronger-regularized variants (e.g., MobileNetV2 V2, EfficientNet-B1 V2) have RMS↓ and cosine↑ yet much higher ECE (likely underconfidence). Could you clarify whether ECE is signed vs absolute (Fig. 3 bottom uses color), and add NLL/Brier/Adaptive-ECE to show the full calibration picture? Also compare to post-hoc temperature scaling on these checkpoints.

Could you include small-scale probes with a cosine classifier (e.g., NormFace), focal loss, or MSE classification, and one non-vision dataset (even a small speech/NLP classification task), to test whether cone-shaped regions, norm shrinkage, and alignment–robustness links persist?

Can you provide per-class angular scatterplots between these three candidates and analyze when/why weights deviate (e.g., class imbalance, |b_c|, inter-class angles)? This would help practitioners choose center surrogates when computing true centers is expensive.

Summary:
The paper proposes OWLEYE, a zero-shot, cross-domain graph anomaly detection framework that learns transferable normal behavior patterns and applies them to unseen graphs without retraining. It first aligns heterogeneous node features into a shared space via PCA plus a cross-domain normalization that preserves pairwise-distance structure across graphs (Section 2.1; Figure 1; Eqs. (2)–(4)). It then learns attribute-level and structure-level representations with separate GNNs, storing representative patterns from multiple graphs in a dynamic dictionary to support continual updates (Section 2.2; Figure 2; Eqs. (5)–(9), (10)). For inference, a truncated attention-based reconstruction selectively uses the most representative patterns to rebuild node embeddings and score anomalies, with training guided by reconstruction and triplet losses (Section 2.3; Eqs. (11)–(14)). Across eight test graphs from diverse domains, OWLEYE achieves higher average AUPRC and AUROC than state-of-the-art baselines in zero-shot and 10-shot settings (Tables 1–2, 6–7), with ablations validating each component (Figure 3). The method is efficient (Figure 3 Right; Table 20), improves other models when its feature alignment is reused (Table 10), and exhibits practical continual learning via plug-and-play pattern augmentation and robust performance under domain shift (Section 3.4; Tables 3–5, 12).

Strengths:
Strengths
1. Clear, well-motivated problem setting with concrete evidence of prior limitations. The paper pinpoints why cross-domain GAD is hard—heterogeneous feature spaces, lack of continual updates, and reliance on target labels—and substantiates misalignment issues with ARC/UNPrompt via TSNE and pairwise-distance diagnostics (Figure 1; also Figure 5). This grounds the method design in observed failure modes rather than abstract claims.

2. Principled cross-domain feature alignment that preserves structural patterns. The normalization uses pairwise-distance statistics with a robust median aggregation and a scaling factor f (Eqs. (2)–(4)), explicitly aiming to maintain inter-node distance structure across graphs. The design choice is validated by (i) improved separability in visualizations (Figure 1/5), (ii) performance gains when plugged into ARC (Table 10; +0.57 AUROC, +1.01 AUPRC on average), and (iii) robustness of the median vs mean choice (Table 17) and projection alternatives (Table 15).

3. Separation of attribute- and structure-level signals with structure-only similarity to counter camouflage. The model learns attribute H and structure R embeddings via two GNNs (Eqs. (5)–(8)) and uses structure-only similarity for cross-graph pattern weighting (Eq. (10)) to avoid being misled by camouflaged anomalies. This choice is empirically justified: using attribute+structure similarity degrades AUPRC (Table 13), and removing structural patterns hurts performance (Table 14).

4. Truncated attention for contamination-robust reconstruction. The reconstruction leverages attention with top-k truncation (Eq. (11)) to minimize the influence of potentially anomalous patterns. Its necessity is confirmed by an ablation replacing truncation with standard attention (OWLEYE-T) showing a clear drop (Figure 3 Left), and by a systematic sensitivity study over k (Table 22) that identifies stable ranges (10–30% of dictionary size).

5. Continual learning via a dynamic, plug-and-play pattern dictionary—no retraining required. The dictionary design enables pattern augmentation that steadily improves performance without fine-tuning (Table 3) and shows predictable scaling with dictionary size until saturation (Table 5). Even when fine-tuning is allowed, the plug-in addition of patterns is more reliable than multi-graph fine-tuning (Table 4), aligning with the demonstrated optimization difficulty when many graphs are added (Appendix C.3; Figure 6 Right).

6. Strong, broad empirical support across settings and splits. On eight diverse test graphs, OWLEYE improves average AUPRC in zero-shot (36.17 vs 30.74 for ARC; Table 1) and matches/exceeds AUROC (75.42 vs 74.04; Table 6), and remains competitive in 10-shot (Tables 2, 7). The gains hold under alternative train/test splits (Tables 8–9), increased anomaly rates (Table 11), and domain shift where an entire training domain is removed (Table 12), where performance degrades moderately only for the affected domain (Amazon).

7. Interpretability of decisions via attention maps. The cross-attention visualizations (Figure 4; Figure 7) show a consistent pattern: correctly detected normals exhibit high attention to normal patterns, while anomalies exhibit low attention, and the behavior flips for misclassifications. This provides a transparent, faithful account of model behavior tied to the dictionary.

8. Efficiency with minimal architecture complexity. Despite using two simple 3-layer GCNs (Appendix A), OWLEYE achieves competitive or better training/fine-tuning times vs. generalist and classical baselines (Figure 3 Right; Table 20). The model also shows robustness to key hyperparameters (τ, τ_a, λ) with narrow performance bands (Table 21), lowering tuning burden.

9. Demonstrated reusability of components beyond the proposed model. The cross-domain feature alignment is not just an internal trick; it improves a strong baseline (ARC) across most datasets (Table 10), indicating broader utility of the alignment mechanism for cross-domain GAD.

10. Careful ablations and diagnostics that isolate what matters. The paper systematically disables each component—normalization, structural patterns, truncated attention—and quantifies the impact (Figure 3 Left). It further quantifies benefits of multi-graph patterns vs. single-graph patterns (Table 16), and analyzes design choices like median vs mean aggregation (Table 17) and different projection methods (Table 15), making the method’s empirical rationale persuasive.

11. Practicality for real deployments. The zero-shot capability (Section 2.3; Eq. (12) with truncated attention), the plug-and-play continual updates (Section 3.4; Tables 3–5), and robustness under domain shift (Table 12) directly target operational constraints of anomaly detection systems that face heterogeneous, evolving graphs without labels.

12. Reproducibility support. The method is fully specified with equations (Eqs. (2)–(14)), hyperparameters, and hardware details (Appendix A), and a public code link is provided, facilitating adoption and verification.

Weaknesses:
1. Test-time “normal pattern” usage risks anomaly leakage and self-reconstruction.
   - Section 2.3 (Inference) states “we extract and store n_sup normal patterns from G_i” for the test graph, yet no labels exist at test time. Earlier, pattern extraction in training is “random” (Eq. (9)), not “normal-only.” This creates two issues: (i) ambiguity/inconsistency about how “normal” is guaranteed at test time, and (ii) potential contamination of the dictionary with anomalies from both training and test graphs. The heatmaps in Appendix C.2 show test graphs “heavily rely on the patterns extracted from its own graph,” which can enable anomalies to reconstruct themselves and reduce anomaly scores.
   - Actionable: (a) add a control that forbids using self-graph patterns at inference (reconstruct only from T_train dictionaries) and report the delta on Tables 1–2, 6–7; (b) add a controlled contamination study where a known fraction of anomalous nodes are injected into the dictionaries (both training and test) and quantify robustness; (c) during training, build DictH/DictR using only normal-labeled nodes (Section 2.2), and report the gain over random (Eq. (9)); (d) if self-graph patterns are needed, enforce conservative gating (e.g., remove top-entropy or low-similarity patterns per Eq. (10)/(11)) and ablate.

2. Scalability of cross-domain normalization is unclear and likely super-linear.
   - Cross-domain feature normalization computes pairwise distances over all node pairs (Eq. (2): O(n_i^2) per graph). This could dominate runtime on large graphs; yet Figure 3 (Right) and Table 20 report only training/fine-tuning time on ACM, excluding preprocessing. No complexity or wall-clock breakdown includes Eq. (2).
   - Actionable: (a) add asymptotic and end-to-end cost analysis separating projection (PCA), pairwise-distance computation (Eq. (2)), dictionary construction, and attention-based reconstruction (Eq. (11)–(12)); (b) evaluate on at least one substantially larger graph than ACM with timing for each stage; (c) add approximations (node subsampling, blockwise/sketched distances) and quantify the error/performance trade-off.

3. Cross-graph reconstruction cost and memory footprint are not analyzed.
   - The reconstruction (Eq. (11)–(12)) computes attention between all test nodes and m dictionaries of size n_sup each, repeated for attribute and structure embeddings. The overall complexity scales with n_test × m × n_sup × d. There is no analysis of memory or latency vs. m and n_sup beyond Table 5 (accuracy saturation).
   - Actionable: provide complexity/memory formulas and measure latency/VRAM across n_sup ∈ {10,…,2000} and m, alongside the accuracy curve in Table 5; add a streaming/batched inference recipe.

4. Weaknesses in supervised/few-shot baselines and protocol clarity.
   - In Tables 1–2 (AUPRC), the supervised 10-shot GHRN/BWGNN results are extremely low (e.g., 3–17 on most datasets), and Table headers are duplicated (“Supervised (10-shot)” appears within zero-shot tables). It is unclear whether these models received (i) any pretraining on T_train, (ii) class imbalance handling, or (iii) proper validation. As is, they are underpowered relative to their design.
   - Actionable: (a) add a few-shot protocol where supervised models are pretrained on T_train then adapted with 10-shot on T_test, with class-balanced loss/early stopping; (b) report tuning details; (c) include confidence intervals or tests (e.g., bootstrap) to confirm OWLEYE’s advantages are not due to under-tuned baselines.

5. Alignment design validated primarily via aggregate pairwise distances; lacks class-conditional analysis and stronger baselines.
   - The normalization uses global pairwise-distance statistics and median aggregation (Eqs. (2)–(4), Table 17). While Table 10 shows gains when plugging this into ARC, the analysis does not examine whether intra-/inter-class separations (on labeled training graphs) are preserved or improved. Also, comparisons focus on PCA/SVD/Kernel PCA/NMF (Table 15), but not on alternative alignment objectives that explicitly match distributions.
   - Actionable: (a) on labeled training graphs, report pre/post alignment changes in Normal–Normal vs Normal–Anomaly distance distributions (as suggested by Figure 1 second row) and class-conditional Fisher ratios; (b) compare against at least one additional alignment baseline beyond dimensionality reduction (even a simple per-graph whitening/z-score + scale matching) to isolate the value of Eq. (4)’s scaling.

6. Evidence for contamination-robustness of truncated attention is narrow.
   - The truncated attention is designed to mitigate anomaly contamination (Section 2.3; Eq. (11)), but robustness is only probed via k-sweeps (Table 22) and a single dataset with injected anomalies (Table 11). There is no study of how performance degrades as the fraction of anomalous patterns in the dictionaries increases, nor of how often anomalies are erroneously retained by attention.
   - Actionable: (a) simulate varying anomaly fractions in the dictionaries and report AUPRC/AUROC; (b) measure the share of retained patterns by label under different k and τ_a (Eq. (11)); (c) add an automatic k-selection heuristic (e.g., per-node attention entropy or top-ρ% by similarity) and compare with fixed k.

7. Limited analysis of failure modes where performance remains very low.
   - On Facebook and Reddit, AUPRCs are ∼5 and ∼4 for most methods including OWLEYE (Tables 1–2). The paper does not analyze why these graphs remain hard post-alignment and with truncated attention.
   - Actionable: provide per-dataset diagnostics (e.g., post-alignment TSNE, attention maps as in Figure 4/7, and similarity heatmaps as in Figure 6) and structural statistics (degree heterogeneity, homophily) to identify conditions where OWLEYE underperforms and guide improvements (e.g., augment structure-only similarity in Eq. (10) with motif/egonet features).

8. End-to-end effectiveness claims would benefit from statistical testing and clearer metric reporting.
   - Some tables mix metric labels (e.g., Table 10 has “AUROC 74.65 ± 0.55” in the BlogCatalog column header row), and Appendix B.1 text references “AUPRC” next to AUROC tables (Tables 6–7). Results are reported over 5 trials without statistical tests despite modest deltas on some datasets.
   - Actionable: fix labels/headers, add PR/AUC confidence intervals and paired tests (e.g., Wilcoxon signed-rank across datasets) to substantiate average gains (e.g., Table 1: 36.17 vs 30.74).

9. Dictionary construction overlooks label information during training.
   - Section 2.2 selects patterns “randomly” (Eq. (9)) even though training graphs have labels. The later Appendix B.6 shows structural patterns help (Table 14), but there is no ablation on “normal-only” vs random sampling for dictionary building.
   - Actionable: construct DictH/DictR from normal-labeled nodes on training graphs and report the change vs random; alternatively, use low-reconstruction-error nodes under L_recon (Eq. (13)) as “pseudo-normal” seeds.

Suggestions/Questions:
1. Clarify test-time “normal pattern” usage and potential leakage.
   - In Section 2.3 (Inference), “we extract and store n_sup normal patterns from G_i” for the test graph, but zero-shot implies no labels. Please specify exactly how these “normal” patterns are identified at test time. If they are randomly sampled (as in Eq. (9) during training), quantify contamination risk and how truncated attention (Eq. (11)) mitigates it.
